articles.title: Germany news: Merz rails against extremism, AfD sympathizers
articles.summary: Political extremism threatens Germany's existing social order, Chancellor Merz has said. The Transport Ministry has proposed a five-year plan to improve Germany's ailing railroad infrastructure. DW…

image.caption: Image: Michael Kappeler/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Published October 7, 2026last updated October 7, 2026
Merz rails against extremism, AfD sympathizers in own ranks

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz on Wednesday addressed the threat of political extremism to the existing social order, accusing the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) and far-left BSW parties of wanting to wipe out "the DNA of our democracy."
"Extremism," said Merz, "is forcing its way into our state legislatures with a vengeance."

Merz, speaking in Berlin, called this week’s election of an AfD politician as speaker of Saxony-Anhalt's state parliament — the first time a far-right politician has been tapped to lead a statehouse since 1945 — a "historic break."
Moreover, Merz slammed politicians — potentially from his own conservative CDU party — for casting ballots in favor of Tobias Rausch in the Saxony-Anhalt vote.
Rausch received 48 votes but the AfD and BSW only have 44 between them. It is unclear from whom Rausch picked up four extra votes — he was elected in a secret ballot.

Observers assume these came from within the CDU, but Merz said "false flag" attacks also occur in politics, implying the Social Democrats, the Left party and the Greens, all of which are also represented in the state's parliament, could be attempting to weaken or sow division in the CDU.
"Anyone ‌who ​casts their vote for the AfD is ​playing the extremists' game and undermining ⁠credibility," ​said Merz. "In any ‌case, this is incompatible ​with ⁠the values of my party, ⁠the ​CDU."

articles.title: Artists including Noel Gallagher show support for Garvaghy Road residents
articles.summary:
Actors and musicians sign open letter urging government to protect residents amid impasse over Drumcree parade

Dozens of artists, actors and musicians including Susan Sarandon and Noel…

blocks.text: Dozens of artists, actors and musicians including Susan Sarandon and Noel Gallagher have expressed support for Garvaghy Road residents in the impasse over the Drumcree parade in Northern Ireland.

In an open letter to the secretary of state, Chris Bryant, they urged the government to protect residents and to appoint an international mediator to resolve the dispute between the Catholic residents and the Orange Order in County Armagh.

“Central to any just resolution must be the primacy and protection of the local community,” said the letter, which urged authorities to safeguard residents from “any form of forced processions that disregard their consent, safety and right to live in peace free from intimidation”.

It was signed by the writer Irvine Welsh, the film-makers Ken Loach and Jim Sheridan, the actors Adrian Dunbar, Maxine Peake and Siobhán McSweeney and the musicians Paul Weller, Johnny Marr and Imelda May, among others.
Twenty MPs and members of the House of Lords signed a separate letter exhorting Bryant to cancel the march.

The 11-day-old dispute fuelled fresh political tension on Wednesday when three unionist parties tabled a motion of no confidence in Michelle O’Neill, the Sinn Féin first minister, and other Sinn Féin ministers. The motion lacks cross-community support and is expected to fail when debated at the Stormont assembly on 12 October.

In the Dáil in Dublin, the Sinn Féin leader, Mary Lou McDonald, accused Bryant of allowing the stalemate to fester and leaving Garvaghy Road residents in “dangerous limbo”. She urged the Irish government to “apply all necessary pressure” on British authorities to prevent the parade.

The taoiseach, Micheál Martin, said he had discussed the impasse with Andy Burnham on Monday and urged renewed talks in Northern Ireland. “We need a mediated resolution,” he said. “The talks that have happened could result in an outcome if we maintain dialogue.”

The march around Drumcree is one of hundreds of parades that the Orange Order holds in Northern Ireland each year to commemorate Protestant forefathers who fell in battles. Critics say they are an attempt to intimidate Catholics.

Attempts by Garvaghy Road residents to block the march in the 1990s led to pitched battles between Orange Order supporters and police and sectarian violence. The dispute subsided after 1998 when the Parades Commission prohibited the route through Garvaghy Road, but last month the commission ruled that a scaled-down parade of 35 Orangemen could march down Garvaghy, reigniting protests by residents.
after newsletter promotion

In a statement on Wednesday, the Orange Order’s Portadown district lodge said its members were ready to exercise a legal right to march the route – for the first time in 28 years – and urged the police to deal with the protesters who impeded them.

“We will not give up that legal right, as to do so would be to legitimise mob rule. We will continue our dignified, peaceful and lawful stand,” it said. “We have yet to see any action taken, as Michelle O’Neill and her comrades continue to flout the law.”

articles.title: Christa Pike’s lawyers hold press conference after she regains consciousness in hospital – latest updates
articles.summary: Tennessee prisoner awake and speaking after surviving state’s attempt to execute her last Wednesday

blocks.text: Christa Pike's lawyers hold press conference after saying she is 'conscious' following execution attempt
Christa Pike’s lawyers are holding a press conference today after revealing last night that their client was “conscious and speaking” following last week’s botched execution attempt in Tennessee.

The 50-year old death row inmate is still receiving critical care in a hospital while “handcuffed and shackled to the bed,” her lawyers said on Tuesday, adding: “Her recovery is medically unprecedented. Her prognosis remains unclear but, at a minimum, we expect a long recovery.”
Speaking to the BBC, an anaesthesiologist advising Pike’s team said that she is able to communicate in a “basic way” but did not seem to remember last Wednesday’s execution attempt.

Her legal team will ask a court on at a hearing on Wednesday to require the Tennessee department of correction to preserve all “relevant physical, written and electronic evidence” related to the failed execution, court documents said.
The press conference is scheduled for 12pm ET.
Stay tuned as we bring you the latest live updates from the press conference.
Key events

items: 29m agoChrista Pike's lawyers hold press conference after saying she is 'conscious' following execution attempt

blocks.text: Tennessee’s top prison official is resigning following Christa Pike’s botched execution attempt.

Over the weekend, governor Bill Lee announced that Frank Strada, the department of correction commissioner, will leave his position in late October amid an independent investigation into Pike’s failed execution attempt.

Despite calling the case “deeply disturbing,” Lee told reporters last week: “So far as we know, the department of correction followed exactly the protocol that was outlined.” Meanwhile, Strada said that his resignation would “be in the best interests” of the state as the investigation goes underway.
Death penalty lawyers said that Strada oversaw five “botched” executions, with common threads including prolonged suffering among prisoners and questionable injection procedures.
On September 30, Christa Pike, who was set to be the first woman executed in Tennessee in more than 200 years, survived two doses of pentobarbital, a sedatative.

Witnesses to the attempt to execute Pike described how they heard she was choking and struggling for an hour after receiving the first injection. She was then hospitalized after a second dose failed to kill her. In the hospital, she was put on a ventilator and had been in critical condition.
Speaking to the BBC, Joel Zivot, an anaesthesiologist advising Pike’s team, said: “She has some memories of being in the hospital but no memory, I believe, of the execution attempt.”
Zivot added that Pike was able to remember her name but incorrectly guessed the current month as September.

articles.title: Canada’s Weston family buys Boots for $8.9bn
articles.summary:
Former Selfridges owners buys UK high street institution from long-term backer Stefano Pessina

The Canadian family that once owned Selfridges department store has bought UK pharmacy and…

blocks.text: The Canadian family that once owned Selfridges department store has bought UK pharmacy and beauty retailer Boots for $8.9bn (£6.74bn).

Wittington Investments, the holding company of the Weston family that controls the Loblaws grocery chain and Drugmart pharmacy chain in Canada, will own Boots’ UK and Irish retail operations and opticians chain, the No7 beauty brand and a franchise arm in Thailand.

The acquisition of the Nottingham-headquartered chain, which has 1,800 stores across the UK and employs 50,000 people, is also being backed by the investment firm Fairfax, which owns The Sporting Life Group and Sleep Country, Canada’s largest mattress retailer which owns Simba Sleep in the UK.

Galen Weston, the chair of Wittington who is likely to become chair of Boots, said: “Boots is one of Britain’s most enduring businesses, with a rich heritage, a trusted name and a vital role in everyday life across the UK and Ireland.

“We see a meaningful opportunity to make a great business even better through stable long-term ownership, further capital investment, and the renewed operating focus required to serve customers with excellence for generations to come.”

The transaction, which sees the exit of Boots’ long-term backer Stefano Pessina and his latest backer, the financial firm Sycamore Partners, is subject to regulatory approval and is expected to close in the first quarter of 2027.

In 2022, the US pharmacy groupWalgreens put Boots up for sale with a suggested price tag of up to £10bn but later dropped the plans as potential buyers, including Mukesh Ambani’s Reliance Industries, the US private equity investor Apollo Global Management and Asda’s owners TDR Capital, struggled to raise funds. A plan to float the business at a valuation of about £7bn was dropped in 2024.
“Boots is an iconic brand and a British institution,” said Pessina, who took Boots private with the backing of investment firm KKR in 2007. He has since merged and demerged it from Walgreens.

“It has been one of the privileges of my and [my wife] Ornella’s life to have been so closely associated with Boots over the last 20 years. We are delighted to be passing on a thriving Boots to strong and reliable owners who understand the value of its great heritage.”
Pessina will retain ownership of Boots’ interests in the Farmacias Benavides pharmacy chain in Mexico and the Alliance Healthcare Deutschland, a German drug distributor.
after newsletter promotion
The acquisition of Boots marks the return of the Weston family’s Canadian branch to the UK high street, after the family sold off the Selfridges department store chain for £4bn in 2022.
The separate UK branch of the family is known for holding a majority stake in Primark through the parent company Associated British Foods, which is led by family member George Weston.

articles.title: Man pleads guilty to sexually assaulting woman drugged by her husband
articles.summary:
Sean Peers admits offence against woman who was drugged and attacked for more than two decades

A man has pleaded guilty to sexually assaulting an unconscious woman, whose husband had drugged…

blocks.text: A man has pleaded guilty to sexually assaulting an unconscious woman, whose husband had drugged her and invited other men to abuse her.
Sean Peers, 38, had been due to stand trial alongside 11 other men, but admitted one count of assault by penetration on 15 September 2024 when he appeared at Manchester Minshull Street crown court.

The husband, who cannot be named in order to protect the anonymity of his wife, had already admitted to offences, but pleaded guilty to a further two counts – one of rape and one of sexual assault – which took place in August last year.
Another man, Keith Fotheringham, 59, from Dundee, a former technician at the city’s university, has also pleaded guilty to a number of offences.

All three will be sentenced at the conclusion of the trial, which is now due to open on 19 October. The case was due to begin in early September, but has faced several delays for legal and practical reasons.

At a hearing on Tuesday, the jury of three men and nine women were told by Judge Maurice Greene that the husband had provided a witness statement detailing “what it is he says happened,” which had been disclosed to defence lawyers, and meant the trial would be delayed while they went through it.
The jury, including two female reserve jurors bringing their total number to 14, were sent away and told to return to the same court on 19 October.
Eleven men are due to stand trial, denying a range of offences including rape and attempted rape, with the abuse alleged to have taken place between 2018 and November 2025.

They are Philip Wild, 58, from Stockport, Jordan Wallace, 31, afrom Manchester, Alan Keelan, 42, from Manchester, Jonathan Kirk, 43, from Stockport, Robert Stewart, 70, from Stockport, Mohammed Sabir, 28,of no fixed abode, and Graham Brougham, 74, from Northwich, Cheshire.

Richard Townsend, 37, from Heywood in Greater Manchester, has pleaded not guilty to offences including one count of assault by penetration. They are Karl Lindsay, 55, from Taunton, Somerset, Daniel Rayner, 42, from Whitstable, Kent, and David Graves, 59, from, Ilkeston, in Derbyshire.
The trial is expected to last around nine weeks, due to conclude in mid-December.

articles.title: EU enlargement: European Commission tables reforms to prepare bloc for new members
articles.summary: The European Commission is proposing earlier access to EU markets for candidate countries, new voting rules to reduce vetoes and extra safeguards for a bigger bloc. But is the reform fair — or even…

image.caption: EU Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos presented the results of the bloc's pre-enlargement policy review on Tuesday: 'Gradual integration is not a substitute for full membership. It is the accelerator for enlargement,' she saidImage: Romeo Boetzle/EU

blocks.text: The European Commission wants to inject new momentum into its enlargement process, which has seen some candidate countries waiting for decades to join.
Albania, Montenegro, Moldova and Ukraine are currently the frontrunners to join the bloc, with EU officials expressing the hope that Montenegro could do so as early as 2028.
"A larger union is a long-term investment in Europe's peace, security and prosperity," Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos told journalists in Strasbourg on October 6.
One key question is how the EU can take in more countries in the near future without becoming harder to run or running the risk of democratic backsliding in new member states.

The Commission's answer to this question is to simultaneously require candidate countries to meet EU standards and get the bloc itself to reform by removing obstacles in the accession process and protecting its democratic values.
Less unanimity, more qualified majority votes

One of the main stumbling blocks in accession negotiations so far has been the need for unanimous decisions across all 27 members. In the past, individual states have often blocked a candidate's progress because of bilateral issues.
The delays caused by Hungary's blocking of Ukraine's negotiation process are a prominent example.

blocks.caption: EU officials hope that Montenegro could join the union as early as 2028. Pictured here: European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen (left) shakes hands with Montenegro's Prime Minister Milojko SpajicImage: Risto Bozovic/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Now — and not for the first time — the Commission is recommending that member states move away from the principle of unanimity for decisions like the opening of negotiation clusters, replacing it with qualified majority voting.
The unanimity dilemma

"Every cluster that you open is subject to three individual decisions, and every single decision is subject to unanimity. It's mind-blowing, and I think this clearly needs to go," a Commission official, who wished to remain anonymous, told journalists on Tuesday.
The catch is that a shift to qualified majority voting would itself require a unanimous decision.

"I have some reservations as to whether there will be unanimous agreement from the member states to move to qualified majority voting," Tinatin Akhvlediani, head of the enlargement program at the Centre for European Policy Studies (CEPS) told DW, pointing to previous attempts to change voting rules that were shot down by member states.
Gradual access to membership benefits

To incentivize reform in candidate countries, the Commission is proposing gradual integration, which means that these countries could be granted some of the benefits of membership before joining — as long as they meet the EU's criteria.

blocks.caption: Tinatin Akhvlediani of the Centre for European Policy Studies told DW that she had 'some reservations as to whether there will be unanimous agreement from the member states to move to qualified majority voting'Image: privat

blocks.text: "Gradual integration is not a substitute for full membership. It is the accelerator for enlargement," Kos said on Tuesday, underlining that the process would stay merit-based.

This could have a motivational effect on candidate countries, Nina Vujanovic, a research fellow at Brussels-based think tank Bruegel, told DW: "Reforms are important, but it is also important to reward that process a little bit earlier, ahead of accession," she said.
Earlier access to EU benefits is not entirely new: Montenegro, for example, already participates in the Single Euro Payments Area (SEPA) even though it is not yet a member.
Addressing geopolitical realities
The Commission now wants to give candidate countries such early access more systematically and link it to strategic alignment.
"This is not something that will be available [to candidate countries] unless they really orient themselves on the EU," a Commission official told journalists.
Making strategic alignment a condition is new and reflects the EU's efforts to adjust to the geopolitical tensions members and candidates are facing.
Candidates' choice: Russia or the EU?

"The EU is trying to keep candidate countries out of the hands of Russia," Heather Grabbe, a senior fellow at Bruegel, told DW. "Strategic alignment is aimed very squarely at politicians like Aleksandar Vucic in Serbia, who has clearly promoted Russian interests," she said.

The new procedures would demand alignment not only with the EU's foreign and security policy, but also with its standards on economic security. "Trading gas with Russia is simply not something that builds trust with the European Union," said Nina Vujanovic.
The lessons the EU learned from Hungary, Poland

To prevent breaches of democratic rules by new member states, the Commission proposes a 15-year period within which it would be easier to sanction new members by cutting financial support or restricting voting rights.

blocks.caption: The foreign ministers of the 16 countries involved in the Berlin Process (the six candidate countries of the Western Balkans and 10 other European countries) met in Montenegro last weekImage: Regierung von Montenegro

blocks.text: In an interview with The Guardian and other European media, Commissioner Kos made it clear that the EU had learned its lesson from the democratic backsliding it saw in the past in countries like Poland or Hungary: "No more Viktor Orban. We have to have quicker mechanisms than only Article 7."
Double standard or necessary protection?
Critics point out that this safeguard would create unequal conditions within the union.
"It is inherently unfair," says Heather Grabbe. "In the 2040s, why should Montenegro face different conditions to, say, Slovenia?"

Many current candidate countries have a shaky record when it comes to democratic norms, as Tinatin Akhvlediani points out: "They are actually fragile democracies. So, this approach vis-a-vis these countries can be very much justified."

Experts say that while it might be desirable to apply similarly strict rules to all members, it is not realistically feasible as it would have to be approved unanimously and, as Grabbe says, "it's very hard to get turkeys to vote for Christmas."
Although the Commission's push for new rules in relation to enlargement is likely to move the debate forward, it is ultimately up to member states to decide how much of it becomes reality.

The European Council, which is made up of the heads of state or government of the 27 EU member states, the European Council president and the president of the European Commission, is expected to discuss the proposals at its upcoming meeting on October 15–16.
The outcome of those talks will determine how quickly the Commission's new enlargement agenda can move forward.

articles.title: Abortion pill access jumps almost 50% after Australia eases restrictions for pharmacies
articles.summary:
The number of pharmacies stocking the MS-2 Step medication increased from 2,228 to 4,107 after rules relaxed in 2023

  • Get our

blocks.text: The number of Australian pharmacies stocking an abortion pill increased by almost 50% when prescribing restrictions were relaxed, with researchers saying the findings suggest deregulation of abortion promotes safer and faster healthcare.

A study published in the medical journal JAMA Network Open on Thursday examined the impact of changes by the Therapeutic Goods Administration in 2023 which meant the medication, MS-2 Step, could be prescribed by any GP.

Prior to the changes, GPs needed additional training and registration to prescribe it. The requirement for pharmacists to be registered to dispense the drug was also scrapped, and administrative hurdles were relaxed. Appropriately trained nurse practitioners and endorsed midwives also became eligible prescribers.

By comparing pharmacy ordering data in the two years before and after the changes, researchers led by La Trobe University found by mid-2025, 49% more pharmacies were stocking the medication. There were 2,228 pharmacies stocking it before the policy change, rising to 4,107 by mid-2025.

The number of postcodes with a pharmacy stocking the medication rose from 915 to 1,292 – or nearly half of all Australian postcodes – two years after the changes. Regional coverage increased from 23% to 35% of postcodes, while the proportion of stocking pharmacies in remote areas nearly doubled, rising from 12.5% to 22%.

The lead author of the paper, Prof Kristina Edvardsson from La Trobe University’s school of nursing and midwifery, said it showed “Australian women who need access to this medication can access it closer to home”.

“It removes the unnecessary travel and stress around getting the medication once it’s prescribed. That’s super important, particularly for women who might be more disadvantaged, women living in rural, remote areas, and women who might not have the means to travel.
“If you can go to your local pharmacy and pick up this medication, it means getting care quicker.”
Edvardsson said other studies have found improving access to MS-2 Step is safe, and that when access to the medical abortion pill increases, the need for surgical abortion decreases.

“In some European countries, medical abortion accounts for more than 90% of all abortions, and it looks like we’re heading that way here as well with a steady increase in medication abortion versus surgical abortion,” she said.
MS-2 Step, available under the Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme, comprises two drugs used together, mifepristone and misoprostol. It can be taken until up to 63 days of gestation.
after newsletter promotion
At the time of the study, MS-2 Step was the only abortion pill available, but in February an additional drug, Arzestra, comprising the same two medicines, was approved by the TGA.

Dr Anna Noonan, a postdoctoral research fellow and abortion researcher with the University of Technology Sydney, said the data should be “an important signal” to countries where more restricted prescribing was still in place, such as the US.
“There are still pervasive, unnecessary barriers in lots of places, and data like this is an important signal that regulation and overregulation is not the way forward,” she said.

Noonan said there was still work to be done to improve rural and regional access, and that her own research suggested a lot of “invisible work” also occurred by local doctors, nurses and advocates working behind the scenes so that people can confidentially and more easily find healthcare.
“Doctors and nurses are going to pharmacies in advance saying, ‘I’m going to be an abortion provider in this community, will you stock this medication?’

“Overregulation creates extra work for those trying to provide timely care, and it doesn’t work out in the best interests of people seeking care,” Noonan said. “The more we encourage a deregulated environment, the easier access will be, particularly for people with less resources.”

articles.title: British billionaire warned Epstein was a ‘sexual deviant’ decades before FBI closed in on the abuser
articles.summary:
Sir James Goldsmith’s links to Hilton Head, South Carolina, adds to mystery of Jane Doe 4, who claimed she was abused by Epstein in the 1980s

For

blocks.text: For Jeffrey Epstein, the billionaire Goldsmith family was a gateway to elite society and he wanted to be in their circle.

The disgraced financier, who died in prison in 2019 facing sex-trafficking charges, longed for a billionaire’s lifestyle and cultivated the family’s friends, bankers, business associates and advisers.

But Sir James Goldsmith, who was knighted by the Queen in 1976 and became a prominent British politician, remained wary of the American financier and even “despised” him, his daughter Jemima recently told the Guardian.
Two decades before Epstein came under federal investigation, Goldsmith – who died in 1997 – told a confidante that Epstein was a “sexual deviant” who was recruiting children for illicit activities.

Goldsmith “told me not to have anything to do with him, that he was a pervert, and he didn’t want him near any of us. He had four daughters to protect,” recalled the famous French architect Robert Couturier, who designed opulent homes for Goldsmith in New York and Mexico.

Goldsmith’s alleged warning came around 1987, years before complaints about Epstein’s solicitation of young girls for sex began filtering into federal law enforcement. Epstein’s network of pretty “girls” evolved into what authorities describe as a global sex-trafficking ring that catered to the ultra-rich and powerful.
It would become a scandal that touched royals, politicians, businessmen, academics, foreign diplomats and celebrities around the world, leaving more than 1,000 victims in its wake.

“That is the pity of it all. It was all preventable,” Couturier told the Guardian. Epstein, born on Coney Island, had been on the radar of New York’s elite since he first surfaced at society events, often on the arm of heiresses, Couturier said.
“He was a charmer and a talker. Lots of rich people are deeply gullible, as protected as they are from reality. No one did anything about it.”

blocks.caption: Jeffrey Epstein in 1985. Photograph: TT News Agency/Alamy

blocks.text: In the mid-1980s, Sir James Goldsmith – known as “Jimmy” – announced he was making a shift in his US business operations. Goldsmith had hired a new chief executive who would open an office for him in Hilton Head, South Carolina, an emerging luxury resort.

Goldsmith’s Hilton Head office is rarely mentioned in writings about his reign as the “lucky gambler”, as Time Magazine called him, an adviser to US presidents who became one of the world’s richest men by betting on undervalued companies. His conglomerate, with command centers in Paris and London, had its US headquarters in New York, close to his elegant Manhattan townhouse where Goldsmith entertained and where the young Epstein trolled for wealthy clients.

Hilton Head at the time was undergoing a chaotic development boom that brought in a rush of speculators, shady operators and vacationers lured by star-studded golf tournaments and tennis matches. Its population, 11,000 in 1980, doubled in a decade. Its tiny airport was suddenly a busy landing strip for private jets, including a $10m Gulfstream owned by Goldsmith’s company that was parked there for quick hops.
Epstein developed a lifelong fascination with Goldsmith, his family and fortune, an investigation by the Guardian found.

Epstein’s connection to Goldsmith, and the presence of the billionaire’s company and his associates on a South Carolina sea island – which was attracting an infusion of investors – is potentially relevant because of an alleged sexual assault that is said to have occurred there in the 1980s. A woman known only as Jane Doe 4 claimed in four FBI interviews after Epstein’s 2019 arrest that he had assaulted her during his visits to the island in the 1980s, when she was still a teenager. She has also claimed the man she only knew as “Jeff” trafficked her to other men, including Donald Trump.
The White House has vehemently denied the allegation about the US president, calling it “completely baseless” and “backed by zero credible evidence”.

The Guardian has been examining records, digging into archives and conducting interviews to explore intersections of Goldsmith and Epstein and try to understand if Epstein, with decades of secretive movements and a web of global financial ties, might have had reason to be on Hilton Head in the 1980s when those alleged assaults by Epstein occurred. This remains a mystery, but Epstein’s relationship with Goldsmith provides some additional clues.

Those who dismiss the claim of Jane Doe 4 – including Epstein’s brother Mark – have cited the lack of a public record of his presence on the island as proof that her story is untrue. Mark Epstein told the Guardian he has “no knowledge of him being in Hilton Head”.

Understanding how Epstein won and retained access to power and privilege throughout his life is important as criminal investigations of his sexual abuse and financial crimes continue around the globe. Federal prosecutors in New York have opened an investigation into the two overseers – Darren Indyke and Richard Kahn – of Epstein’s $577m estate, according to the Wall Street Journal. Both have denied they knew of Epstein’s criminal behavior. The Department of Justice has said that Epstein “harmed” over 1,000 people, including minors who were sexually abused.

The justice department has released about 3.5m documents under the Epstein Disclosure Act, including reams of emails, letters and bank transactions. But the trove includes almost no records from the 1980s, leaving a large gap in the public’s understanding. Epstein’s alleged victims continue to accuse the justice department of a cover-up for holding back documents that might implicate Trump and other powerful men in Epstein’s exclusive circle. Trump has said he ended their friendship in 2004 after a real estate dispute and kicked Epstein out of his Mar-A-Lago club in 2007 for poaching employees.
It is unclear whether Goldsmith’s concerns about Epstein stemmed from specific encounters, and there is no indication that Goldsmith ever reported his concerns to local or federal law enforcement.

It took decades for the FBI to catch up with Epstein’s crimes. Federal investigators in Florida charged him in 2008 with soliciting sex from minors after a two-year investigation in which they interviewed young women, including some minors, who he paid for sexual encounters in his Palm Beach mansion. He served 13 months in jail under a lenient deal cut with federal prosecutors.

blocks.caption: Epstein abuse survivor Annie Farmer holds up a photo of her younger self with her sister Maria Farmer during a news conference with lawmakers on the Epstein Files Transparency Act outside the US Capitol on 18 November 2025. Photograph: Heather Diehl/Getty Images

blocks.text: Until now, the earliest warning about Epstein’s criminal behavior is believed to have come in 1996, when one alleged victim – an artist named Maria Farmer – claims she alerted authorities that she was sexually assaulted by Epstein, according to a lawsuit she has brought against the FBI. Farmer has also claimed that Epstein stole nude images she had of her two minor siblings, which she kept for her personal use in her artwork. The FBI has said in response to the ongoing litigation, which now includes 34 alleged victims, that agents do not have a duty to investigate “every single tip that comes across their desk”.
A fascination with ‘Sir James’
Since Epstein’s death, Goldsmith has been portrayed as an important influence in his early career.

The New York Times last year described Sir James as a connection Epstein shrewdly calculated was “worth nurturing for the long haul”. It recounted a party scene at Goldsmith’s Upper East Side mansion where Epstein, trained in classical piano, serenaded guests with a piano solo from the grand entry hall.

Goldsmith’s warnings about Epstein came just as Epstein signed one of his biggest clients, Ohio retail magnate Les Wexner, the founder of Victoria’s Secret, who was then ranked by Forbes as the 10th richest person in the US. Wexner says he severed the relationship with Epstein in 2007 after discovering he had stolen funds from Wexner.
Some questions about Epstein and Goldsmith may never be answered given the secrecy surrounding these events and the refusal of key sources to answer questions.

blocks.caption: Posters with photos of acting attorney general Todd Blanche with the words:  ‘Ask Todd Blanche about Epstein’ displayed along a street in Washington, on 17 July 2026. Photograph: Kevin Carter/Getty Images

blocks.text: Meanwhile, the debate over the government’s release of the Epstein files rages on. Attorney general Todd Blanche has declined to release about 2.5m Epstein documents he deemed duplicative. An independent journalist, Katie Phang, is suing Blanche to try to force their release, and Blanche recently quietly turned over some of the documents related to Jane Doe 4 to a federal judge, who is reviewing the documents in his chambers.

Prominent figures caught up in the Epstein controversy include former US president Bill Clinton, former Prince Andrew, former Harvard president Larry Summers and billionaire investor Leon Black. Black was recently held in contempt of Congress for his refusal to comply with subpoenas issued to him by the House oversight committee in connection to its Epstein investigation.

Epstein’s emails about the Goldsmiths sometimes suggested bruised feelings and revealed he was watching the family from afar. He was not among the dozens of invited guests in 1997 to Jemima Goldsmith’s grand wedding party to the cricketer-turned-politician Imran Khan, who served as Pakistani prime minister, according to the guest list.

Just before he finished his lenient 2008 sentence for sex crimes in Palm Beach, Epstein scolded a young Romanian admirer for turning down her exclusive invite to a swanky dinner at Jemima’s Oxfordshire estate.
“That was a BIG mistake,” he wrote in an angry 2010 email.
Epstein criticized daughter Jemima’s choice of husband, calling Khan – who is now divorced from Goldsmith and in jail on corruption charges – a “whacko”.

blocks.caption: Diana, Princess of Wales in Lahore, Pakistan, with Imran Khan and Jemima Khan, during her visit to the Shaukat Memorial hospital, on 21 May 1997. Photograph: Tim Graham Picture Library/Tim Graham Photo Library/Getty Images

blocks.text: In a 2018 text, Epstein wrote of Imran Khan: “makes donald look like einstein. incapable of truth. , devout islamisist . many nuclear weapons. ( not erdogan or khomeni). he was married to two friends of mine. one daughter of jimmy goldsmith.”

After the family distanced itself from him, Epstein gathered gossip about James’s daughter Isabel’s haughty behavior and joked when a hurricane seemed destined to damage Las Alamandas, her posh Mexican resort.
“hurricane will hit isabel goldsmith resort and bye bye,” he wrote to a friend in 2015.

Epstein elevated his access to the British elite when, in 1990, he started dating Ghislaine Maxwell, the daughter of a British media baron, who hobnobbed with British royals and enhanced Epstein’s standing among upper-crust families like the Goldsmiths. Maxwell became Epstein’s closest partner in recruiting young women, according to her federal indictment. She is serving a 20 year sentence.
Three Goldsmith heirs told the Guardian in emails they never met Epstein and doubted their father had any business dealings with him. Isabel Goldsmith did not respond to messages.

blocks.caption: From left: Donald Trump and his girlfriend (and future wife), former model Melania Knauss, Jeffrey Epstein, and Ghislaine Maxwell at Mar-a-Lago club, in Florida, on 12 February 2000.  Photograph: Davidoff Studios Photography/Getty Images

blocks.text: “I’m not sure I had ever heard of Jeffrey Epstein before he hit the news for the first time. So I’m presuming my father did not know him,” said Ben Goldsmith, an environmentalist and investor who was 16 when his father died.
Zac Goldsmith, a conservative member of the House of Lords, said he never met Epstein and was not aware of his fascination with the family.
Jemima Goldsmith Khan, who owns a London-based film production company, said she never met Epstein. “I heard that my father despised him – he was certainly not a friend of his,” she said.

Sir James was a king of US corporate takeovers in a frenetic era of Wall Street deal-making, earning hundreds of millions by seizing control of vulnerable companies and cutting thousands of American jobs. Goldsmith sold his New York investments in 1987 and made a hasty exit back to London after correctly predicting the Black Monday stock market crash.

Epstein was a takeover amateur who concocted his own deals while working as a consultant to a shady Manhattan debt collection company, Towers Financial, whose chief executive Steven Hoffenberg was later convicted of running a $450m Ponzi scheme. Before his death, Hoffenberg accused Epstein of masterminding the scheme. Epstein was never charged.

Hoffenberg’s most ambitious effort was an attempted takeover of troubled Pan Am Airlines, the prestigious international carrier Epstein had fantasized as a boy about one day owning, according to an email from one of his friends.

Working from its Hilton Head office, Goldsmith’s takeover team had already analyzed Pan Am’s books and backed off from making an offer. Developer Donald Trump also flirted with a takeover bid but never made it, media reports show.

Couturier met Epstein through Isabel Goldsmith, the titan’s oldest daughter. Jet-setting Isabel became friendly – but not romantically involved – with Epstein, he said, and Isabel and Epstein both socialized in New York City’s nightlife scene. Epstein kept Isabel’s phone contacts at several addresses in his “little black book” later seized by the FBI as evidence.

Couturier had grown close to James Goldsmith and his long-term girlfriend, who hired him in 1981 to renovate a mansion on East 80th Street. Goldsmith cut famous takeover deals around the dining room table, and his catered parties attracted the cream of Manhattan society.

blocks.caption: Jemima Khan, right, and her sister Isabel Goldsmith at David Frost’s annual summer garden party in Chelsea on 25 June 1998. Photograph: Tom Wargacki/WireImage

blocks.text: Isabel told Couturier that Epstein wanted to discuss hiring him for another renovation at a huge Upper East Side brownstone purchased by Wexner, he said. Epstein later moved into the restored mansion at 9 East 71st Street, about a half mile from Goldsmith’s, and decorated its dark wooded interior with his private art collection and gaudy fabrics. It became a center of his sexual misconduct, an address where the FBI in 2019 carried out boxes of photographs of alleged victims, massage tables and sex toys.

Wexner also owned a dilapidated historic townhome next door at 11 East 71st Street that needed total renovation. The house was eventually bought through a trust by Trump’s commerce secretary Howard Lutnick, who has said he hardly knew Epstein, his next-door neighbor. Under questioning by House investigators, Lutnick acknowledged visiting Epstein for lunch at the predator’s Caribbean island, Little Saint James.

Couturier was approached and interviewed by the FBI in 2010, after Epstein’s first arrest. A record of the interview, which is included in the Epstein files, indicates that Epstein had approached Couturier for a high-paying project on Little Saint James Island, where he was asked to provide “decor and furniture appropriate for teenage girls, with pink furnishings and bunk beds”.
Courturier told the Guardian he remembered Sir Jimmy’s earlier warning. He withdrew from the contract, leading to a legal dispute.

blocks.caption: British financier and businessman Sir James Goldsmith (1933 - 1997) with his family, left to right: Jemima, Sir James, Zac, Ben and his wife, Lady Annabel, on their estate in Marbella, Spain, circa 1987. Photograph: Peter Jordan/Popperfoto/Getty Images

blocks.text: Goldsmith was hardly a prude, Couturier said, but he had no tolerance for inappropriate behavior with children. Goldsmith’s own domestic life was what his daughter Alix once described as “unconventional”, with three wives, numerous girlfriends and eight children. Two children were born in New York to his longtime girlfriend, a French journalist who moved with him to the city.

Another link between Epstein and Goldsmith was Bear Stearns, where Epstein was a junior broker until he was targeted in an internal investigation of his trading practices. He quit in 1981 with an indignant resignation letter that was included in the Epstein files.

Goldsmith remained a major Bear Stearns client, and Epstein, who somehow remained on good terms with the brokerage top brass, invested his own and his clients’ money into the firm, which collapsed in 2008.
Epstein always kept an air of mystery around his business deals. In the 1980s, he described himself to friends as a “bounty hunter” who traveled the world to recover stolen money for rich clients.

He and Goldsmith knew many of the same influential people. Saudi billionaire Adnan Khashoggi, an international arms dealer, hired Epstein in the 1980s for unspecified work, according to published reports. Khashoggi and Goldsmith were both trusted advisers to President Richard Nixon, who met with them after his 1974 resignation to discuss overseas income opportunities, according to a Nixon biographer.

Epstein became friendly with a wealthy international investor Jean “Johnny” Pigozzi, who was in Goldsmith’s circle of advisers and is one of the trustees of Goldsmith’s estate, according to published reports. At one point, Epstein’s girlfriend Maxwell emailed Pigozzi to get price estimates for his French estate and nature preserve in Panama, saying she had an interested potential buyer, the emails show.

Pigozzi, an art collector and heir to an auto fortune, is best known in popular culture as the inventor of the “selfie” because of his candid photographs of the rich and famous, including Goldsmith. He did not respond to messages.

blocks.caption: Bear Stearns brokerage firm in New York in 1998. Photograph: James Leynse/Corbis/Getty Images

blocks.text: Goldsmith’s massive holding company, GOSL, had operations around the world and a corporate office in Manhattan run by his trusted team.

But in 1985, GOSL filed papers with the state of South Carolina seeking authorization to do business in the state, the Guardian found. It opened an office in Hilton Head, the home of Al Dunlap, a notorious corporate raider Goldsmith was hiring to run his US operations.

Dunlap had been living part-time on Hilton Head since the early 1980s when he was running a company that made paper cups. He was among the many corporate bigwigs who had discovered Hilton Head as a sanctuary for executives and government officials who needed privacy. Most exclusive neighborhoods were gated and developed on former rice plantations.

Dunlap – who died in 2019 – had the Wall Street clout to ask investors to come to him. A newspaper account describes one session in 1985 at a new Marriott waterfront resort in Hilton Head where Dunlap pitched a Lily-Tulip stock offering backed by Wall Street firms to 70 out-of-town investors before leaving on a global capital-raising tour.

blocks.caption: An image of Al Dunlap on Hilton Head island from a 1987 Island Packet newspaper article. Photograph: Island Packet

blocks.text: Some locals say the atmosphere on the island was so frenetic, with investors and deal makers arriving for meetings, that anyone could slip in and out without notice.

Goldsmith’s office in Hilton Head was tasked with selling millions of acres of forest land the company had acquired in takeovers of US paper companies. Its massive new holdings stretched from the Pacific north-west to the Adirondacks, making Goldsmith’s company one of the largest owners of undeveloped US land.

The Guardian tracked down former GOSL executive Phil Lader, who was in charge of land sales, to ask if he recalled seeing Epstein in Hilton Head during the time GOSL had an office there. The short answer was “no”.

Lader was a Hilton Head resident and former chief executive at Sea Pines. In 1981, he founded the prestigious Renaissance Weekends that drew luminaries to the island for private invitation-only retreats. He was especially close to Bill Clinton, who was governor of Arkansas when he and his wife, Hillary, began coming to Lader’s exclusive gatherings. Other featured guests included Wall Street executives, university and government officials and leaders in the arts and sciences.

blocks.caption: Bill Clinton is greeted by the Lader family after arriving in Hilton Head, South Carolina, for the annual intellectual retreat known as ‘renaissance weekend’ on 30 December 1996. Photograph: Wilfredo Lee/AP

blocks.text: Goldsmith hired Lader as a GOSL vice-president in 1986, just after he lost a Democratic party bid for the South Carolina governorship. Lader was appointed Clinton’s deputy White House chief of staff in 1993 and moved to London four years later when he was appointed ambassador to the court of Saint James.

Lader said he never met Epstein and “never heard the name Jeffrey Epstein in my years on Hilton Head”. Epstein reportedly made 17 visits to the Clinton White House and later flew Clinton on his private jet.

A partially redacted 2011 exchange in Epstein’s emails shows he was aware of Renaissance Weekends, which are promoted on social media as gathering places for “thought-leaders”. An unnamed friend asked if Epstein had heard of the gatherings.
“Of course,” Epstein wrote. Asked if it was “something i should do?”, Epstein wrote “yes”.
Renaissance Weekends were held in Hilton Head for 20 years, then moved to Charleston. Similar programs are also held in other cities.

The woman who would come to be known as Jane Doe 4 first called an FBI victim hotline to report her alleged abuse on 10 July 2019. It was four days after Epstein’s arrest at a New Jersey airport. The agent manning the phones recommended that she be interviewed in person, near her home in Vancouver, Washington. One of her close friends made a separate call to anonymously report Jane Doe 4’s abuse.

Jane Doe 4’s federal class-action lawsuit, filed later in New York against the Epstein estate, alleges she met Epstein around 1984, when she was a teenager, and had sex with him for several years when he visited the island. She said he rented properties, including a villa at Sea Pines, from her mother’s realty firm.
In four FBI interviews in 2019 she described her abuser’s specific sexual quirks – including his use of butt plugs. Several were seized when the FBI gathered evidence in Epstein’s home in 2019.

Some details squared with accounts given by other young victims who came forward during the previous Florida investigation. She described how he allegedly asked her to recruit friends and took nude photographs of her, also part of a pattern, and repeatedly plied her with drugs and alcohol. The FBI seized thousands of photographs and videos depicting victims when it searched his various properties.

The Marriott hotel on Hilton Head figures heavily in her allegations. She told the FBI about a pool party there with local teenage girls and older males. She claimed the older man she knew as “Jeff” made a brief appearance at the pool before taking her back to his rented villa. She also mentioned a neighbor she had talked with during the period of alleged abuse.

Her local attorney told the Guardian he sat in on the FBI interview and interrupted when she began describing telling other girls about “Jeff”. The lawyer said he feared the FBI might accuse her of aiding her abuser in soliciting other minors.

FBI notes in the case, which were first reported by the Post and Courier in Charleston, South Carolina, repeat the woman’s allegation that at one point, Epstein transported her to New York or New Jersey where she claims he introduced her to Trump, who forced her into a sex act. She estimated she was about 13-15 years old, which would place the dates between 1983 and 1985, but she acknowledged a fuzzy memory. Trump said in a 2002 interview with New York magazine that he had known Epstein for 15 years, which would date their relationship to 1987. The White House has denied Jane Doe 4’s allegations.
Jane Doe 4 also offered names of some of her high school friends who might have seen her with Epstein.

But there is no evidence the FBI ever followed up on the leads Jane Doe 4 gave investigators. Its interest in her case appears to have died abruptly when she asked agents what the point was of her continued cooperation and told them she intended to join a class action lawsuit, filed by the Bloom Law Firm in December 2019.

A relative of Jane Doe 4 told the Guardian that she had been scarred by “layers of trauma” as a young girl from family tragedies and upheavals. She had spent time in foster care and had just finished elementary school when the family made its way south.

Jane Doe 4 declined to answer questions from the Guardian relayed through the relative, who considers her account “plausible” because she was often unsupervised in her early teens. Three friends contacted by the Guardian did not respond to messages.
Jane Doe 4’s attorney at the Bloom Law Firm told the Post and Courier she ultimately reached a settlement with Epstein’s estate but declined to give an amount.

Court records show a claim she filed with the Epstein victims’ compensation fund, a formal review panel funded by the estate, was denied. The dates of her alleged abuse are much earlier than most other victims who have come forward with claims.

In response to lawmakers’ questions about whether Jane Doe 4 had received a settlement from the estate, an attorney for Epstein’s accountant, Richard Kahn, said he could not recall details of all 60 women who settled with the estate outside of the compensation fund.

blocks.caption: Richard Kahn, an accountant for convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, arrives for a House oversight committee deposition about Epstein, on 11 March 2026.  Photograph: Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc/Getty Images

blocks.text: The record is far from definitive about whether Epstein ever visited Hilton Head during this time. He did not own a private plane in the 1980s, so no travel logs are available. Epstein did have other real estate development interests at that time, including a long friendship with a developer who was building an oceanfront golf course on nearby Kiawah Island.

Later records in the Epstein files show his plane landing at the nearby Savannah airport several times from 2013 to 2019, for unknown reasons. The emails show a redacted exchange in 2014 suggesting he was on Hilton Head for a March visit.

Kenneth Lannon, a retired FBI expert in child sexual victimization who has trained hundreds of law enforcement agents to investigate abusers, said it is “highly likely” Epstein had victims pre-dating his Florida arrest and that he probably “started out slowly and just got better and better at it as time went on.

The typical child sex abuser, he said, begins targeting and grooming potential victims soon after puberty, although they may come across as “nice guys” in regular social interactions. Money and the ability to travel freely makes the crimes easier to pull off, he said.
Child victims are often so starved for attention they become compliant and have more than one encounter with the abuser.

Jane Doe 4 had a troubled life after leaving Hilton Head. She married several times and moved to the west coast. She returned to be with family in Georgia and was arrested in 2023 for stealing money from a dying man. She pleaded guilty and spent a year in jail. Her brothers were well educated; one worked for a few years as a Bear Stearns trader before the brokerage collapsed in 2008.

A family member told the Guardian in June that Jane Doe 4 is “staying off the grid” and lives in fear of retaliation from the Trump administration amid the ongoing controversy over the handling of the case.
Additional research by Sophie Sullivan

articles.title: Why music in Iran is more than just entertainment
articles.summary: Iranian authorities are trying to persuade prominent singers in exile to return home. While the state seeks to harness music as a political tool, music has also become a powerful expression of…

image.caption: Since the 1979 Islamic Revolution, there has been an ongoing conflict between the Iranian state and musicImage: Sobhan Farajvan/Pacific Press/picture alliance

blocks.text: After spending 47 years abroad, Iranian musician Bijan Mortazavi returned to his homeland at the end of September.
Mortazavi is one of Iran's most renowned violinists, singers, and composers.
In July 2026, he performed with his famous white violin at the closing ceremony of the FIFA World Cup alongside the New York Philharmonic Orchestra.

In the videos that he and his wife have now posted on social media, the couple can be seen taking walks through the city of the Iranian capital, Tehran, while passersby greet the musician warmly and welcome him.
Singer Mohsen Namjoo also recently returned to Iran after about 20 years in exile.
Internationally renowned for his experimental Persian music, he blends traditional Persian singing and poetic lyrics with elements of blues, rock, jazz, and folk.
In 2009, Namjoo was sentenced in absentia by a court in Tehran to five years in prison.
He was accused of insulting holy sites and mocking verses from the Quran, among other things.
In a video posted online after his return to Iran, Namjoo said he had returned to the country to spend more time with his family and friends.

blocks.caption: Women are prohibited from singing solo in Ira, but many young female musicians play and sing on the street without headscarves, defying the existing banImage: Morteza Nikoubazl/NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: Return as a political tool

On August 27, Abbas Salehi, Iran's minister of culture and Islamic guidance, said in an interview with the prominent Iranian media outlet Farhikhtegan that his ministry had compiled a list containing the names of more than 100 distinguished Iranians living abroad.
The goal, he said, was to remove obstacles to their travel or return to Iran.

Salehi stressed that even "critics of the Islamic Republic" could return at any time. He added, however, that the return of artists does not necessarily mean they would perform in Iran. Instead, they could simply visit the country, the minister said.
Sina Yousefi, a human rights lawyer, pointed to international law, specifically Article 12 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, to which Iran is also a signatory.
According to this provision, no one may be arbitrarily prevented from entering their own country. This right cannot be made contingent on a citizen's level of loyalty to the government, he told DW.

"The idea of seeking out certain well-known figures — who the reformists, in particular, believe are less likely to cross the red lines — and winning them over to collaborate or bringing them back to the country is not new," said Sepideh Raissadat , an ethnomusicologist who has been studying the history and development of Persian music for years.

As an internationally renowned performer of classical Persian music, she combines her artistic work with scholarly research, with her dissertation focusing on the lives of Iranian female singers since the 1979 Islamic Revolution.
Iran uprising seen through the eyes of Iranian women
Between control and resistance

"The 1979 revolution in Iran was a revolution against music. Music was one of the red lines," said Raissadat, referring to statements by the leader of the revolution, Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini, who as early as July 1979 had publicly described music as harmful to society and called for its complete abolition.

In a speech to employees of Radio Darya on July 21, 1979, Khomeini is said to have described music as "a betrayal of the country" and "a betrayal of the youth." A few days later, the Iranian newspaper Keyhan quoted him as saying that music was "like a drug” and must be completely eradicated.

During the Iran-Iraq War from 1980 to 1988, however, music made a comeback in the form of revolutionary and religious songs. It was also used to stir up feelings of national pride and a sense of belonging.

The regime also failed to completely banish the female voice from the public sphere. "They couldn't completely eliminate the voice of women. The female voice returned through choral singing," said Raissadat.
But the conflict between the state and music continued.

For years, musical instruments were not allowed to be shown on Iranian television. Instruments were confiscated or destroyed on the streets. Fearing repercussions, musicians did not carry their instruments in public, while some hid them in their cars.

"Listening to banned music at home was a political act. And when women began to sing, that, too, became a political act," Raissadat noted. The development of Iranian pop music was also part of this political and cultural tension, she underscored. "People began producing new domestic pop music to compete with music from Los Angeles."
Over the past ten years, social media — which is not entirely under government control — has become increasingly important and now wields considerable influence.
This change is particularly evident among young people, with young women now even playing the guitar without headscarves and performing in public.
Iranian singer finds voice in Germany
Music as an expression of protest
Raissadat observes a particular trend among the families of the young people who were killed during the nationwide mass protests in late December 2025 and January 2026.
The demonstrations began on December 28, 2025, and were violently suppressed by security forces.
Human rights organizations report that thousands of protesters were killed, but the exact figures are unknown due to the extensive information blackout imposed by the regime.

"The most important thing we've seen in recent years has been the use of music by the bereaved families of those killed in the protests. This stands in complete contrast to Shiite tradition and our history," said Raissadat.
At some funerals, families turned the memorial service for their loved ones into a new form of protest.
Instead of religious hymns, music played, and the mourners sang and danced along to it. In doing so, they created a deliberate contrast to traditional religious mourning rituals, the musician said.

"Music became a weapon. Those who were mourning were able to connect with it on their own, and at the same time, it stood in opposition to what the political system stands for," Raissadat pointed out, adding, "Dancing in white clothing also became an expression of this resistance."
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: Satellite images show attack jets at Chinese military facility in Laos
articles.summary:
New ‘support and training centre’ prompts concern in region but China says it is ‘not directed at any third party’

Satellite images show attack jets stationed at a new overseas Chinese…

blocks.text: Satellite images show attack jets stationed at a new overseas Chinese military facility in Laos, which opened last week and gives Beijing’s air force its first foothold in mainland south-east Asia.

Images provided by the commercial satellite provider Vantor show eight light attack aircraft positioned at Ban Keun airport alongside what appear to be more than a dozen military vehicles lined up in rows.

The planes’ shape matches that of the Chinese-made Hongdu JL-8 jet, a two-seat trainer that can be deployed in combat to carry bombs. Laos is reported to have four such aircraft, according to the London-based International Institute for Strategic Studies.
In a rare example of Beijing’s overseas military expansion, China opened what it said was a joint “support and training centre” at Ban Keun on 29 September.

The airport, about ⁠50km (30 miles) north of Vientiane, the capital of Laos, has been significantly expanded over the past year. Satellite images taken just months ago show farmland and dirt paths where there are now new buildings and a paved runway.

Aside from its island bases in the South China Sea, Beijing does not have a significant network of military outposts in other countries and the Laos airbase would be its first facility in another country capable of handling fighter jets.

The satellite images, taken a day after the announcement and first reported by Reuters, show extensive construction work that appears to be focused on a future runway extension, which could make the airport capable of handling larger planes such as bombers.
In its September announcement, China’s defence ministry said the new centre would “help Laos strengthen the training of its air force pilots” and was not “directed against any third party”.

blocks.caption: Construction under way at the site on 2 September. Photograph: Vantor/Reuters

blocks.text: Governments will be watching closely for signs of deployments or the installation of defence equipment that may serve wider military ambitions. After the announcement, the Singapore-based security analyst Collin Koh said it “may not be wrong to conclude this is the first full-fledged PLA [People’s Liberation Army] overseas base in south-east Asia”.

Over the past two decades, China has built up an extensive network of outposts on islands in the disputed South China Sea, including airbases with air defence installations. Otherwise, its navy’s sole overseas military base is a logistics base in Djibouti, on the coast of the Horn of Africa.
The Laos agreement follows a similar programme established in Cambodia, at the Ream naval base on the Gulf of Thailand, although that facility has no runway.

After years of speculation and denials, China announced in April last year that it had created the “joint logistics and training” facility in Cambodia. It said the centre would support the two militaries in “conducting regional counter-terrorism, disaster prevention and mitigation, humanitarian assistance, joint training and other operations”.

US forces are believed to have used Ban Keun airport in Laos during covert military operations at the height of the Vietnam war in the 1960s and 1970s. Its development will be monitored by Vietnam, which maintains disputes with China over the South China Sea, and Thailand, which shares a border with Laos.

After the announcement last week, Thailand’s defence ministry spokesperson said Bangkok considered itself a close partner of both Laos and China and saw it as Vientiane’s sovereign right to decide whether to grant permission for a Chinese base.
“Nevertheless, Thailand will continue to closely monitor developments and how the matter proceeds, particularly with regard to building mutual trust,” said R Adm Surasant Kongsiri.
China’s government did not mention sending aircraft to Laos in its initial announcement, while government of Laos has not commented on the project.

The US-based Institute for the Study of War has described the Laos base as the “first PLA overseas military facility focused on air power”. In its assessment, the thinktank said the base was “not yet equipped to provide the PLA with the ability to execute major combat operations, unlike US military bases”.
The base would, however, give the Chinese military alternate routes to access to the South China Sea and strategic air routes, it added.
Reuters contributed to this report

articles.title: Could the UK really rejoin the EU?
articles.summary:
The big question facing ​A​ndy Burnham is not whether Brexit has harmed Britain, but if a rapidly changing Europe will keep the door open​ if the UK decides it wants back in

•…

blocks.text: It was lobbed into the national conversation without fanfare or warning, almost a footnote in the UK prime minister’s first speech as leader to his governing Labour party’s annual conference. But Andy Burnham has kicked off a quiet U-turn on Brexit.

By stating bluntly that the decision to leave Europe’s core political community had done “more harm than good”, Burnham broke a taboo in his own party, in effect, discarding his predecessor’s paralysing ‘red lines’ on Europe, and signalling he will not be bound by these constraints after the next British election.

Over the coming six weeks Burnham will gauge public support before setting out future options for the UK’s long term relationship with the UK’s largest market. Rejoining the 27-nation bloc will be one of them, opening the door to Britain reversing Brexit.

The famous red lines, or non-negotiables, enshrined by Starmer in Labour’s 2024 election manifesto, were meant to reassure Brexit-supporting voters that under Labour there would be no return to a single market, customs union or the free movement of people. These pledges left Starmer with little room for manoeuvre with Europe beyond warm words.

The evidence that Brexit has stunted the British economy is not new. Estimates for the damage quitting the single market has already done range from 6% of 8% of GDP. What is new is a prime ministerial readiness to publicly acknowledge that harm and conclude that an ambitious new path is required.

“This is the first time that a UK politician in power has been willing to stand up and say that Brexit is a failure that we must address or redress in some fundamental way,” Joël Reland, an analyst with the UK In a Changing Europe thinktank, told me. “Keir Starmer’s public message was that we will be sticking with Boris Johnson’s [2019] Brexit deal, but we’re going to improve it to make Brexit work. Burnham is saying Brexit doesn’t work and that we need a different form of deal. That has never been said before.”

Burnham is not yet committing himself to fighting the next election on a particular course of action. Much will depend on the response he gets. But all options – Lisa O’Carroll details them here – are on the table, from a customs union to re-joining the single market and becoming, like Norway, a rule-taker, to “going all the way”.

But crucially, Burnham has already departed from the orthodoxy that makes questioning Brexit a heresy. Instead of shutting down the topic to limit his exposure to Eurosceptic attacks, the PM is meeting it head-on, Reland said. “And I don’t see why you would do that unless you wanted to take on the political argument”.
Why would Burnham choose this juncture and risk drawing down what Rafael Behr calls the Brexit curse?

The economic rationale is the obvious one. “Burnham’s ten year domestic agenda for the country promises radical reform of such things as the social care system, and somebody is going to have to pay for that,” argues Reland. “One of the ways you can get economic growth is by rejoining your largest and closest trading partner.”

The modest ‘re-set’ agenda launched by Starmer in May 2025 is stuck, bogged down in disputes, such as that over fees for EU students in the UK. A pencilled-in 20 November summit is still up in the air. Britain’s big impediment from outside the club is its lack of bargaining power. A cherrypicking attempt to coax the EU into a selective single market for goods only (without free movement of people) was firmly rebuffed by Brussels in May. And even if this reset were fully delivered, the government’s own figures estimate it would add at most 0.3% to GDP by 2040.

Labour meanwhile has lost votes to its left, particularly to the Greens, so a more progressive offer on Europe might be a gamble worth taking. New polling, as Pippa Crerar and Rowena Mason revealed at the weekend, shows that if Burnham’s preference is for rejoining the EU, almost half of the country already agrees.

Gaby Hinsliff noted that among Burnham’s opponents the only one to react to the surprise move with “unfettered glee” was Nigel Farage. Yet, she suggested, the Conservatives, also obsessed with economic growth, may not side with Farage given that most voters think Brexit has made them economically worse off. “It’s not in Tory long-term interests to strangle this at birth” wrote Hinsliff.
after newsletter promotion
A warm welcome?

blocks.caption: Emmanuel Macron’s French government is being hardline about Britain’s involvement in ‘Made in Europe’. Photograph: Ludovic Marin/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Events in Europe are also dictating the pace. “Welcome back!” was the French president Emmanuel Macron’s possibly tongue-in-cheek response to Burnham’s remarks. But it is a French-led project called “Made in Europe” that is both concentrating the PM’s mind and could ultimately undermine his ambition.

Made in Europe is a highly protectionist idea for remaking the EU as an industrial powerhouse, able to withstand competition from China. UK-made goods, if legally classified as non-European under the law, would be locked out, spelling trade devastation for the British car industry. France, facing its own domestic upheaval and crunch elections next April, is hardline about Britain’s exclusion: Macron’s ministers insist that if you’re not paying the costs of the internal market you don’t get to claim the benefits. Made in Europe is emerging as a symbol, Reland explained, of how geopolitics is driving the EU’s agenda, and widening its range of competencies to such areas as industrial policy, AI and tech sovereignty. “It is no longer just food and environment policy that is set at EU level but the big, strategic, hard security decisions too,” he said.

The more that EU countries strategically pool sovereignty to respond to shocks such as US antagonism or Russian hybrid warfare, and the more aggressively they protect that cooperation, the steeper the costs of being outside the club become. With Norway and Switzerland, both non-EU members with single market access, now also facing the Made in Europe battle, it’s no wonder Burnham is mulling the full rejoin option.

But, as Mujtaba Rahman’s prescient column advised, the coming debate will need to go beyond the question of whether Britain could contemplate rejoining, to an honest assessment of what Europe has become in the years since it left.
