articles.title: Is Sara Duterte unaware of BPI accounts with father Rodrigo?
articles.summary: The defense team also distances the Vice President from the insurance policies linked to her

blocks.text: SARA DUTERTE. Accompanied by her brother, Davao City 1st District Rep. Paolo Duterte, Vice President Sara Duterte arrives at the Quezon City RTC on September 11, 2026, to attend arraignment proceedings for a grave threat case.
Jire Carreon/Rappler
The defense team also distances the Vice President from the insurance policies linked to her

Amid the prosecution team’s attempt to prove the authenticity of bank accounts and insurance policies linked to Vice President Sara Duterte, the latter’s defense team had a strategy: distance the Vice President from these transactions.

Defense spokesperson and counsel Michael Poa wrote a letter to the Bank of the Philippine Islands (BPI) to clarify matters about Duterte’s accounts with her father. Poa floated this letter during the impeachment trial on Wednesday, October 7, which was later read out loud by Senator-judge Risa Hontiveros during her interjection.
The letter was flashed on screen as Hontiveros read it out loud.

“Certain public statements have referred to purported bank accounts allegedly maintained with your institution bearing various account numbers hereto attached as Annex A. In light of these allegations and considering that our client has no knowledge, participation or recollection of maintaining or having any beneficial interest in such accounts, we respectfully request confirmation of the following,” the letter said, seeking clarification about the existence and status of the BPI accounts.
Poa addressed the letter to BPI senior vice president and legal counsel. Paul Rodrick Ysmael.

On Day 35 of the trial, BPI division head for central Manila branches Marwin Galvez confirmed that former president Rodrigo Duterte and daughter Sara had a joint time deposit account opened in January 2010 with a principal amount of P40.65 million.

The account was opened in the BPI Julia Vargas branch in Pasig City, rolled over 12 times, and eventually reached P41.72 million. When the time deposit matured in March 2011, the funds were converted into a manager’s check.

Prosecutor James Bryan Ibrahim explained that if funds were used to acquire a manager’s check, they will not reflect on the account’s year-end balance as they are considered “floating.” A manager’s check is valid for six months.

blocks.caption: Sara, Rodrigo Duterte hid P96M through unutilized manager’s checks — prosecution

blocks.text: So by saying that Duterte had no recollection of these accounts, did the defense say that this manager’s check transaction was all the idea of the former president?
“Well, to better phrase it your honor, our client, does not have any recollection of this account,” Poa told Hontiveros, who had the same question in mind.

The defense counsel added that his client only knew about the said bank account during the House quad committee hearings in 2024, which investigated Philippine offshore gaming operators, war on drugs, and illegal drugs.

“I was asked by the Vice President to verify kasi hindi niya natatandaan na may ganitong account at wala daw siyang transaksyon, ‘no (because she cannot remember that such an account exists and she is not aware of that transaction). So, in fact, that’s why we wanted to show even the response of the BPI to my letter,” Poa added.
But this was not the only thing that the Vice President is supposedly unaware of — or at least has no knowledge of.

During their cross-examination of witnesses from several insurance companies, the defense lawyers highlighted that the Vice President — although named in the policies — might not be directly involved in the transactions done by her husband.
For example, defense lawyer Carlo Joaquin Narvasa read to a witness section 3 of Republic Act No. 10607 or the law that amended the Insurance Code.

“The consent of the spouse is not necessary for the validity of an insurance policy taken out by a married person on his or her life or that of his or her children,” Narvasa said, reading the provision.
The consent of the spouse in insurance policies and other similar questions were repeated by defense counsels during the Wednesday trial. But for the prosecution, these excuses were unacceptable.
“Because, the SALN is a SALN. There are requirements for the SALN,” said prosecutor Terry Ridon.

“You have to ask your co-depositors, the co-joint accounts, whether that’s your spouse, your father, the content of these bank accounts before writing your SALN. That’s the process for all government officials preparing their SALN. So, hopefully, that’s what the Vice President should have done,” he added in Filipino.

What did the defense team — and the Vice President, for that matter — accomplish in claiming that Sara had no knowledge of the joint bank accounts with her father, who was detained in The Hague? Ridon had a response that mirrored the though balloon of many trial observers that day: “Magandang araw po, Pangulong Duterte. Nilalaglag po kayo rito.”
(Good morning, President Duterte. They’re throwing you under the bus here.) – Rappler.com

articles.title: Weston family's holding company to buy U.K. pharmacy chain Boots for $12.7B
articles.summary: The Weston family holding company Wittington Investments said Wednesday that it will purchase the U.K. chain Boots for $8.9 billion US, including debt, from private equity firm Sycamore Partners.…

image.caption: A sign outside a Boots location is seen in London on May 16, 2011. The family behind Canada's biggest pharmacy and grocery chains is growing its empire with the acquisition of the U.K. drugstore. (Luke MacGregor/Reuters)

blocks.text: Business·New

The Weston family holding company Wittington Investments said Wednesday that it will purchase the U.K. chain Boots for $8.9 billion US, including debt, from private equity firm Sycamore Partners. Boots is one of Britain's most prominent retailers.
U.K pharmacy chain Boots is one of Britain's most prominent retailers
· The Canadian Press
· Posted: Oct 07, 2026 10:40 AM EDT | Last Updated: 20 minutes ago
The family behind Canada's biggest pharmacy and grocery chains is growing its empire with the acquisition of U.K. drugstore Boots.

The Weston family holding company Wittington Investments said Wednesday that it will purchase Boots for $8.9 billion US (almost $12.7 billion Cdn), including debt, from private equity firm Sycamore Partners.
Along with Boots's retail operations in the U.K. and Ireland, Wittington will acquire its operations in Thailand and franchised businesses, its optical division and No7 Beauty Company.

Toronto-based holding company Fairfax Financial Holdings Ltd. will partner with Wittington on the acquisition and after its closing, expected in the first quarter of 2027, Galen Weston will become Boots's chairman.
Boots is among Britain's most prominent retailers and has many similarities to Shoppers Drug Mart, the Canadian pharmacy giant with ties to the Westons.
The Westons are best known in Canada for building Loblaw Companies Ltd. and George Weston Ltd., and owning luxury department store Holt Renfrew.

items: Loblaw boosts profit on generic GLP-1 drug sales, bargain hunting shoppers

blocks.text: They also have a stake in Associated British Foods, the parent company of value retailer Primark and the makers of Twinings tea, Mazola oils, Mazzetti vinegars, Ovaltine and Fleischmann's yeast.

It's unclear whether the acquisition will bring Boots, which was founded in 1849 and operated for a time in Canada, back to the country. If Boots made a Canadian return, it could become a competitor with Shoppers, which counts about 1,350 stores in Canada.
Boots has roughly 1,800 locations. When a Boots acquisition by the Westons was rumoured in late September, RBC Capital Markets analyst Irene Nattel said the deal made some sense.

"We believe there is substantial organizational knowledge and understanding of retail pharmacy within the Weston family of businesses and investments, knowledge that would prove extremely useful should a transaction come to fruition," she wrote in a Sept. 30 note to investors.
She didn't see a potential deal as having much impact on Loblaws or George Weston, if it was completed through the family's private investment arm Wittington.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Tara Deschamps is a business reporter with The Canadian Press

articles.title: ‘Another coup d’état’: fears grow as Flávio Bolsonaro vows to ‘re-democratise’ Brazil
articles.summary: After a surprise first-round victory, critics suggest son of disgraced ex-president could seek to continue his father’s authoritarian rule
articles.byline: Tom Phillips in Rio de Janeiro

blocks.text: Flávio Bolsonaro, the far-right frontrunner to become Brazil’s next president, has vowed to “re-democratise” the South American country, fuelling fears over a move into authoritarian rule if he wins power.
Brazil was re-democratised in the 1980s after a brutal 21-year dictatorship that Flávio’s father, the disgraced ex-president, Jair Bolsonaro, has long praised.

Last year, Jair Bolsonaro, a former soldier who served under that military regime, was jailed for 27 years for trying to engineer a coup after he lost the 2022 election to the current leftwing president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva.

But Flávio, 45, beat Lula, 80, in Sunday’s presidential election first round and goes into the 25 October run-off as favourite. On Tuesday, the rightwinger vowed to capitalise on the hugely increased far-right presence in congress after the election to change the constitution and “re-democratise this country”.
“The only thing standing in the way of Brazil becoming a barbarity is called Flávio Bolsonaro as president,” he claimed at a campaign event in Goiânia, a city near the capital, Brasília.

The incendiary comments caused outrage among historians and opponents of Bolsonaro’s radical populist movement, who have accused him of co-opting the language of democracy to disguise an illiberal shift.

blocks.caption: Flavio Bolsonaro raises hands with former presidential candidate Ronaldo Caiado (left) and Sao Paulo governor Tarcisio de Freitas during a rally in Goiania, Goias state, Brazil. Photograph: Sérgio Lima/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Talíria Petrone, the leftwing congresswoman, wrote on X: “This is the announcement of a coup.”

Marcelo Freixo, a newly elected congressman from Lula’s Workers’ party (PT), said: “Brazil was re-democratised in 1988. The person who tried to undo this was his father, who was convicted of an attempted coup. What they want, once again, is a coup.”

Bolsonaro did not spell out what he meant by “re-democratising” Brazil, a vibrant if polarised multi-party democracy which the Sweden based V-Dem institute ranks 28th on its liberal democracy index, two places ahead of the UK and 23 ahead of the US.
But Jair Bolsonaro, who has praised authoritarian leaders including Chile’s former dictator Augusto Pinochet, has long hankered for a return to military rule.

Last September, the supreme court found Jair Bolsonaro guilty of trying to convince military chiefs to help him cling to power at the end of his 2018-2022 presidency. The conspiracy culminated in the 8 January 2023 riots in Brasília, a far-right insurrection seemingly inspired by the January 6 storming of the US Capitol.

Writing in the O Globo newspaper, Míriam Leitão, a prominent political and economic journalist, warned that, if Bolsonaro won, Brazil faced “the extreme and concrete danger of … another coup d’état attempt”.
“Flávio follows the same ideas as his father and has already said that an intervention in the institutions is necessary,” Leitão wrote.

“If Flávio Bolsonaro is elected, he will have more tools at his disposal to carry out his father’s authoritarian project: robust caucuses in the lower house and senate, a weakened supreme court, and the support of the Donald Trump administration. Political science shows that it’s in the second term that an autocrat doubles down on their plan. Look at the case of Donald Trump. The risk isn’t of the son repeating the father, it’s that he surpasses him,” Leitão said.

blocks.caption: Supporters of Brazilian presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro flash victory signs during a rally ahead of the presidential election runoff. Photograph: Adriano Machado/Reuters

blocks.text: Political scientist Miguel Lago said Sunday’s far-right election triumph – in which Bolsonaro’s Liberal party (PL) secured the senate’s largest caucus, with 28 of its 81 seats – would permit radical changes, including the impeachment of supreme court ministers considered enemies of the Bolsonarismo movement.

Jair Bolsonaro and his jailed co-conspirators are also likely to be freed if his son wins, with the former president expected to become an influential minister able to select the new heads of the armed forces.
“It’s better than a coup d’état … it’s almost like a coup d’état with the support of the majority of the population,” Lago said.

Nayib Bukele, El Salvador’s authoritarian president, has been accused of “killing” democracy by using control over the country’s congress and institutions to approve sweeping constitutional changes, including scrapping presidential term limits so he can seek indefinite re-election.

Flávio Bolsonaro recently met Bukele’s security minister, Gustavo Villatoro, in São Paulo, hailing the Central American country’s hardline security policies, which have seen thousands jailed during a state of exception that has lasted nearly five years. Bolsonaro told reporters that during their conversation, Villatoro “stressed the importance” of using control of congress to make the “necessary legal changes”.

On Tuesday, the president of Bolsonaro’s party, Valdemar Costa Neto, said that if Flávio Bolsonaro became president, he would release his father, who would then be “a strong candidate” in the 2030 presidential election.

articles.title: More than 200,000 people displaced as renewed fighting grips Yemen, UN agency says
articles.summary: More than 200,000 people have been displaced across Yemen as fighting between Houthi rebels and Saudi-backed government forces has intensified in recent weeks, the United Nations's migration agency…

image.caption: Displaced Yemeni women wait to receive aid supplies at the Al-Salam camp in Dar Saad district, Aden, Yemen, on Tuesday. At least 201,217 Yemenis have been forced out of their homes in recent weeks amid escalating fighting between Houthi rebels and Saudi-backed government forces, the UN migration age

blocks.text: World·New

More than 200,000 people have been displaced across Yemen as fighting between Houthi rebels and Saudi-backed government forces has intensified in recent weeks, the United Nations's migration agency says.
Speed of crisis 'alarming,' says International Organization for Migration
· CBC News
· Posted: Oct 07, 2026 10:00 AM EDT | Last Updated: 26 minutes ago

The International Organization for Migration (IOM) said on Wednesday that the speed of the displacement was "alarming," with at least 201,217 people now forced out of their homes — up from 76,000 in mid-September.
Yemen's southwestern Ta'iz governorate, on the Red Sea coast, accounted for more than half of all those displaced throughout the country of some 43 million people.
"People are running for their lives and finding nowhere safe to go," IOM director general Amy Pope said in a statement.

A years-long civil war reignited in July when Yemen's internationally recognized government said it bombed the airport in the capital, Sanaa, which is under the control of the Iran-aligned Houthis, to prevent an Iranian plane carrying Houthi officials from landing.
The Houthis blamed Saudi Arabia, which backs the Yemeni government, for the attack and launched a series of strikes on Saudi targets.

The fighting escalated dramatically last month when the Houthis seized the country's entire Red Sea coast from government forces, which this week launched a counter-offensive with the support of a Saudi-led coalition, aiming to keep the Bab el-Mandeb strait open to shipping.

items: How Yemen’s Houthis could supercharge global trade disruptions
Britain to give limited military support to Saudi Arabia to defend against Houthi rebels

blocks.text: The Saudi Foreign Ministry has stressed the need to ensure freedom of navigation in the strait, a critical waterway off Yemen's southwestern coast that leads to the Red Sea. The Houthis had declared a naval blockade of Saudi Arabia in July.

"Riyadh apparently believes that diplomacy has failed and previous efforts to appease the Houthis have merely caused their ambitions to expand," Annelle Sheline, a non-resident senior fellow at Arab Center Washington DC, a think-tank, wrote this week.
"The Yemeni population, many of whom are already on the edge of survival, are paying the price."
Displaced Yemeni children from Al-Kadha, west of Taiz, sit in the Al-Akdaf camp in Taiz on Sept. 26. (Abdulnasser Alseddik/The Associated Press)
Food insecurity rising
The IOM said displaced Yemenis have sought shelter in makeshift camps, or with relatives and neighbours, in 10 governorates across the country so far.

More than 3,700 others have reached nearby Djibouti by sea. "They arrive exhausted, in overcrowded boats, with little food or water. Families are leaving with almost nothing. Many flee at night, carrying what they can. Most are women and children," the agency said.
Last week, the World Food Programme (WFP) also warned that food insecurity was "accelerating rapidly" in Yemen amid the escalating violence.
LISTEN | The rise of Yemen's Houthi rebels:
Front Burner28:07How did the Houthis become so powerful?

Nearly three out of four Yemeni families in areas where the WFP is able to operate "are unable to meet their basic food needs today," WFP official Matthew Hollingworth told reporters on Friday. "That's a record number for this year in just a few weeks."
Hollingworth also said many Yemenis have been forced to walk for "days without any water or food" to seek safety.
"Some are surviving largely on bread that they brought with them and a simple soup made from anything they can find — leaves, grass, et cetera."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Jillian Kestler-D'Amours is a senior writer at CBC based in Montreal. You can reach her at jillian.kestler-d.amours@cbc.ca.

articles.title: ‘Palestinians will bear the cost’: UK consulate in East Jerusalem prepares to shut its doors
articles.summary: Forced closure marks low point in UK-Israeli relations, with reports UK is considering retaliatory expulsion of Israeli diplomats from London
articles.byline: William Christou and Sufian Taha in Jerusalem

blocks.text: The UK consulate in East Jerusalem gave few signs that it was at the centre of a geopolitical controversy this week, with little movement around the high-walled building save the fluttering of the union jack and the occasional car exiting the compound.

The mission is to shut its doors on Thursday after Israel ordered its closure in response to a UK ban on trade with illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank and sanctions on those who help build or finance them.
The forced closure marked the lowest point in UK-Israeli relations for decades, with reports of the UK considering a retaliatory expulsion of 27 Israeli diplomats from London.

It would be the Palestinians who pay the price for the consulate’s closing, warned Amjad Iraqi, the International Crisis Group’s senior analyst on Israel and Palestine. The UK consulate in East Jerusalem is separate from the UK embassy in Tel Aviv – which remains open – and provides services to Palestinians in East Jerusalem, the West Bank and Gaza, services they will now lose.

“It’s quite telling that the Israeli government response was primarily about blocking the UK’s ability to support Palestinians, rather than the core of UK-Israeli relations themselves,” Iraqi said. “For [the Israeli] foreign minister, Gideon Sa’ar, the response is low-cost, in their minds it’s just Palestinians bearing the cost.”
Israel has already curtailed the diplomatic activities of countries like the Netherlands, Spain and Norway in the occupied West Bank.
Palestinian residents of Sheikh Jarrah, the East Jerusalem neighbourhood that is home to the consulate, appeared resigned when asked about the impact the closure might have on their lives.

“I mean, it was the British that were the basis of the issue wasn’t it? They were the ones who signed the Balfour declaration?” said Abu Abdo, a 79-year-old former repairman and resident of Sheikh Jarrah, referring to a 1917 document by the British foreign secretary Arthur Balfour, which expressed support for a Jewish state in Palestine.
It was a dramatic end for the consulate’s tenure in East Jerusalem, which since its move to the Sheikh Jarrah neighbourhood in 1967, had seen its fair share of political upheaval.

The UK government first bought the plot that would become its consulate in 1963, when East Jerusalem was still under Jordanian control. It was meant to be a direct liaison between the UK government and the Jordanian-administered West Bank and East Jerusalem. The compound took four years to build and was finally ready for the UK consul-general to move into by 1967.

But by the time the consul moved into, however, East Jerusalem was no longer under the control of the Jordanians. Just weeks before the new consul-general, John Henry Lewen, was to move into the building, the six-day war broke out, and Israel captured East Jerusalem from the Jordanian forces.

Lewen assumed his post at the present day consulate in a changed East Jerusalem under Israeli control. The consulate he oversaw occupied a unique position, as the UK did not recognise Jerusalem as being under any single country’s control.

As the UK foreign secretary told parliament in June 1967: “Our consul-general in Jerusalem is subordinate neither to the ambassador in Tel Aviv nor to the ambassador in Amman, but directly to the Foreign Office.”

Lewen’s tenure was marked by the political problems that plagued Jerusalem in the aftermath of the six-day war, and the birth of Israel. In 1969, a bomb was placed under the window of a consul secretary, harming no one but damaging the compound.
Years later, Palestinians would present their grievances to the British consulate in Sheikh Jarrah.

In 2017, protesters demonstrated outside the consulate to mark the centenary of the Balfour declaration. Men placed flags in the consululate windows reading “Balfour is a crime”, while schoolgirls carried thousands of letters written by Palestinian students asking Britain to apologise for the declaration.

This week, however, there was little sign of the political turmoil which the British consulate had waded through during its 60-years on the site. The neighbourhood, mostly made up of diplomatic missions and UN and other international organisations’ offices, was quiet.
Residents in the area expressed disappointment over what they saw as a lack of international support for the Palestinian people in recent years.
“We have seen very little but studies and words, no action from the international community,” said Abu Abdo.

articles.title: Overseas, Albanese sees ‘the very definition of climate injustice’ – but at home, he still wants coal
articles.summary:
It isn’t hard to see a contradiction between the PM’s message in Fiji and his opposition to legal action to stop a NSW coalmine

  • Get our

blocks.text: There are unlikely to be many bigger moments in Australian action on the climate crisis this year than a judgment by the high court on Wednesday.

In what is likely to prove a historic victory, the court sided with community members in the Hunter Valley to strike down a state regulator’s approval of a massive coalmine expansion that could have kept it operating until 2048.
This doesn’t happen every day and the central implication may yet have ramifications for other fossil fuel expansions.

If comments he made in May are taken at face value, the judgment may not please Anthony Albanese. Speaking on 2HD radio in Newcastle, the prime minister said the renewable transition was needed, but the government supported “existing industries” – that is, coal. He hoped the community group would lose as the Mount Pleasant mine expansion had “been through appropriate approvals”.
Well, not according to the high court.

Critics were quick to note the contrast between Albanese’s language opposing legal action to stop a coalmine and the message he delivered over the past three days at a climate conference in Fiji in preparation for the Cop31 summit in Turkey next month.

With Pacific island counterparts, the prime minister helped lead a delegation of about 50 dignitaries to the atoll and reef island nation of Tuvalu. Remote and tiny doesn’t do Tuvalu justice. It is described as the least visited country on the planet. Its land totals just 26 sq km, mostly narrow strips less than 2 metres above sea level. And the distance between the ocean and where most of its people live is getting smaller.

The rate of sea level rise around Tuvalu is about twice the global average, according to Nasa researchers. It means the edges of the nation are being eroded. The delegation was given a presentation illustrating the escalating threat of floods and storm surges washing through homes and infrastructure in the years ahead.

They also saw an example of what the country is doing to give itself the best chance to survive, visiting a land reclamation project on the main atoll of Funafuti that is mostly funded by the Australian government. Sand and gravel dredged from the lagoon is being used to create more than 20 hectares of new, higher ground.

blocks.caption: Australian PM Anthony Albanese and Chris Bowen, who is the president of the formal negotiations. Photograph: Huang/Menders/ZUMA Press Wire Service/Shutterstock

blocks.text: It is a project of hope, and a way to buy time. Possibly the most powerful moment on the quick trip came when the delegation was addressed by a 13-year-old, Melelusi Sokotia, who spoke powerfully about how her friends’ aspirations to be “teachers, doctors, builders” was being overridden by the basic question of whether they could “grow safely here in Tuvalu”.
Melelusi made a plea: “Please work together to protect small islands like ours.”

Later, back in Fiji, a leaders’ plenary heard from the Nepali foreign affairs minister, Shisir Khanal, who travelled for the pre-Cop meeting while his country staggers under the fallout from devastating flooding in August.

While the Pacific confronts a crisis of rising tides and more fierce cyclones, Khanal said Nepal was threatened by melting mountain ice bringing havoc from above. He pointed out the two threats were linked. Melting glaciers ultimately add to rising seas.

The minister said Nepal and the Pacific had something else in common. Neither contributes much at all to the global emissions causing these catastrophes. “Yet our people pay with their lives and development gains for a crisis they had no hand in creating,” he said. “This is the very definition of climate injustice.”

Albanese didn’t ignore this. He took Khanal’s message on enough to repeat part of it – that Nepal faced “extraordinarily traumatic” climate events despite running entirely on hydroelectricity – in a speech before flying out on Wednesday.

He described other examples of extreme events becoming less predictable and more intense as “the science told us would occur”. Climate change wasn’t an abstract future challenge, but “a daily reality that communities are dealing with”. “We saw that first-hand yesterday in Tuvalu,” Albanese said.

The point of Albanese’s speech was to argue for more international investment in the Pacific Resilience Facility, a fund designed to help people in the region cope and live that has received A$100m in Australian government support. He didn’t mention coal.
after newsletter promotion

But when held up against his commentary about the high court judgment, it wasn’t hard to see a screaming internal contradiction – a case of a leader sending conflicting messages to different audiences.

Does Albanese disagree with the high court judgment and still support coal expansion, given its contribution to the crisis he has accurately identified? There was no chance to test this on Wednesday. He left pre-Cop without taking questions from journalists.

None of this is to dismiss the work being done in Fiji. Despite the focus in Australia on the number of leaders who flew to Nadi and Funafuti for the meeting, there is little sense on the ground of it being the failure some have described.

Pre-Cop meetings usually barely make a blip on the public radar. They’re not meant to. They’re a chance for diplomats and bureaucrats to gather before the big end-of-year UN climate summit to lay groundwork and hopefully give it some chance of success.

This year is something else entirely. It is being held in the Pacific in an attempt to bring focus to the plight and needs of its peoples. In that, it has had at least some success. Ministers and their representatives from about 50 governments, including India and European nations, attended. So did thousands of diplomats and civil society members. They talked about Pacific needs.

The trip to Tuvalu included only two national leaders from outside the region – but the EU climate commissioner and the heads of the Asian Development Bank, the Green Climate Fund and the UN climate secretariat were on board. They saw and heard things people doing their jobs should see and hear.

Pacific national and community leaders are not uniform in their views, but they have largely applauded the focus and Australia’s support. Some are also critical, and cynical, about what they see as Australia’s hypocrisy on fossil fuels. That issue isn’t going away.

The ultimate test of this week’s success is whether it helps Cop31 pull off a meaningful agreement on issues to limit climate catastrophe and better direct finance to those that need it to survive, including in the Pacific. To describe that as a challenge in the current geopolitical climate is a spectacular understatement.

One upside of this week has been that the two men responsible for trying to pull that off – the president of the formal negotiations, Australia’s Chris Bowen, and the Turkish Cop31 president, Murat Kurum – have had a few days together to build their relationship and consider how they might do that.
And they have had a consistent and forceful reminder from those around them of why it matters.

items: Adam Morton is Guardian Australia’s climate and environment editor and writes the Clear Air newsletter

articles.title: Mayor of Turkish opposition stronghold Izmir defects to Erdoğan’s party
articles.summary:
Cemil Tugay joins ruling AKP after vowing he would never switch sides in boost for Turkish president

The mayor of Izmir, Turkey’s third city and an opposition stronghold, has defected to the…

blocks.text: The mayor of Izmir, Turkey’s third city and an opposition stronghold, has defected to the ruling AKP in a move hailed by Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, the Turkish president.
Turkey’s opposition is battling an increasingly intense crackdown, with a barrage of what observers say are politically motivated arrests and lawsuits targeting its mayors and elected officials.

Cemil Tugay’s decision to join the Islamic-rooted Justice and Development party (AKP) was announced by Erdoğan at a parliamentary group meeting in Ankara, where he welcomed the mayor amid a party-like atmosphere broadcast live on TV.
“I welcome Izmir mayor Cemil Tugay, who is today joining the AKP family,” Erdoğan said, presenting him with a party pin.

The scene caused anger and disgust on the streets of Izmir, a secular resort city of 4.5 million people on Turkey’s Aegean coast. Kadir Öztürk, 52, said of Tugay: “If I were his mother, I wouldn’t be able to show my face in public. His wife should divorce him. A person needs a backbone.” Tugay had vowed in January that he would never switch to the AKP and that if he did, his mother would disown him and his wife would leave him.
Taking control of the mayorship of Izmir, which has been governed by social democrats since 1999, is a big coup for Erdoğan, although opposition parties retain a majority on the city council.

The centre-left Republican People’s party (CHP) won a resounding victory in the local elections of March 2024, but it has since faced a growing intimidation campaign. Six of its provincial mayors have been arrested, including Ekrem İmamoğlu, the mayor of Istanbul, and 29 of its district mayors, according to figures published on Wednesday by the independent Diken news website.
There has been a growing number of defections to Erdoğan’s AKP, which had gained at least 17 opposition mayors before Tugay’s defection, the Medyascope news website said last week.
“This is a continuation of AKP’s strategy to reverse its major defeat in the 2024 local elections through force and repression,” said Berk Esen, a political analyst.
He said mayors were not changing sides because they had changed their ideology or been won over by the ruling party. Rather, many were doing it “out of fear”.
“This is a continuation of AKP’s strategy to reverse its major defeat in the 2024 local elections through force and repression,” added Esen.
after newsletter promotion
Tugay took office as mayor in April 2024 just after CHP’s local election victory, but in June he resigned from the party after its leadership was replaced in a controversial court ruling.

The former CHP leader, Özgür Özel, went on to found the Yeni party, taking 90 lawmakers with him and becoming Turkey’s main opposition. Tugay said he would remain independent, leading to rumours he was planning to defect.

On Tuesday Özel spoke of the campaign of pressure, threats and blackmail faced by Izmir’s elected officials. “Those who do not bow to this pressure ... will remain our brothers until the day they die. But those who sell out and leave are traitors,” he said.

articles.title: South Sudan's road to elections remains uncertain
articles.summary: South Sudan's first general election is set for December 22. Insecurity, political tensions and failure to begin voter registration have raised doubts over whether the poll can be held credibly.
articles.byline: James Shimanyula, Eddy Micah Jr., Isaac Mugabi, Isaac Kaledzi

image.caption: South Sudan's President Salva Kiir is set to contest in the December electionImage: Brian Inganga/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: South Sudan has scheduled a general election for December 22. It will be the first since the country gained independence from Sudan in 2011.

But political tensions are high as preparations lag. Debate over the election intensified after President Salva Kiir dissolved the transitional unity government on September 22 to form a caretaker administration.
Some voters are skeptical that the election will take place
Many are worried not only about the electoral logistics and insecurity in the country known for violent power struggles and political instability, according to Denis Logonyi, a Juba-based journalist.
Will elections happen in South Sudan?
To play this audio please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 audio

"People are having different views on these elections," Logonyi told DW. "You hear discussions in political circles and on social media, but ordinary people are not talking much about elections," Logonyi told DW.
"There has been no voter education, no voter registration, and only a few months remain," one voter said.
Another voter told DW that while South Sudanese are eager for a credible election process, the country was not adequately prepared.
Food prices are rising, civil servants are not being paid, and displaced people are struggling, the voter said.
Politicians admit to 'obstacles' but agree to adhere to election timeline
Political parties have until October 22 to present their manifestos and register.
On October 7, South Sudan concluded a two-week Inter-Party Dialogue. Thirty-nine parties took part in discussions on the critical issues ahead of the election.
The meeting was initiated by Kiir, with some civil society groups left out, according to Logonyi. Minister of Cabinet Affairs Dr. Martin Elia Lomuro outlined a few of the challenges.

"Delayed funding could severely affect civic education and election infrastructure. There is need for a clear legal framework to govern the participation of the country's administrative areas. The three administrative areas are not clearly reflected in the National Election Act, which is necessary for the election outcomes to be accepted," Lomuro said.

"A credible election requires security readiness throughout the entire cycle — including campaign rallies, polling stations, voting, counting, and results transmission. The unified security forces have not yet been fully deployed."

According to Albino Akol Atak, the Deputy Rapporteur of the Inter-Party Dialogue and Minister of Humanitarian Affairs and Disaster Management, the parties unanimously agreed to adhere to the election timeline.
"The election train has left the station, and it has no reverse gear. We are trying to smooth the pathway for this train to arrive on December 22, 2026, without obstacles," Atak said.
Meanwhile, Changkuoth Bichok Reath, Secretary General of the South Sudan Opposition Alliance (SSOA), said the success of the election would depend entirely on urgent, comprehensive collaboration.

"The South Sudan Opposition Alliance strongly believes that successfully conducting the election on December 22 requires coordinated, inclusive action from all national institutions, political parties, security actors, civil society, and other stakeholders," Reath said.

"Given the limited time remaining, priority should be placed on resolving outstanding legal issues and ensuring constructive dialogue among political actors. Furthermore, political parties must be funded to meet key requirements, because a lack of funding will only draw us backward."
Sudan has a history of planning then postponing elections
South Sudan has endured decades of conflict, from long wars that preceded independence to a devastating civil war that erupted just two years after it became a sovereign state.

Power-sharing transitional governments have been in place under fragile peace deals — including the Revitalized Peace Agreement of September 2018. Elections have repeatedly been planned then put off since.
Armed opposition groups remain active, and many citizens fear political tensions could trigger renewed violence.
"The absence of Riek Machar from the political process is a major concern," Logonyi said. "If there is to be an election or a meaningful political dialogue, many believe he has to be part of it."

The 2018 power-sharing deal that saw Kiir become president and Machar — his long-time rival and main opposition leader — vice president briefly stabilized the country. However, tensions between the two persisted.
In March 2025, Machar was placed under house arrest and later put on trial for offences that include treason and murder.

blocks.caption: South Sudan's former Vice President Riek Machar pictured in court in Juba in September 2025Image: Peter Louis Gume/AFP

blocks.text: Key conditions envisioned for elections under peace deal not fulfilled yet

"The government has demonstrated that it is keen for the election to happen," said Wambui Njehu Nzigo, an analyst with Control Risks. "But there are important processes that have not yet taken place."

The lack of voter registration is among the biggest concerns. "If elections are to take place soon, you would expect there already to be a voter register," Nzigo said. "There is very little time for that to happen."
Security reforms required under the 2018 peace deal are unfinished. These include the unification of armed groups to create the conditions for a stable transition.
Analysts have long been warning that the legitimacy of any election without these key issues being addressed would be undermined.

"The elections would be taking place in an environment where there is still active fighting in some parts of the country," Nzigo said. "The fact that the main opposition leader is under house arrest raises questions about whether this will be a true competition."
According to Logonyi, civil society groups are calling for greater dialogue, political inclusion and protections for journalists and activists before the vote is held.
How instability persists in South Sudan
Ongoing flooding could interfere with the vote
South Sudan is facing severe flooding, displacement and food insecurity. These conditions could make it difficult for some citizens to reach polling stations, Nzigo said.
For communities displaced by conflicts in particular, there's uncertainty over how they would register and cast their ballots.
Floodwaters, oil and health fears in South Sudan

Analysts argue that the focus should be not only on ensuring elections take place, but also on creating conditions that make them credible.

articles.title: Nepal search for missing after flash floods officially ends, with nearly 5,300 people still unaccounted for
articles.summary: The families of thousands of people who remain missing in Nepal weeks after catastrophic floods devastated the country have expressed mixed feelings after the government said this week that it is…

image.caption: A search and rescue team member, along with a sniffer dog, looks for missing people along the banks of the Trishuli River in Nepal's Nuwakot district, on Sept. 30. (Prakash Mathema/AFP/Getty Images)

blocks.text: World·New

The families of thousands of people who remain missing in Nepal weeks after catastrophic floods devastated the country have expressed mixed feelings after the government said this week that it is stopping the search for victims.
While many families are upset by decision, others need death certificates for insurance, other purposes

The office of Prime Minister Balendra Shah decided on Monday that search and rescue operations for victims of the Aug. 26 floods will cease. Instead, authorities will concentrate on rehabilitation and reconstruction, including restoring roads and bridges cut off by floods, particularly in remote areas where damaged infrastructure has made aid deliveries difficult.
Rescuers have so far recovered the bodies of at least 1,455 people, but 5,285 others remain missing, including hundreds of foreign nationals.

Two weeks ago, Global Affairs Canada told CBC News that it was aware of 29 Canadians and permanent residents in Nepal and the Tibet autonomous region whose whereabouts and well-being after the flash floods have not yet been confirmed, but cautioned that the number could fluctuate based on new information. CBC News has requested an update from the department, but did not immediately hear back.

Hopes for finding survivors were briefly revived after two Nepalese workers were rescued from an underground tunnel at the Trishuli hydropower project on Sept. 4, and again two days later when rescuers found a Chinese man at the same location.
2 more people found alive 10 days after devastating Nepal floods
Families of victims have held protests and vigils in Nepal, calling for search efforts to be improved.

"I am so angry at the government for giving up on search and rescue with thousands of people still missing. I just don't understand how they can do that when we still have hope left that our loved one can still be found," said Usha Khatri, who has spent days searching for her husband in multiple towns where the river flows and bodies have been recovered.
A general view on Sept. 28 shows damaged houses covered in sludge in the aftermath of the Aug. 26 flash flood, at Betrawati Bazaar in Nepal's Rasuwa district. (Prakash Mathema/AFP/Getty Images)
During her ongoing search, she has checked photos of bodies that were recovered but buried for preservation until identification is made.
"Either they have to give up the body or show some solid proof that my husband is gone, and only then can they declare him dead," Khatri said.

"They have abandoned us and they should not have stopped the search," said Mahesh Shrestha, whose brother was an engineer at a hydropower plant that was hit. "Our family demands they continue looking for him."
Death certificate, burial requirements
Others welcomed the decision and said they are seeking government-issued death certificates.

"After so many days and weeks, there is little or no hope of finding anyone alive. We are sure that none of our family members survived and we are just looking for a closure," said Nirajan Poudel, who lost five family members in the flood.
Satellite images show glacier collapse that triggered flooding at Nepal-China border

Several people whose relatives remain missing have performed symbolic funerals. Cremation is an important final rite in the Hindu tradition and performing the ceremony even without a body provides a sense of spiritual release for some families.

Poudel said the government has so far refused to issue death certificates, saying laws need to be amended first. Death certificates are necessary in Nepal for families to receive compensation, insurance and inherit properties.
Nepal's government did not immediately respond to a request by The Associated Press for more information about the death certificates.
The government estimates reconstruction and recovery will cost $4.77 billion US. Nearly 33,000 people have been affected and about 7,500 homes were damaged or destroyed.
With files from CBC News

articles.title: China's Golden Week reveals cautious consumer spending despite travel surge
articles.summary: Chinese visitors are returning from trips after the 13-day Golden Week holiday. Their subdued spending has raised fresh questions about domestic demand in the world's second-largest economy.

image.caption: Golden Week is typically a time of high levels of travel and spending in ChinaImage: Ryohei Moriya/The Yomiuri Shimbun/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Ya Xi just returned to Shanghai on a red-eye flight after her Golden Week trip to Southeast Asia. "I can stay up all night for a cheaper ticket," she told DW.
She was among the 31.19 million passengers who traveled during the 13-day holiday period that followed the Mid-Autumn Festival on September 25 and China's National Day on October 1.
Many of them spent their budgets more cautiously this year.

"I earn less this year, so I'm lowering my budget for this year's Golden Week," said Xi, who is in her mid-20s. "I spent 5,000 yuan (about €660) on my flight, which was the largest expense of my trip."

Golden Week is viewed as a barometer of the Chinese economy with Beijing using it as an opportunity to showcase the world's second-largest economy's spending power. State media, for instance, reported a record-breaking 25.204 million passenger trips on China's railway network on October 1.

blocks.caption: State media reported record-breaking train passenger numbers over Golden WeekImage: CFOTO/picture alliance

blocks.text: However, early data indicated more moderate spending per traveler and broadly flat passenger traffic, according to Citigroup analysts. Traffic volume during the first four days of the holiday rose just 0.1% year over year, far below the 3.5% increase seen during this year's Labor Day vacation.
Selective spending among younger consumers
Lizzi C. Lee, a fellow on the Chinese Economy at the Asia Society Policy Institute, told DW that Chinese consumers are becoming increasingly selective.
"My read is that people are willing to get out and spend. They're just being much more careful about how much and what they spend on," Lee said.

But being cautious doesn't mean staying frozen, she added. "They'll spend on travel, concerts, restaurants, experiences, and tech… if they think it's worth it, they'll economize pretty aggressively elsewhere."

Xi's Golden Week trip followed this pattern, paying more for significant experiences and economizing elsewhere: "Eat, drink, and be merry," said Xi, indicating she was willing to spend more on food. For example, she set a 200-yuan (about €26) budget for each meal.

blocks.caption: Many Chinese are opting for budget travel options instead of luxury tripsImage: CFOTO/picture alliance

blocks.text: Guo-Chen Wang, an associate research fellow at the Chung-Hua Institution for Economic Research, told DW that the budget-travel trend among Chinese visitors was ongoing.
"The number of trips is increasing, butconsumption remains strained, as I saw in past years," Wang said.

The Chinese government attempted to boost Golden Week spending by providing coupons worth more than 310 million yuan (€41.2 million). Wang remained unconvinced about the effectiveness of such a measure: "That's an old solution to an old problem."
A sign of China's weak domestic demand

It isn't the first Golden Week to see weak consumer demand. During last year's holiday season, the average spending per trip was 911.04 yuan (around €121), the lowest in three years, according to Reuters.
"Beijing still believes the low spending was due to consumers' reluctance [to spend]," Wang said. "In fact, we think Chinese consumers are unable to spend."

While savings kept increasing in Chinese banks, Wang said the vast majority of the savings are held by a small proportion of the population. "In other words, the majority of Chinese people don't have savings."
"The fundamental issue is the wealth gap in Chinese society," he said. "I don't know whether Beijing really neglected this problem or was simply unwilling to face it."
China’s tourism surge: expansion, regulation and challenges

A recent International Monetary Fund publication, Toward a New Economic Growth Model for China, once again noted that China's domestic demand has been weak since the pandemic, when the property market correction began.
Lee, however, saw weak spending during this Golden Week as a confidence problem.

"Theproperty downturnhas hit household wealth, income and job expectations are still pretty soft, and several years of weak prices have trained people to wait for discounts and hunt for value," she told DW.
Tightened cross-border rules played a limited role

Weeks before the Golden Week, China's tightened travel restrictions took effect on September 15. The new restrictions ban citizens from leaving the country if they are deemed to pose a risk to national as well as industrial or technological security.

Wang expected Chinese tourists to turn to domestic travel under the new rules, but the outcome did not match his expectations. "The volume of travel abroad is in fact growing, though not by much," he said.
Lee said she saw little evidence of a broad chilling effect on ordinary outbound tourism, with the Golden Week numbers serving as a "useful reality check."
"The September rules give authorities more room to verify travel purposes and ask for additional information in some cases," Lee said. "They still leave plenty of room for ordinary overseas tourism."
Mi Tang in Taipei contributed to this article.

The Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) observed that there were more than 20 Chinese vessels spotted in the vicinity waters of Pag-asa Island, Palawan on Wednesday, GMA News' Ivan Mayrina reported in "24 Oras."
The ships that are from the Chinese Maritime Militia and the Chinese Coast Guard were hovering in the island’s waters.
The PCG said they observed that there were more ships earlier and that some already left Pag-asa Island’s waters.
Last month, according to the Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP), there have been more than 100 Chinese ships recorded within the West Philippine Sea (WPS).

“Month of September, we monitored 101 different vessels ng Coast Guard at ng PLA (People’s Liberation Army) Navy. Ito naman, if we look at it over a longer period of time, let's say six month period kagaya ng first sem assessment natin, na dumami ang kanilang Coast Guard vessels...based on their posture, they will be focusing on enforcing maritime law, 'yung maling pananaw niya sa maritime law, utilizing 'yung China Coast Guard ships para i-push nila ang kanilang mandato,” AFP spokesperson for the WPS Rear Admiral Roy Vincent Trinidad said.

(For the month of September, we monitored 101 different vessels of the Coast Guard and of the PLA Navy. Here, if we look at it over a longer period of time, let's say six month period of the first semester assessment, there have been more Coast Guard vessels… based on their posture, they will be focusing on enforcing maritime law, their wrong view of the maritime law, utilizing the Chinese Coast Guard ships to push their mandate.)
Pag-asa Island is a hotspot for these Chinese ships, together with Escoda Shoal and Bajo de Masinloc.
Last week, Chinese Coast Guard vessels blocked Philippine officials from responding to a Chinese fishing vessel performing illegal dynamite fishing at the Sandy Cay near Pag-asa Island.
Meanwhile, PCG Commandant Admiral Ronnie Gil Gavan led the activation of the Coast Guard Auxiliary District in the Kalayaan Island District on Wednesday.
Gavan said that these citizens have an important role in overseeing the country’s sovereignty.
“Hindi tayo nahihinaan ng loob. We will match them hangga't kaya natin. Ship for ship, patrol for patrol. 'Yung mga maling naratibo nila, kino-correct natin sa tamang naratibo,” Trinidad said.
(Our resolve will not weaken. We will match them as much as we can. Ship for ship, patrol for patrol. Their wrong narratives, we will correct it with the right ones.) — Jean Mangaluz/BAP, GMA News

articles.title: Sara, Rodrigo Duterte hid P96M through unutilized manager’s checks — prosecution
articles.summary: Senator-judge Vicente “Tito” Sotto III claims the practice is called 'tinikling' in banking circles

blocks.text: VEEP. Vice President Sara Duterte addresses an event in Pagadian City, Zamboanga del Sur, in late May 2026.
Sara Duterte Facebook page
Senator-judge Vicente “Tito” Sotto III claims the practice is called 'tinikling' in banking circles

items: House prosecutors presented P96 million in manager's checks to establish a pattern of concealment involving Vice President Sara Duterte and former President Rodrigo Duterte.

Bank of the Philippine Islands confirmed a joint time deposit account for the Dutertes, which was opened in 2010 and reached P41.72 million after multiple renewals, with funds later converted into manager's checks.

Senator-judges questioned the relevance of the transactions, with discussions on the practice of leaving manager's checks unutilized, while it was noted that the P96 million was not reflected in the Vice President's Statements of Assets, Liabilities and Net Worth.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – House prosecutors on Wednesday, October 7, presented P96 million in manager’s checks as they sought to establish a “pattern of concealment” involving the year-end balances of Vice President Sara Duterte and her father, former president Rodrigo Duterte.

On Day 35 of Duterte’s impeachment trial, Bank of the Philippine Islands (BPI) division head for central Manila branches Marwin Galvez confirmed the father and daughter had a joint time deposit account opened in January 2010 with a principal amount of P40.65 million.
The account, opened at the BPI-Julia Vargas branch, was renewed 12 times and reached P41.72 million after its final rollover in February 2011.
When the time deposit matured in March 2011, a settlement account was opened and the funds were converted on the same day into a manager’s check for P41.72 million.
Defense lawyer Michael Poa initially objected to the presentation of the bank records, questioning their relevance to the case.
Senator-judge Panfilo “Ping” Lacson then asked the House prosecutors whether they were trying to establish through their direct examination a “pattern aimed at proving concealment.”
Private prosecutor James Bryan Ibrahim Alih answered in the affirmative.
“We wanted to establish a pattern,” Alih said. “Our point is that the manager’s checks being circulated did not reflect on the year-end balance because they were considered ‘floating.’”

In the interjections of Senate impeachment court presiding officer Francis “Chiz” Escudero, Galvez explained that when a manager’s check is issued, the amount is deducted from the client’s account and transferred to the bank’s settlement account — an account separate from the customer’s account.

The funds will then remain in the settlement account to back the manager’s check while it is unitized. If the manager’s check remains unused for six months, the amount may be returned to the client’s account, Galvez said.

“A similar time deposit that became a manager’s check in the amount of P55 million was also running during the same years, simultaneously with this P41 million. It’s a total of P96 million,” Alih said.
The prosecution presented three more manager’s checks dated April 19, 2012 and October 17, 2012; and October 7, 2013 purchased by the Duterte patriarch. It has a total value of P41.72 million.

Senator-judge Bam Aquino said it was the first time he had heard of such transactions and asked Galvez whether deliberately purchasing manager’s checks and leaving them unutilized was a known practice in banking circles “to keep money.”

Galvez said it was usual for some manager’s checks to be unutilized and requested to be returned. However, he could not determine whether some clients were deliberately purchasing manager’s checks for the purpose of having the funds returned after six months.
“I cannot answer… if some clients are purposely buying manager’s check to return it after six months,” said Galvez.

Senator-judge Vicente “Tito” Sotto III later said the practice is allegedly called “tinikling” in banking circles. Tinikling is a traditional Philippine folk dance wherein a dancer or dancers step, hop, and jump between two moving bamboo poles.

Senator-judge Sherwin Gatchalian said he reviewed Duterte’s Statements of Assets, Liabilities and Net Worth (SALNs) for 2010 and 2011 but did not find the P96-million time deposit accounts in the documents.
Poa came to the defense of Duterte, saying she may have been unaware of the accounts.

“The operative word is if she’s aware… And as we demonstrated during cross, all these time deposits and transactions wala pong prima ng bise presidente (there’s no signature of the Vice President) and all off them were done by the former president,” Poa added.
The Vice President declared zero cash in hand and bank deposits in her SALNs from 2019 to 2024. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Ten people linked to Kenya's first-ever Ebola case quarantined as screening concerns grow
articles.summary: The patient passed through multiple cities in DR Congo, drove to Uganda and eventually flew to Kenya.

blocks.text: Ten people who came into contact with a man who died of Ebola in Kenya have been quarantined, health officials in the East African nation say.
They are also trying to trace 57 other contacts of the Kenyan patient after he travelled from the Democratic Republic of Congo, dying in hospital in Nairobi on Monday.
This is the East African nation's first-ever Ebola case and there is now growing concern about the country's screening measures.

The Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention chief has told the BBC that despite being sick for a month, the patient passed through multiple cities in DR Congo, driving to Uganda and eventually flying to Kenya without his sickness being detected.

"We know that he left Buta, a city in [northern] DR Congo, to drive to Kisangani. And from Kisangani, he took a flight to Beni. From Beni, he drove to Uganda. And from Uganda, he took a flight to Nairobi," Jean Kaseya told the BBC's Focus on Africa programme.
"What are symptoms he was presenting? Why was he not detected?" he asked.
The Ebola virus spreads through contact with infected bodily fluids such as blood or vomit.

The current outbreak in DR Congo, which began in May, has been caused by the Bundibugyo species of Ebola, which is relatively rare, with no approved vaccine or treatment - though trials are under way.
Kaseya said the Africa CDC was investigating the case, alongside the Congolese authorities. A team from the organisation was also due to meet the Kenyan health authorities.
Kenya's health ministry official Patrick Amoth said the patient might have passed screening after taking medications that masked his symptoms.
After arriving at the airport in Kenya's capital, he was transferred by a relative to a hospital in the city where he died, and was buried on Tuesday in line with health safety guidelines.
Kenyan authorities have urged people not to panic, with the health ministry assuring of heightened surveillance at airports and border crossings.
But Dr Dennis Miskellah, a representative from Kenya's main doctors' union, said the Ebola case did not come as a surprise to him and most health workers.
He told the BBC's Newsday programme that he had witnessed "lapses" at various border points, including with neighbouring Uganda and Tanzania, as well as at Kenyan's main airport.

"How could you have been sick for almost a month plus in DR Congo, come all the way to the country through not just any small border point, but the main entry point, the main gateway into the country and pass unnoticed?
"That's the question that most Kenyans are asking."
The health ministry says it has intensified measures to contain the spread, with a joint response involving county administrations, humanitarian partners and others.
President William Ruto has said that surveillance and rapid response teams are on the ground, building on the systems that the country adopted following the outbreak in DR Congo in May.
His spokesman said Kenya had the capacity to detect, isolate and manage suspected cases, adding that so far more than 650,000 travellers had been screened and 267 samples tested.
Facilities in four main hospitals have been designated for the management of Ebola patients, including at the Nairobi Hospital, where the first Ebola patient died.

In June, a US plan to establish an Ebola treatment facility at a military base in the central Kenyan town of Nanyuki sparked concern, with Kenyans reacting furiously about the risks of cross-border infection. The plan was halted by the courts.

On Wednesday, Health Minister Aden Duale told local television station NTV that pending the outcome of the court case, the government was considering turning the facility into the "first" infectious disease hospital in the region, to deal with outbreaks like Ebola.
More than 4,000 people have died from Ebola in DR Congo this year, in what is the second most deadly known outbreak of the disease.
Shortly after DR Congo declared an outbreak of Ebola in May, it was also reported in Uganda, where two people died.
However, the World Health Organization (WHO) declared that county free of the disease in August.
On Tuesday, Uganda's health ministry emphasised that the country remained free of Ebola and was continuing to "maintain strong surveillance measures to protect public health".
It said the Kenyan Ebola patient had transited through the country for less than 24 hours and screening teams had "observed he had a normal temperature at the time of departure".
According to Africa CDC chief, his organisation was working with all the countries in the region to reinforce response mechanisms.
Kasiye said Kenya was "well prepared" and was therefore able to immediately receive the case, "but it is not the case for all other countries".
"It means the regional approach is more important today to stop this outbreak."
However, Kasiye said there was no quick testing available at border points and the taking of temperatures was unreliable as medication is able to stop a fever.
"I have to make it clear - we don't have diagnostics to test for Ebola. It's just about temperature," he said.

Dr Miskellah, from the Kenyan doctors' union, said he was concerned that governments were counting on the "honesty and full co-operation of the travellers to self-declare, to say the truth" about their health.
This was however undermined by a lack of proper health education to destigmatise the virus, meaning people often wanted to hide their symptoms, he said.

articles.title: German spy scandal threatens national security
articles.summary: The arrest of Germany's former intelligence chief August Hanning could undermine national security, experts warn, as allies may reconsider their intelligence relationships.

image.caption: The arrest of August Hanning, former president of Germany's foreign intelligence service, the Bundesnachrichtendienst (BND), is threatening to cause a major rupture in Germany's intelligence relationshipsImage: Sebastian Gollnow/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: The arrest of August Hanning, former president of Germany's foreign intelligence service, the Bundesnachrichtendienst (BND), and his former chief-of-staff, Manfred D.*, is threatening to cause a major rupture in Germany's intelligence relationships, according to analysts, as the full scale of the scandal begins to be understood abroad.

Manfred D. is accused of having sold around 2,000 highly classified documents to Hanning over a period of 12 years, long after the latter stepped down from the BND in 2005, after seven years as its chief. Manfred D. continued to serve all of Hanning's successors, including the current BND chief Martin Jäger, before retiring in March this year.
On one occasion, the state prosecutor said, Hanning "used classified intelligence provided by Manfred D. to draft an analysis for an officer of a foreign intelligence service."
DW's Michaela Küfner looks at Germany's espionage scandal

According to Florian Flade, reporter for public broadcaster ARD, most of these documents were weekly intelligence briefings delivered to the German government by the BND, including the latest findings from partner intelligence agencies in other countries.

"This is very, very sensitive because it involves partner agencies in other countries," Flade told DW's Berlin Briefing podcast. "And we heard this also involves information about the Iranian nuclear program, the Russian military, also the Ukraine war."
Broken trust, broken credibility

Some pundits now say that the biggest concern is what conclusions the intelligence agencies of allied countries will draw from this affair. In the past, the US CIA is known to have shared information on radical Islamists in Germany, which possibly helped to prevent terrorist attacks in the country.

If it now emerges that information was leaving the BND via Hanning, that relationship could be undermined, particularly if it was also eventually ending up in the hands of the intelligence agencies of Russia and China (though there is no suggestion of that as yet).

"There's huge damage being done not only to the outer appearance and image of the BND," said Flade. "There's a damage assessment now happening within the BND. Also, they're talking to partners about this because they want to know if their information was given to other countries."

That could also potentially have consequences for Germany's national security in the growing confrontation with Russia. The BND, which is currently subject to more legal restrictions than other intelligence agencies around the world, considers its relationship with its US counterpart as vital.

"There might be a change in the amount of information that is coming from the US and others," Flade added, though ultimately, he pointed out, it might be difficult for the BND to know what they're not being told.
Security loopholes in Germany's parliament spark concern

Only a day before the scandal broke, current BND President Martin Jäger reiterated his concern that Germany could slide into a military conflict with Russia, telling a parliamentary hearing that the Kremlin was already waging a "shadow war," and that further military rearmament was "unfortunately necessary" — though he did say that there was currently no indication of active preparations from Russia.

Flade said that, behind the scenes, Jäger is furious about the leak of information from Manfred D., and called a meeting on Tuesday of all BND officials to underline the how serious the consequences of sharing information could be. New internal security measures are also being put in place.

The new case could not have come at a worse time for Jäger or the BND. For one thing, new laws are currently being prepared to expand the agency's powers, partly to improve the BND's standing among its foreign partners.

For another thing, another BND agent, Carsten L. and a businessman named Arthur E., are currently on trial in Berlin on treason charges for passing on classified documents to the Russian secret service in 2022.

blocks.caption: Florian Flade is an espionage expert and guest in DW's Berlin Briefing podcast this weekImage: DW

blocks.text: New rules for old officials?

The case has also raised questions about what former intelligence officials should and shouldn't be allowed to do once they leave office. Hanning founded his own security consultancy business after he left the BND, for which he apparently used his contacts and knowledge to advise his clients. This is legal and tolerated, but many think it shouldn't be.

Timo Lange, of the NGO LobbyControl, said that the Hanning case shows why former intelligence officials must be prevented from working as security consultants in any capacity for the rest of their lives.

"It is fundamentally problematic when high-ranking officials from the intelligence or military sectors, after leaving government service, act as consultants for various — and in some cases unknown — clients from abroad," Lange said in a statement. "This is an obvious gateway for illegitimate foreign influence and jeopardizes the security interests of Germany and the European Union."

But as Flade pointed out, Hanning's career path is not exactly unusual. "These people are trying to just make some money with what they can do best, which is networking and then selling the security assessments that they do," he said. "And yeah, working for companies or even for other countries as a consultant."
Edited by Rina Goldenberg

Editor's note: DW follows the German press code, which stresses the importance of protecting the privacy of suspected criminals or victims and urges us to refrain from revealing full names in such cases.

articles.title: Sara Duterte denies hand in joint bank account with dad Rodrigo
articles.summary: The defense panel on Wednesday said Vice President Sara Duterte does not recall having or participating in transactions involving a joint Bank of the Philippine Islands (BPI) account under her name…

blocks.text: The defense panel on Wednesday said Vice President Sara Duterte does not recall having or participating in transactions involving a joint Bank of the Philippine Islands (BPI) account under her name and that of her father, former President Rodrigo Duterte, which was supposedly used to purchase a P41.7-million manager’s check.

Defense counsel Michael Poa made the statement on Day 35 of the impeachment trial after Senator-Judge Risa Hontiveros asked whether the flagged P41.7-million manager’s check was owned and controlled by Rodrigo Duterte, and not the Vice President.
“To better phrase it, our client does not have any recollection of this account,” Poa said, adding that the matter was only raised during a previous hearing of the House Quad Committee.

“Nung lumabas ang mga accounts, tinitignan namin itong mga accounts na ito and I was asked by the Vice President to verify kasi hindi niya natatandaan na may ganitong account at wala daw siyang transaksyon,” he added.
(When these accounts surfaced, we examined them, and the Vice President asked me to verify them because she did not recall having such an account and said she had no transactions involving it.)
If that is the case, Hontiveros asked whether the Vice President was attributing the flagged transactions solely to her father.
“Ang sinasabi lang po niya ay wala siyang naging partisipasyon dito,” Poa answered.
(What she is saying is that she had no participation in these.)
The defense counsel also said they did not wish to prejudice the former president or his counsel regarding whatever legal defenses they may have concerning the accounts.
The prosecution earlier flagged a P41.7-million manager’s check linked to Rodrigo and Sara Duterte that was supposedly “floating” for years and was not reflected in year-end balances.

A prosecution witness, BPI division head for Central Manila branches Marwin Galvez, confirmed the existence of a joint peso time deposit opened on January 22, 2010, at the bank’s Julia Vargas Branch in Pasig City under the name “Rodrigo Roa Duterte or Rodrigo Roa Duterte and Sara Z. Duterte,” with a principal amount of P40.65 million.
Galvez said the time deposit had 12 rollover periods or renewals. At the last renewal in February 2011, the amount had increased to P41.7 million, including interest.

The witness said that in March 2011, a credit and debit memo showed that a manager’s check worth P41.7 million was purchased. The manager’s check, however, remained unutilized after its six-month validity period.

The transaction was among the financial records being presented in support of Article 2 of the Articles of Impeachment, which centers on the allegation that Duterte accumulated unexplained wealth and failed to fully disclose her assets and interests in her SALNs.

Private prosecutor James Bryan Alih said the prosecution intended to prove a “pattern,” in which a transaction in 2011 moved around for several more years and was later used to purchase insurance policies.

Responding to an inquiry by Senator-Judge Francis Pangilinan, Senate impeachment court presiding officer Francis Escudero confirmed that while the signature of the Vice President did not appear in any transaction involving account ending in 9539.

"We confirm, as well, the statement made by Attorney James that the signature of the Vice President appears in the document that opened the account, as well as in the signature sheet or KYC (know-your-client) documents for July 2020 and July 25, 2017.
The signature of the Vice President also appears in the KYC document for June 13, 2023, Escudero said.
'Why involve Rodrigo?'
In his interjection, Senator-Judge Robin Padilla questioned the repeated mention of former President Rodrigo Duterte’s name during Galvez’s direct examination.

“Kanina pa po kasi nababanggit ang pangalan ng dating Pangulong Rodrigo Roa Duterte. Hindi ko alam bakit kailangang idamay pa dito ang matanda. Masasabi po niyan, may ginawa bang kalokohan ’yung matanda?” Padilla asked.
(The name of former President Rodrigo Roa Duterte has been mentioned repeatedly. I don’t know why it is necessary to drag the old man into this. Did the old man do anything wrong?)
The bank official answered, “Not in the documents that we submitted, Your Honor.”— MCG, GMA News
Follow GMA News Online on Facebook for real-time news and developments in the Philippines and around the world.

articles.title: France suspends use of stun grenades against protesters
articles.summary: France is suspending the use of stun grenades against protesters as allegations of student brutality draw more anger. Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu is also set to address the nation later this…

image.caption: Police have fired tear gas to break up demonstrations in several French cities since protests beganImage: Fred Tanneau/AFP

blocks.text: France is suspending the use of stun grenades at student-led protests as people report allegations of police brutality at demonstrations that have widened over the weeks.
"I am suspending their use in the high school student protests until the facts of the incident have been clarified," Interior Minister Laurent Nunez told RTL radio broadcaster on Wednesday.
He emphasized that the suspension was "only for the high school student protests" and for "just long enough to understand what happened."
Nunez announced the measure to curb growing anger after reports about teenagers having lost their hands or teeth during protests drew anger.

French regional newspaper La Voix du Nord reported this Monday that a 15-year-old had his hand and a part of his lower arm blown off after picking up a police stun grenade that then detonated during protests.
Last week, a 14-year-old student in northwest Paris was hit in the jaw as a tear gas canister was fired during protests, with the officer having been charged on Tuesday.
The order also comes before an address by Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu to protesters later Wednesday evening.
More to follow.
