articles.title: How did Christa Pike survive execution attempt - and what happens next?
articles.summary: The convicted killer of Colleen Slemmer is said to be awake and speaking in hospital in Tennessee after surviving two lethal injections.
articles.byline: James FitzGerald, Kayla Epstein, Brandon Drenon

blocks.text: Watch: What we know about Christa Pike’s "unprecedented" recovery after failed execution
ByJames FitzGeraldKayla Epstein and Brandon Drenon
Convicted murderer Christa Pike has woken up and begun speaking from her hospital bed almost a week after authorities in the US state of Tennessee botched her execution, her lawyers said.
Pike, 50, was sent to hospital after surviving two attempts to execute her via lethal injection for the 1995 murder of a 19-year-old she met at a summer camp for troubled teens.
An independent review of what went wrong in the Nashville execution chamber on 30 September has been ordered by Tennessee Governor Bill Lee.
He has also halted executions in the state for the rest of the year.
Warning: This article contains details that readers may find distressing
How did Pike survive?
The Tennessee Department of Correction is yet to say why the execution did not go as planned, though it has defended the method it used.

Dr Joel Zivot, an anaesthesiologist advising Pike's defence team, says it was not the case that Pike had some "special immunity" but suggested it was simply that not enough of the drug pentobarbital reached her bloodstream to kill her.
Pike was injected with a second dose of the drug, according to the prison authorities' protocol, after the first did not kill her.
In interviews with the BBC, Zivot has suggested the pentobarbital was more likely to have spread across the tissue under Pike's skin than to have entered her bloodstream.
"Most of the pentobarbital, instead of circulating in her body, ended up in her arms, and that's how she lived," Zivot said.

Pike's medical condition of thrombocytosis, a blood-clotting condition, was highlighted in advance by Pike's legal team as an additional issue that could scupper the process. Before the attempted execution, they had filed a legal case challenging the injection protocol.
If clots of blood formed at the injection site as a result of thrombocytosis, they would potentially have blocked the chemical from entering her veins, the lawyers warned.

As the attempted execution took place, prison officials used at least seven needles on Pike during their efforts to establish intravenous (IV) lines, Pike's lawyers said afterwards. The woman could simultaneously be heard "crying, whimpering, and breathing loudly".
May Martinez, the mother of Colleen Slemmer who was murdered by Pike and her then-boyfriend, told NBC the failed execution had been "a mess".

blocks.caption: Image caption, Colleen Slemmer was tortured and brutally killed by Pike and her then-boyfriend

blocks.text: Image source, Family handout
Colleen Slemmer was tortured and brutally killed by Pike and her then-boyfriend
The Tennessee Department of Correction has defended the method it used, saying "the protocol does not allow for additional procedures beyond what was carried out".
The state protocol does not clearly specify what should happen if an inmate remains alive after a second dose, according to the AP news agency.

After it became clear that Pike was not going to die from the two doses, she was taken to hospital for life-saving treatment. States have a legal obligation not to deny medical treatment to prisoners.
What is pentobarbital?

Pentobarbital is a potent sedative that slows down the body, including the nervous system. Doctors sometimes use it as a treatment for certain conditions, but in high doses it can also be used as a lethal injection to cause death.

Its use in lethal injections came under renewed scrutiny last year after a US federal government review during the Biden administration raised concerns about the drug's potential for "unnecessary pain and suffering".
The Biden government banned its use in federal executions, but that did not bind individual states such as Tennessee, which can choose their own methods.
In recent years, states have found some drugs needed for lethal injections harder to come by, because pharmaceutical companies have opposed the use of their products for such purposes.
The Tennessee correction department has not specifically addressed an allegation from Pike's legal team that the pentobarbital it used was "degraded".
But the department said the lethal injection chemical had "consistently been effective".
What happens next?
The full picture of Pike's current physical condition is unknown.

Although she was said to be awake and speaking in hospital as of 6 October, is it unclear whether she has any long-term health defects. Medical staff have been working to clear the drug from her body, a process that they expected to take about a week. She has been removed from a ventilator.
Zivot said Pike had been able to communicate in a "basic way", including by giving her name and making an incorrect attempt to guess the date.
Meanwhile she is reportedly handcuffed to her bed.
Watch: Witnesses recount Christa Pike's failed execution attempt
There is then the question of what happens to Pike next.

Authorities are yet to say whether they will try again to execute Pike, though executions in the state have been paused for the rest of the year. Meanwhile, it has been announced that the state's Department of Correction Commissioner Frank Strada is stepping down.
Pike's lawyers have made repeated calls for Lee, the state governor, to commute her sentence to the lesser punishment of life in prison without the possibility of parole.
Historically, the US Supreme Court has not halted second attempts at executions, said John Mills, a lawyer who works with inmates sentenced to death.

In 2024, it allowed Alabama to proceed with a second execution of Kenneth Eugene Smith, using an experimental oxygen deprivation method, after their attempt to kill him by lethal injection failed two years earlier.
The Supreme Court has already been involved in Pike's case: it allowed the lethal injections to go ahead after a legal battle.
Has this happened before?
While there is a lengthy history of botched executions across the US, Pike is believed to be the only person to have survived after receiving a lethal injection.
Deborah Denno, a criminologist and professor at Fordham Law School, said she was "absolutely astonished" that Pike is conscious and speaking.
There had been seven previous cases in which prisoners survived slated executions, but in those cases, executioners were not able to inject anything into the inmates' veins, Denno told the BBC.
Pike "is the only person for whom some kind of toxin has been injected", she said.
The attempted execution of Pike was not the first in Tennessee in 2026 that did not go to plan.

The execution of Tony Carruthers, who was convicted of kidnapping and murdering three people in 1994, was postponed in May after staff were unable to find a vein for a lethal injection. He was granted a year's reprieve by the governor.
In 2022, more than a third of executions across the US were botched or highly problematic, according to the Death Penalty Information Center, which does not take an ethical stance on the penalty.
What did Pike do? Who was Colleen Slemmer?
Pike, now 50, was sentenced to death in 1996 for the murder a year earlier of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, which was perpetrated along with her then-boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp.
Pike killed Slemmer at a camp for troubled teens, after accusing Slemmer of insulting her and attempting to steal Shipp from her.
Two other residents at the camp later testified that Pike had bragged about the murder and showed them a piece of Slemmer's skull.

Shipp was given a life sentence with the possibility of parole and he remains in prison. He was spared the death penalty for his part in the attack because he was not yet legally an adult at the time.

Correction 1 October: This article originally referred to the inmate executed by the state of Louisiana in 1947 as Willie Smith. We have amended the article to make clear that his name was Willie Francis.

articles.title: [DECODED] What a fake Duterte tells us about our bigger AI problem
articles.summary: Disinformation spreads rapidly because it’s becoming easier and cheaper to create fakes, while the systems behind them are outpacing the safeguards meant to mitigate the risks

blocks.text: Disinformation spreads rapidly because it’s becoming easier and cheaper to create fakes, while the systems behind them are outpacing the safeguards meant to mitigate the risks

items: Lance Duterte is a synthetic online persona claiming to be related to former president Rodrigo Duterte, gaining significant social media attention despite being a creation of AI.
The persona has evolved over the years, with recent posts utilizing videos to enhance believability, highlighting the growing ease of creating fake identities online.

Concerns about the unchecked development of AI and its potential dangers have been raised by researchers and former employees in the field, emphasizing the need for safety standards similar to those in other industries.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
Have you ever heard of a “Lance Duterte”? He’s a Facebook persona claiming to be a grandson of former president Rodrigo Duterte and the son of Vice President Sara Duterte.

Like his supposed family members, Lance has attracted a huge following on social media. He has over 382,000 followers on Facebook, and his posts rack up thousands of engagements each — many of which come from fans and supporters who gush over his conventionally attractive features. Some even tout him as a future celebrity or politician.
But as our researcher Alex Culla found out, Lance is not real. He’s a synthetic online persona made from AI.

When Alex pitched the story, I thought the name sounded familiar. Then I remembered: six years ago, I wrote a fact-check article about a Facebook account with the name “Lance Kurt Dong Duterte.” He falsely claimed that Tricia, daughter of former vice president Leni Robredo, sent a hate message to him via private message.

But this happened back in 2020, before consumer AI chatbots like ChatGPT became publicly accessible. And as Alex pointed out in her Decoded piece, the profile picture of the 2020 version of this persona looked different from the one currently active today.
So the persona has been around for years, but its posts today now include videos to make the lie appear more believable, thanks to the accessibility of AI.

Lance isn’t the first AI piece built around the Duterte name. Back in 2025, we also reported on how AI-generated images of Duterte statues were being shared by Facebook pages known for glorifying the Dutertes. These fakes were created a few months after the former president was arrested over a warrant issued by the International Criminal Court.
These things happen because it’s becoming easier and cheaper to create fakes, while the systems behind them are outpacing the safeguards meant to mitigate the risks.
Over the past week alone, news reports have quoted different AI researchers, employees, and former staff on the lack of safety culture in AI companies.

From OpenAI to Google DeepMind, current and former employees have expressed concerns about the risks of self-improving AI systems and warned that companies are doing too little to protect the world against AI’s potential dangers.

Another former OpenAI safety employee said that “the time for trial and error is over,” because AI capabilities have far outpaced the systems’ ability to act in ways that match human goals and values. He even argued that advanced AI systems should have safeguards in place comparable to those used in the nuclear power and aviation industries.

Even Anthropic, the company behind Claude, warned its potential IPO investors that AI could exhibit “self-preserving behaviors.” The company said in its IPO prospectus: “Our development of highly advanced models, platforms, and applications and expansion of use cases could further increase the risk that our models cause harm.”

These warning bells echo concerns that advocates have long raised about social media. Cambridge Analytica whistleblower Chris Wylie once said that digital products should have moral standards and safety testing like those imposed on consumer goods. “We do not allow any other consumer product to just be released without any kind of safety standards,” Wylie said in a Rappler+ briefing back in 2023.
Three years later, we’re still grappling with the same concerns, now made worse by the unchecked development of AI.

Which is why Rappler built MUNI, a platform where facts and trusted voices can thrive. It’s a community space for verified information, where you can read news, chat with reporters, and talk with like-minded individuals who share your interests.

MUNI is not limited to Rappler. You can also find other newsgroups there, including Daily Guardian in Iloilo and SunStar in Cebu, so you can also join their chat rooms and take part in their discussions.
You can explore MUNI by downloading the Rappler app for free from the App Store or Play Store. MUNI is a tab on the Rappler app where you can join as many chat rooms as you want.

articles.title: Nunavut’s Kitikmeot and Kivalliq regions aim to join neighbours not turning back clocks
articles.summary: With the N.W.T. and Manitoba ending daylight savings, Nunavut's Kitikmeot and Kivalliq regions will be out of sync with their provincial and territorial neighbors. Now, some officials in the regions…

image.caption: Cambridge Bay MLA Fred Pedersen said he alongside other Kitikmeot MLAs want to end the time change. This year, when Nunavut turns back the clock, the Kitikmeot and Kivalliq regions will have a different time than the N.W.T. and Manitoba. (Rafael Ferraz/CBC)

blocks.text: North

With the N.W.T. and Manitoba ending daylight savings, Nunavut's Kitikmeot and Kivalliq regions will be out of sync with their provincial and territorial neighbors. Now, some officials in the regions say it's time the regions ended the practice.
Government of Nunavut says it’s looking into ending the time change
Come Nov. 1, the time zones in Canada will look a little bit different — especially in Nunavut.
With the Northwest Territories, Alberta and now Manitoba ending the practice of turning back the clock, Nunavut's Kitikmeot region will share the same time as the Yukon.
Meanwhile, the Kivalliq region will be aligned with the Northwest Territories.
This means both regions will be out of sync with their provincial and territorial neighbours, despite being right next door.
Time zones in Canada as of Nov. 1, 2026:

“It's a concern for us for sure,” said Cambridge Bay MLA Fred Pedersen. “We rely on a lot of trade with the [Northwest Territories] and Alberta. We're on the same time. We've always been on the same time zone as them and this year it'll be the first time that we're not.”

items: Time zones in Canada are getting complicated. These maps lay them out

blocks.text: Impact on flights and travel
What happens when you no longer share the same time as your neighbour?
For Joe Savikataaq, mayor of Arviat in the Kivalliq region, he worries about people mixing up flights and medical appointments because people often fly to Winnipeg for health care.

"The vast majority [of Arviat residents] were concerned about our connections to Manitoba," he said. "All of the medical patients that do go there and that's our main connection and there will now be an hour time difference."
Because of the time difference, Pedersen said there’s going to have to be a new flight schedule.
“Now, it'll be a little bit different,” Pedersen said. “The flights might look like only one hour flights now or something like that because of the time change.”
Gjoa Haven Mayor Raymond Quqshuun Sr. said residents regularly fly to Edmonton or Yellowknife for medical travel and with the time zone change this travel could be disrupted. (Samuel Wat/CBC)
Raymond Quqshuun Sr., mayor of Gjoa Haven in the Kitikmeot region, said residents don't want to be in a different time zone, but rather want to share the same time as their neighbours.

"Everybody saying in my community that they would like [to] stick with the N.W.T. time and also Alberta time because we do a lot of medical businesses with them, like every day, every month, every year," he said.
Nunavut looks to end daylight savings
At the Kitikmeot mayors forum last month, the mayor drafted a resolution to end the time change.

Pedersen said he hasn’t seen the resolution yet, but wants to table it at the next sitting of the legislative assembly. He said he's hopeful the time change can end this year, and he alongside other Kitikmeot MLAs will be asking about the possibility.
"We'll all be bringing this issue up with the minister again in hopes that the government of Nunavut can pass legislation prior to Nov. 1," Pedersen said.

In an email, Nunavut’s Justice Minister George Hickes said the Department of Justice is accessing the feasibility of ending the time change and that the review will be complex and could take several months.
No decision has been made at this time.
Still, Savikataaq said the time is right to get away from seasonal time changes.

"Every time there is a time change twice a year, it gets like, what time is it and what's your time and all that,” he said. “It's getting easier now with cell phones, but people don't want to change."
Nunavut's annual time change is set for Nov. 1.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Bianca McKeown is a reporter with CBC North in Iqaluit. Previously, she worked at CBC Ottawa. Have a story idea? Email her at: bianca.mckeown@cbc.ca

articles.title: Researchers probe Prairie wetlands for signs of 'epidermal epidemic' in Manitoba frogs, salamanders
articles.summary: There's a deadly disease that threatens to infect Manitoba frogs and salamanders — and it could wreak havoc if left unchecked. That's why Brandon University researchers are sampling amphibians to…

image.caption: A grey treefrog rests on a rock at the edge of a lake near the Manitoba-Ontario border. The fungal pathogen Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis gives rise to chytridiomycosis, which is plaguing amphibians worldwide and has been confirmed in northwestern Ontario, but not yet Manitoba. (Bryce Hoye/CBC)

blocks.text: Thickening skin falling off lethargic frogs and toads in flecks. Struggles with breathing and eating. An immune system under attack shutting the body down.
Those are telltale signs of chytridiomycosis, a lethal fungal disease that's been called an "epidermal epidemic" leading to the extinction of dozens of amphibian species worldwide.
It hasn't been detected yet in Canada's middle province — but that isn't necessarily because it isn't in Manitoba.
"It is quite literally everywhere on our continent …. There's no way we don't have this pathogen here," said Jackie Tran, a graduate student sampling frogs and salamanders across southern Manitoba.
"There's reported presence everywhere around our province. Now, that doesn't mean we don't have the pathogens here, it just means we haven't been on top of surveillance up until now."
Chytrid in frogs is caused by the fungal pathogen Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis; in salamanders, by Batrachochytrium salamandrivorans.
The latter, believed to have originated in East Asia, surfaced in the past couple decades and has decimated local populations of salamanders in parts of Europe.
It hasn't made the leap to North America yet, that scientists know of.
Researchers probe Manitoba wetlands for deadly frog, salamander disease

Where the variety that infects frogs and toads first emerged remains unclear, though there are signs it was present in Brazil and Asia for more than a century before popping up around the world, in large part because of the trade in exotic pets.
Chytrid is directly responsible for the extinction of at least 90 species, and tanking numbers in more than 500 others.

That's one of the reasons it's been described as "the worst infectious disease ever recorded among vertebrates" (any creature with a spine). It's become more established in the U.S. and Canada in recent years.
A blue-spotted salamander emerges from beneath a woodpile in northwestern Ontario last summer. The fungal infection hasn't been confirmed in salamanders in North America yet. (Colby McGilvray/CBC)

Nearly half of Alberta frog populations sampled between 2006-10 came back positive for chytrid. Studies from around the same time in British Columbia found it present in one of 10 amphibians sampled, with northern leopard frogs among those worst hit.
That species is federally listed as endangered in parts of Western Canada. In Manitoba, it's listed as a species of special concern.

The leopard frog — one of 16 amphibian species in Manitoba historically — has seen population declines across Canada in recent decades. And there's suspicion that chytrid might have been the culprit behind a marked drop in Manitoba numbers five decades ago.
The leopard frog range in Manitoba contracted after "heaps of dead and dying frogs" up to a metre high were observed along shores of some wetlands in Manitoba.
A northern leopard frog lurks along the edges of a lake near the border of Manitoba and Ontario in September 2026. (Bryce Hoye/CBC)
No one sampled or scooped up any of those frog corpses for posterity, so while chytrid is considered a plausible explanation, it remains speculation.
Tran suggests the thus-far chytrid-free designation for Manitoba might be more of a mirage than a mirror of any special conservation action going on in the province keeping the disease at bay.

Jackie Tran, a master's student at Brandon University, stands next to a wetland in Sandilands Provincial Forest in south eastern Manitoba on Oct. 1. His research is focused on determining for the first time whether a deadly fungal pathogen has infected populations of amphibians in Manitoba, such as northern leopard frogs and tiger salamanders. (Bryce Hoye/CBC)
"That's kind of been taken as a sign to not prioritize this research," he said.

It's been confirmed in frogs in Ontario, including in the northwest, not far from the Manitoba border, as well as in the Northwest Territories, North Dakota and Minnesota. Saskatchewan had one confirmed case in 2007, Tran says.
Tran swabs a gray treefrog as part of his research focused on confirming whether Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis has made it into Manitoba amphibian populations. (Submitted by Jackie Tran)
There's reason to believe the risk to amphibians on the Prairies could be increasing.
"With a changing environment, a changing climate, things could get a lot worse," Tran said.

items: Reptile and amphibian researchers meet in Manitoba in shadow of troubling report
Interest waning in Manitoba reptile, amphibian project, biologist says

blocks.text: He used geographic modelling data to identify a range of wetland amphibian habitats where the pathogens could thrive.
Tran's work marks the beginning of a proactive monitoring program at Brandon University that his supervisor plans to carry on.
"If we can get out front of this, this can help sort of limit some of these declines," said Pamela Rutherford, associate professor in the department of biology at BU.
Tran is her first graduate student doing this kind of work, which is part of a broader pathogen monitoring program that started in the U.S., Rutherford says.
Tran sampled a variety of the 16 amphibian species that call Manitoba home, including wood frogs, such as those shown here in a southern Manitoba wetland. (Submitted by Jackie Tran)
Pathogens spread well in wetlands degraded by human activity, Rutherford says, which is why the component of Tran's work identifying those kinds of habitats could have value beyond his project.

"This also gives us a more general sense of what the health of wetlands are now for the systems that he [Tran] looks at, but that has much broader implications for the health of everything," Rutherford said.

items: 'Deadliest disease in all time' wipes out 90 species of frogs and toads
Frogs are dying and Korea gets the blame

blocks.text: "The health of the wetland tells you about not just how the frogs are doing, but it tells you how the fish … how the insects are doing, how the plants are doing, and so it's all interrelated," she said.
"The health of wetlands is also directly connected with human health as well: healthy wetlands, healthy environments."
Rutherford says if Brandon researchers confirm the pathogen in amphibians in Manitoba, there's a glimmer of hope that those amphibians might not be consigned to oblivion after all.
A baby American toad crawls across moss in northwestern Ontario in August 2017. (Bryce Hoye/CBC)
Results emerging from field experiments run by the Wilder Institute and the Calgary Zoo suggest young leopard frogs can be inoculated against the worst effects of chytrid.
They gave a few dozen young frogs, from a B.C. population overrun with chytrid, baths in a diluted itraconazole solution.

More than a quarter of the frogs they treated survived winter, says Lea Randall, senior manager conservation programs at the Wilder Institute, compared with an estimated half a per cent of untreated frogs.
"We had about 60 times the overwinter survival for treated frogs, which confirms that chytrid fungus is what has hampered our reintroduction efforts until now," Randall told CBC News via email.
"We are scaling up this treatment in 2026 and are optimistic that this will lead to improved success in our reintroduction efforts."
An American bittern eats a barred tiger salamander. (Bryce Hoye/CBC)
Tran hopes Manitoba is in a position to leverage that success, should its cold-blooded critters need help.
"We tend to mourn things when we've already lost it, and this disease research is just one component of trying to protect that and prevent that from happening," he said.

articles.title: Trump to speak to Putin about plague lab worker's death in Russia
articles.summary: Fears that the death may have been caused by pneumonic plague has prompted calls for more transparency from Russia.

blocks.text: US President Donald Trump has said he will speak with his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin soon about the death of a lab worker at a plague research centre in Siberia.
"So far we are in very deep discussions," Trump said, adding that he would be able to report on his talks with Putin "probably" on Thursday.

Russian officials say they are investigating the cause of the 28-year-old's death. They say that those who came into contact with the victim all tested negative and have not confirmed that the suspected disease is pneumonic plague - a serious lung infection, often described as the most virulent form of plague.
The head of the World Health Organization (WHO) has called for transparency from Russia.

"Timely, complete and transparent information sharing under the International Health Regulations is essential to clarify conflicting reports and enable an accurate assessment of potential public health risks," Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said.
According to the WHO, pneumonic plague has a very short incubation period - sometimes just 24 hours - and can be fatal, if not diagnosed and treated early.
People can be infected through:

items: infected flea bites
contact with bodily fluids or contaminated materials
the inhalation of respiratory particles

blocks.text: Symptoms include shortness of breath and coughing, often with blood-tainted phlegm.
Reports first emerged on Friday of almost 200 people being placed under observation in Siberia's Irkutsk region following the death.
The lab worker, named in Russian media as Darya Shipilova, had reportedly fallen ill a couple of days earlier.

Unconfirmed reports suggested that she had become ill after breaking a test tube containing the pathogen at the Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia and the Far East where she worked - or following a field trip to a region where plague occurs naturally among wild rodents.
But Russian officials have played down those reports. The country's health watchdog Rospotrebnadzor said the woman had died of "pneumonia of an undetermined etiology".
Ongoing speculation into the lab worker's death has sparked a back and forth between Russia and the US, with questions about a possible spread outside of Russia.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the US had "measures" available to help Russia if the situation turned out to be more serious than claimed.
The bacterium that causes the plague, Yersinia pestis, found among rodents such as marmots in the area.
It killed up to half the population of Europe in the 14th Century when it was known as the Black Death.
It was in response to an outbreak in the 1920s that the Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia and the Far East, was founded just over 100 years ago.

articles.title: Ferdinand Marcos Jr. unplugged: Why the President needs music
articles.summary: 'I’ve come to the conclusion that my life was lived with a soundtrack. When I hear a song, I remember when I first heard it, what I was doing, how I was feeling. Every big event in my life there was…

blocks.text: 'I’ve come to the conclusion that my life was lived with a soundtrack. When I hear a song, I remember when I first heard it, what I was doing, how I was feeling. Every big event in my life there was an accompanying track ongoing,' Marcos says in an interview with Gary Valenciano

items: President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. has a history of music-related controversies, including using a presidential helicopter to attend a Coldplay concert, which he described as 'unmissable.'
Marcos views music as an essential part of his life, associating significant events with specific songs and expressing admiration for the Filipino audience's enthusiasm for live performances.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
MANILA, Philippines – Back in September 2024, President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. had caused an uproar for hiring a band to play at his private birthday party.

While the Philippines is known as a music-loving country, it wasn’t just any band, that Marcos hired — it was acclaimed British pop-rock outfit Duran Duran, which was flown in just for his 67th birthday celebration.

But the Presidential Communications Office (PCO) had attested that the party, held at a Pasay City hotel, was thrown by “old friends,” and that the Duran Duran performance had merely come as a surprise to Marcos. Then-communications secretary Cesar Chavez had even told reporters in a message that the band’s appearance came “at no cost to the government.”
This wasn’t the President’s first music-related controversy, however.

Just a few months before that, in January 2024, the son of the former dictator had also found himself in hot water when the public caught wind of him using the presidential chopper to get to British band Coldplay’s concert at the Philippine Arena in Bulacan.

blocks.caption: Coldplay concert ‘unmissable’ for chopper-riding, ‘music lover’ Marcos

blocks.text: It was “unmissable,” he had told reporters in a chance interview several days after the show.
“It was, by the way, fantastic. Ask anybody who attended the concert. The show they performed was spectacular. I haven’t seen anything like it,” he said.
It seems, then, that the country’s biggest music fan happens to hold the state’s highest position. And Marcos was always one to make his affinity for music known.

Around the time of the 2022 presidential elections, an old clip of him playing the saxophone had gone viral. He had revealed in an interview with Gary Valenciano that premiered on October 5 that this, along with the flute, were instruments he had picked up in his youth. He had even gone on to join several orchestras.

blocks.caption: Ferdinand Marcos Jr. unplugged: Why the President needs music

blocks.text: Marcos had first studied music while he was pursuing his secondary education in England in the ’70s. He was a self-confessed troublemaker then, and was sent to his housemaster to receive his punishment.
“He said, ‘You’re here all the time. You’re always in trouble. Go find yourself a hobby so that you can occupy your time by doing something constructive,’” he recalled.

blocks.caption: Ferdinand Marcos Jr. unplugged: Why the President needs music

blocks.text: Back then, he had been listening to a lot of music anyway, so it only seemed like the natural choice. What had served as his musical awakening, he shared, was Lou Reed’s “Walk on the Wild Side,” which he had heard another student play out loud while he was making his rounds before class. Aside from playing the flute and the saxophone, he would later also study music theory.

“It’s a fascinating thing because unlike any other art form, music doesn’t exist anywhere else except in your brain. Think about it. A sculpture you can touch, a painting, you can look at and you can see the brushstrokes. All the other forms. This is just sound and it only becomes music because your brain interprets it as music. But the universality of it, everyone understands,” Marcos told Valenciano in the interview.
The President views music as an integral part of his life — as something he cannot live without. If anyone were to take it away from him, he tells Valenciano, he wouldn’t know how to manage.

“I just don’t know how I would get through the day,” he explained. “It’s the only thing that can change my mood. There are two things that can change my mood. Music’s one of them. The other one’s my children.”

Even Marcos’ big life events have specific songs associated with them. He and this art form have long been intertwined. “I’ve come to the conclusion that my life was lived with a soundtrack. When I hear a song, I remember when I first heard it, what I was doing, how I was feeling. Every big event in my life there was an accompanying track ongoing.”

But even as a big music fan, the President can’t seem to figure out why Filipinos excel so much at holding a note. He said that whenever his foreign friends would ask him why his countrymen were such good singers, he had never been able to give a proper answer.
Apparently, what he does know, though, is that Filipinos make the best concert audiences.

“I’ve heard it from Elton John, I’ve heard it from Sting. I’ve heard it from The Corrs. I’ve heard it from many of these artists that come. And they said, ‘The audience does all the work for me. I don’t have to sing. I don’t have to perform because the audience is singing for us,’” Marcos explained.

Most Filipinos are lauded for always enthusiastically singing the lyrics back to the performing artist as loud as they can. It’s become a big indication of who the Filipino people are as enjoyers of music.

In Marcos’ case, perhaps much of his repertoire as a music fan reflects in his willingness to do anything to catch his favorite bands perform live — even if it means flying a high-profile music act in for a private show or riding the presidential chopper to the Philippine Arena to beat the evening traffic, much to the ire of taxpayers. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Sri Lanka's ex-first lady arrested over alleged misuse of children's hospital donations
articles.summary: The 73-year-old has been arrested over allegations that a charity she is linked to misused donations.

blocks.text: Sri Lanka's former first lady Shiranthi Rajapaksa has been arrested over allegations that a charity she is linked to misused donations raised for a children's hospital.
Anti-corruption authorities arrested the 73-year-old wife of former President Mahinda Rajapaksa at their Colombo home on Wednesday.

They are questioning her over the 10 million rupees ($30,300; £22,800) of donations collected by the Siriliya Saviya charity, meant to be spent on a specialised scanner for Colombo's Lady Ridgeway Children's Hospital.
But officials say such a scanner had already been donated by the Chinese government.
Shiranthi Rajapaksa has denied any wrongdoing and says the money has not been appropriated.
She returned to Sri Lanka on Monday from Singapore, where she was receiving medical treatment. She had filed a court petition to try to prevent her arrest, but the hearing was set for 12 October.
Ex-President Mahinda Rajapaksa's spokesperson, Manoj Gamage, has said the money is safe in Siriliya's accounts and that no fraud has occurred.

Mahinda Rajapaksa served as president of Sri Lanka from 2005 to 2015 and for years, his family held a tight grip over the country's politics. He was hailed by many as a hero for bringing an end to nearly three decades of civil war when Tamil Tiger rebels were crushed in 2009, during his first term as president.
But in 2022, protests broke out across the country as inflation surged and Sri Lanka ran out of fuel, food and medicine.
Mahinda's brother Gotabaya Rajapaksa, who was serving as leader at that time, was eventually toppled.
Sri Lanka's current government, under President Anura Kumara Dissanayake, has since revived long-stalled corruption investigations involving various members of the Rajapaksa family.

Mahinda and Shiranthi's eldest son, Namal Rajapaksa, was arrested earlier this year over allegations linked to an aircraft procurement deal made during his father's presidency. He is currently held in remand.
His brother Yoshitha was also arrested earlier this year on corruption charges.

articles.title: Israelis mourn on anniversary of Oct. 7 attack as Palestinians grapple with war it sparked
articles.summary: Israelis gathered on Wednesday to commemorate the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas-led attack that killed 1,200 people, saw 251 taken hostage, and sparked a devastating war in Gaza that has left much of the…

image.caption: The family of Hilly Solomon visits her memorial photo and plaque at the Nova festival memorial site early Wednesday in Reim as Israel marks the third anniversary of the Oct. 7, 2023 attacks. (Alexi Rosenfeld/Getty Images)

blocks.text: Israelis gathered on Wednesday to commemorate the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas-led attack that killed 1,200 people, saw 251 taken hostage, and sparked a devastating war in Gaza that has left much of the territory in ruins and its two million people living in dire conditions.

In southern Israel, families mourned at intersections, bomb shelters, and the site of a music festival that Hamas-led militants overran three years ago in the deadliest attack against Israel. It is the first anniversary that all the hostages are home, marking a new stage of grief.

For Palestinians, the anniversary brings another day of life of misery and difficulties after an Israeli retaliatory campaign in Gaza that has killed tens of thousands of people. Most of the population of about two million people live in vast, squalid tent camps, with large parts of the strip's cities reduced to rubble.
More than half the territory remains in the hands of the Israeli military, and despite a ceasefire deal reached nearly a year ago, Israeli strikes continue almost daily.

items: 1 year since Oct. 7, the lives of these Israelis and Palestinians are forever changed
U.A.E. warned Netanyahu of major Hamas operation days before Oct. 7 attack: Israeli newspaper

blocks.text: For the region, the day highlights a startling transformation over the past three years. Israeli troops occupy a large chunk of southern Lebanon in their conflict with Hezbollah, which began firing on Israel in 2023 in support of Hamas.
Commuters in Tel Aviv conduct a moment of silence on the highway as part of a memorial ceremony on Wednesday. (Jack Guez/AFP/Getty Images)

Iran and the United States are locked in a confrontation that has seen attacks across Arab Gulf countries and has shaken the global economy — a conflict that Israel helped launch and that the Gaza war paved the way for even if they weren't directly connected.
Families mourn at music festival site

In Reim, the town where the music festival was underway on the day of the attack, families gathered around photos of their killed relatives. They hugged at 6:29 a.m. local time — the exact time the first rockets were launched three years ago — as booms from explosions in nearby Gaza were heard.
Anya Davitashili, who lost her 25-year-old son, Sean, said she comes to the site every Saturday because it's where she feels closest to him.
"I have a video of him dancing here that ends at 6:29 in the morning, it's in front of my eyes all the time," she said. "Every morning, you wake up and there is just endless missing."
Hundreds of people came to pay their respects to the more than 350 people killed in and around the festival site.
Released hostage marks 1st anniversary of freedom

Elkana Bohbot, 37, is marking the anniversary in Israel for the first time, after being released from 738 days of captivity last year. For most of that time, he said, he was held 50 metres underground in a dark, damp tunnel.
People attend a memorial service in Kibbutz Kfar Aza, southern Israel, where many community members were killed and abducted on Oct. 7, 2023. (Ariel Schalit/The Associated Press)

Bohbot, who was abducted from the Nova music festival , was kept in a small cell with other hostages, given very little food, and allowed to bathe only every few weeks, he said. His captors forced him to take part in several propaganda videos, including one where he acts out a fake call to his family.

In the 11 months since his release, Bohbot has undergone physical and emotional rehabilitation, written a book, begun a speaking career, travelled with his family, and celebrated all the holidays and birthdays he missed.
What Netanyahu knew before the Oct. 7 attacks
In August, his wife, Rivka, gave birth to a daughter, fulfilling a fierce promise that Bohbot made to himself in the tunnels to give his five-year-old son, Reem, a sibling.

The newborn Michele is "not a symbol for my people, she is more of a symbol for the enemy," Bohbot told The Associated Press. "So this child is the message for you that we were here, and we will always be here forever."
Palestinians struggle to recover in Gaza

No events are expected on Wednesday in Gaza, but Hamas in a statement praised the Oct. 7 attack as an example of "heroism, resilience and national solidarity" and said it had returned the Palestinian cause to the world's attention.
"The conflict with the enemy did not begin on that day, as its final chapters are not written yet," it said.
Palestinians in the territory said the extent to which their lives had deteriorated over the past three years was previously unimaginable.
"We witnessed death, destruction, and bombardment that we had never known before," said Walid Akram, a Gaza City resident who, like most in Gaza, has been displaced by the war.
Raed Khozeiq's coastal neighborhood in Tel al-Hawa was largely flattened. Nothing about his life now is the same, he said.
"No country in the world has gone through what we have experienced here," he said. "A war of extermination, starvation, the absence of schools and universities — nothing remains."

Israel's offensive has devastated the narrow strip and displaced around 90 per cent of its population, often multiple times. Restrictions on the entry of goods and aid have contributed to a severe hunger crisis.

More than 74,000 Palestinians have been killed in Gaza, according to the territory's Health Ministry, which does not distinguish between civilians and militants in its figures but says around half were women and children. The numbers from the ministry, part of the Hamas-run government, are seen as generally reliable by UN agencies and independent experts.

While a ceasefire that took effect on Oct. 10, 2025 has halted the heaviest fighting, Israeli strikes have continued, targeting what Israel says are Hamas militants. Since the ceasefire, 1,460 Palestinians have been killed in Gaza, according to the ministry. Seven Israeli soldiers have been killed in that period.
Palestinians walk along a street in Gaza City on Tuesday, surrounded by buildings destroyed by Israeli military strikes in the Israel-Hamas war. (Jehad Alshrafi/The Associated Press)

Hamas portrayed the Oct. 7 attack as a response to decades of Israeli military occupation, land seizures and settlement construction. But the Palestinians' dream of an independent state appears even more distant.
Middle East altered

A contentious election in Israel at the end of the month hangs over this year's anniversary. The government's official memorial services took place on Oct. 5, closer to the Hebrew-calendar anniversary of the attack. The separate commemorations are indicative of the deep divisions over Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's handling of the war and his reluctance to launch an official inquiry into failings of the day.

The attack set in motion a cascade of events that led to wars across the Middle East as Israel confronted Hamas, Hezbollah and their backer Iran. Israel has seized swaths of territory in Syria and Lebanon, where more than 300,000 Lebanese remain displaced.
The United States joined Israel in attacking Iran's military and nuclear program in two rounds, battering Iran and upending global markets far from the battlefield.
Violence has also risen across the Israeli-occupied West Bank, where Israel's far-right government has emboldened extremist settlers who have attacked Palestinians and destroyed their property.

articles.title: Japan beer giants raided over alleged price-fixing cartel
articles.summary: Asahi and Kirin confirmed their premises were searched by Japanese competition authorities.

blocks.text: Japanese officials have raided the country's biggest beer makers over allegations they worked together to raise the price of their beverages.
Asahi and Kirin confirmed to the BBC their premises had been searched by the Japan Fair Trade Commission, adding that they would fully cooperate with the government authority.
There are reports Sapporo Breweries and Suntory Spirits were also raided. Both firms have been contacted for comment.
Asahi, Kirin and Sapporo all saw their share price fall after news of the investigation broke on Wednesday. Suntory is not publicly-listed.
According to the Japan Times, the investigation centres on the companies raising their prices in April last year and in October 2022.
All four companies announced increases, citing the rising cost of raw materials as well as other factors such as energy and transportation.
Kirin Holdings said its subsidiary, Kirin Brewery Company, was searched "on suspicion of a violation of the Antimonopoly Act".
It said it takes the matter "very seriously", adding it would "fully cooperate with the Japan Fair Trade Commission's investigation and any requests for cooperation".
Kirin Holdings said: "At present, the impact of this matter on the company's financial results has not been determined. The company will promptly disclose any material developments as they arise."

Asahi Breweries said it was "subject to investigation by the Japan Fair Trade Commission regarding a suspected violation of the Act on Prohibition of Private Monopolization and Maintenance of Fair Trade".
It added: "We will fully cooperate with the commission."
The Japan Fair Trade Commission has been contacted for comment.

articles.title: [In This Economy] Cesar Virata, technocrat who helped finance a dictatorship
articles.summary: How should we remember a capable technocrat who helped keep such a government going?

blocks.text: Cesar Virata, who died on October 2 at age 95, was a familiar presence at big events of the UP School of Economics, attending in his wheelchair.
That is the extent of my personal acquaintance with him. I did not know him closely, and I leave the intimate recollections to his family, friends, and colleagues.

He may well have been as wise and kind as those who knew him remember. On Facebook, I saw an outpouring of condolences from my friends for whom Virata was a tito (uncle/respectful title for an older person), ninong (godfather), mentor, friend. Those qualities deserve their place in the tributes and obituaries.
But Virata’s long service to the Marcos dictatorship deserves equally serious attention.

The fact is that Virata headed the finance department/ministry from 1970 to 1986 and served as prime minister from 1981 until the dictatorship fell. These were positions at the very heart of a government that, in the end, impoverished Filipinos and left the country with debts that outlived the regime.
How should we remember a capable technocrat who helped keep such a government going?

In my 2023 book False Nostalgia: The Marcos “Golden Age” Myths and How to Debunk Them, I discussed how Marcos’ technocrats helped make the regime’s massive foreign borrowing possible. Virata was a central figure in that group.

To the uninitiated, technocrats are officials whose authority rests on specialized expertise. Under Marcos, they included economic managers with advanced degrees and international connections, people who could speak the language of bankers and development institutions.

This mattered enormously for the Marcos dictatorship. Borrowing requires lenders willing to believe that you can repay. Officials like Virata helped present the Philippines as a country whose economy was being managed competently—even as political power became increasingly concentrated in the hands of the dictator and his cronies.

The technocrats’ credibility helped the regime obtain money from foreign banks and institutions such as the World Bank and International Monetary Fund (IMF). The backdrop is that the economic managers were confronted with the task of maintaining a fixed exchange rate and maintaining an ample supply of dollars. The borrowings, totaling more than $25 billion over the Marcos years, helped finance the government and prolonged its ability to operate.
In the book, I described this as effectively “deodorizing” the Martial Law regime. Technical competence gave international creditors reasons to keep dealing with a dictatorship.

Of course, the technocrats and Marcos’ cronies were often at odds. They were characterized once as separate if opposing spokes in a wheel, connected by the hub that was Marcos. Political scientist Teresa Encarnacion Tadem’s research documents how crony interests undermined Virata’s group, even as its relationships with international financial institutions strengthened its position within the government.

Those conflicts show the limits of the arrangement. Marcos retained the power to accommodate his cronies and disregard technical advice, while continuing to benefit from the credibility lent by his economic managers. Both groups could serve the same regime while disagreeing bitterly about its policies.

Eventually, some technocrats left one by one. Gerardo Sicat, for instance, left his position as director-general of the National Economic and Development Authority in 1981, just as the economy was tumbling into decline and crisis. Virata remained to hold the fort.

Many years later, Sicat would write a tome of a biography for Virata, titled: Cesar Virata: Life and Times Through Four Decades of Philippine Economic History. Published in 2014, it offers a sympathetic account of Virata’s predicament as the chief technocrat during the crisis years. As Hal Hill’s review explains, it portrays a reformer battling Imelda Marcos and the cronies, attempting to restrain spending, and eventually offering a resignation that Marcos refused.

But this defense leaves important questions unanswered. The disappearance of congressional opposition after Martial Law may have made economic reforms easier to implement. It also removed democratic checks on the borrowing and spending that helped bring the country to ruin. Economists should count those costs to our institutions as well.

As well, the unsuccessful offer to resign doesn’t erase the consequences of remaining in office. Virata’s credibility continued to help Marcos obtain foreign financing even as the regime’s abuses and economic failures became increasingly evident.

Truthful reminiscences of Virata’s life and times must acknowledge the fact that technocrats like him were crucial in propping up the dictatorship and the crony capitalism that flourished at that time.

Consider an admission by Virata himself that I quoted in False Nostalgia, drawing on economist James Boyce’s account. In 1984 Virata admitted, “We were quite liberal in guaranteeing loans,” referring to “behest loans” or loans that were granted by president Marcos to select friends and family members, obtained from government financial institutions.

Virata explained that some companies had been interested in making money from equipment purchases rather than operating the businesses those purchases were supposed to support. He called this “one of the major faults in our system.”

A loan guarantee is a promise to pay if the borrower cannot. It can help a worthwhile project obtain financing, but it also exposes the guarantor to losses. When public institutions extend guarantees too freely, as Virata admitted to doing, private business failures can become public financial obligations.

That is why Virata’s admission matters. It points to a gross failure in how the Marcos regime assessed and assumed financial risks. The public was left exposed to projects whose supposed developmental benefits might never materialize.

Indeed, state-owned banks like the Development Bank of the Philippines, and even the old Central Bank, were left with deteriorating balance sheets as it became impossible to collect the behest loans that they gave out to cronies. Rescuing crony businesses in the 1980s weakened the institutions financing them, which themselves needed rescuing. The costs, in short, spread far beyond the favored borrowers.

Then there’s the 1983 debt moratorium. In October that year, not long after senator Benigno “Ninoy” Aquino Jr. was killed on the tarmac, Virata and then-Central Bank governor Jaime Laya had gone to New York to seek a 90-day moratorium on principal payments to private creditors. By that time, the country could no longer meet its debt obligations as scheduled.
The same government that had borrowed so heavily was now asking for more time to pay.

Sure, the Philippines faced a hostile international environment: higher global interest rates and the international debt crisis also battered other developing countries. Virata alone did not cause the Philippine crisis, and negotiating relief was necessary once the country was in trouble.

But decades of bad domestic decisions had made us weak and vulnerable. Foreign borrowing came with repayment obligations, and politically favored projects could fail to generate the income needed to meet them. In hindsight, therefore, economic managers must be assessed on the risks accumulated during their tenure alongside their efforts to manage the eventual collapse.

It didn’t help that Virata was tone-deaf about people’s increasing economic hardships. In a controversial interview in the June 1, 1984 issue of Mr & Ms Special Edition, Virata was quoted as saying, “Well, I do not know what they mean by crisis… They never had it so good.”
They never had it so good.

He argued that basic needs were being supplied and that people should not mistake the absence of luxuries for a crisis. Recall that this was months after the debt moratorium, amid an economic crisis aggravated by crony capitalism and reckless borrowing. In effect, Filipinos were paying for the failures of a government whose prime minister was assuring them that life had never been better.

Whatever his disagreements with Marcos behind closed doors, Virata was on record publicly defending the regime’s economic record. His own words complicate the picture of a technocrat merely trying to contain the damage.
There is a familiar defense of officials who stay under an abusive leader: they are supposed to have restrained the damage from within.
Sure, sometimes they do. But that defense still leaves a difficult question: How much did their continued service help the government survive and carry on with the very practices they opposed?

For economists like me, this is an uncomfortable question worth asking. Expertise gives us influence, but things get complicated when we lend that influence to institutions and political leaders with dodgy reputations. Technocratic competence can make a government more credible even when its use of power deserves public resistance. Recently, we’ve seen that play out as well in the dictatorial regime of Rodrigo Duterte—the subject of my second book, Twin Plagues.

In Virata’s case, complicity lies in his sustained role in financing and administering the dictatorship. He didn’t necessarily steal public money or order an abuse, but nobody can deny the responsibilities he held and the regime his work helped to sustain.

People can remember his kindness and generosity, and we sympathize with the family and friends. But the country as a whole must also never forget what happened under the government Virata willingly served for so long.

There have been stringent efforts to memorialize Virata in past years, like a biography written by Sicat as well as the 2013 renaming of the UP Diliman College of Business Administration (CBA) into the Cesar E.A. Virata School of Business or VSB (a highly contested move until now; many students and faculty still insist on calling their college the CBA rather than the VSB).

At any rate, Virata’s passing should at least prompt a fuller reckoning with his record as a public servant. His personal virtues belong in his obituary—but so does his complicity in the Marcos dictatorship. – Rappler.com

Jan Carlo “JC” Punongbayan, PhD, is an associate professor at the University of the Philippines School of Economics. His professional experience includes the Securities and Exchange Commission, the World Bank Office in Manila, the Far Eastern University Public Policy Center, and the National Economic and Development Authority. JC writes a weekly economics column for Rappler. He is also co-founder of UsapangEcon.com and co-host of Usapang Econ Podcast.

His first book, False Nostalgia: The Marcos “Golden Age” Myths and How to Debunk Them, was published by Ateneo de Manila University Press in February 2023. His second book, Twin Plagues: How Duterte and COVID-19 Wrecked the Philippine Economy, was published by Penguin Random House SEA in June 2026. Follow him on Instagram (@jcpunongbayan).

articles.title: Suspected pneumonic plague in Siberia: What we know about the disease
articles.summary: After a worker at a Russian plague research institute in Siberia died October 2, 2026, nearly 200 of her contacts were under medical observation. But authorities there denied pneumonic plague had…

image.caption: The ECDC is closely monitoring the situation in Siberia after the death of a Russian laboratory workerImage: Britta Pedersen/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: UPDATE: Following initial reports raising concerns that a lab worker had died accidentally of pneumonic plague, the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) said it was now also "closely monitoring the situation."

However, in a statement published October 6, 2026, the ECDC said that "based on the limited information currently available, there are no reports of secondary cases and no evidence of sustained human-to-human transmission that would cause further spread of the disease."
What you need to know about plague

items: There are three forms of plague, all caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis.
The three forms of plague are bubonic, septicemic and pneumonic.

Bubonic plague is the most common form; it does not spread from person to person. If untreated, the bacteria can move through the body and bloodstream, causing septicemic plague, which causes internal bleeding and organ failure.
If the bacteria reach the lungs, they cause pneumonic plague. Pneumonic plague is highly contagious because it can pass from person to person through the air, for example, via coughing.
If untreated, bubonic plague kills between 30-60% of patients. The septicemic and pneumonic forms are always fatal without treatment.

blocks.text: Speculation over the death in a Russian plague laboratory

Following the death of a Russian laboratory worker, there is speculation about an outbreak of pneumonic plague, a highly contagious bacterial infection of the lungs. Russia denies there is a broader risk to the community.

Russian officials have said the laboratory worker's death was not caused by a plague pathogen. The 28-year-old died of "pneumonia of unknown origin," according to Russia's Interfax news agency, citing Rospotrebnadzor, Russia's disease-control agency. According to that agency, samples taken from the woman showed no microorganisms "related to her professional activities." This contradicts earlier information.
Local media had previously reported that the woman, who worked at an institute dedicated to fighting plague, had dropped a test tube.
She reportedly died on Friday, October 2, 2026, at the district hospital in Shelekhov, a town near Irkutsk in Siberia.

According to official Russian figures, authorities placed two hospitals and a children's clinic under quarantine. Local reports said staff at the institute were being quarantined at their workplace. The US news site Axios has reported that around 200 people who had been in contact with the woman had been placed under observation. There were no further reported infections.
Russia rejects reports of plague in Siberia

Even so, distrust of how Russia handles information persists. On one of DW's Russian-language social media channels, a user wrote: "It wouldn't surprise me if this turns into a disaster now, both in terms of the spread and the quarantine measures."
Pneumonic plague: a fast-moving lung infection
All that is known for certain, at the time of writing and first publication (October 5, 2026), is that pneumonic plague is highly contagious.

Pneumonic plague is a form of plague that infects the lungs. Like every form of the disease, it is caused by Yersinia pestis, a bacterium usually found in small mammals, such as rodents and in the fleas that feed on them.
The World Health Organization describes the pneumonic form as the most virulent type of plague.

Its incubation period can be as short as 24 hours, and it is the only form that passes easily from person to person through respiratory particles released when a sick patient coughs. This is why, according to the WHO, it can trigger severe epidemics.
Symptoms appear quickly: high fever, headache and weakness, followed by a rapidly worsening pneumonia with shortness of breath, chest pain and a cough that often brings up blood.
A person can catch pneumonic plague by breathing in the bacteria directly, or by developing it when bubonic and/or septicemic plague go untreated and spread to the lungs.
Could a Russia plague case trigger wider concern?
What is the difference between bubonic and pneumonic plague?
Pneumonic plague is not a separate disease. It is one of three forms of plague: bubonic, septicemic and pneumonic.
All are caused by the same bacterium.
What sets them apart is where the infection settles in the body, and that shapes how the disease spreads and how deadly it is.

Bubonic plague is the most common form and the one most people think of when they hear the word "plague." It usually follows a flea bite. The bacteria travel to the nearest lymph node, which swells into a painful lump known as a bubo. According to the WHO, it rarely spreads between people.

blocks.caption: The bacteria Yersenia pestis is responsible for the plagueImage: James Cavallini/BSIP/picture alliance

blocks.text: If bubonic plague goes untreated, the bacteria can move further through the body. If they spread into the bloodstream, the disease can become septicemic plague, which causes bleeding under the skin, tissue death in the fingers and toes, and organ failure. If the bacteria reach the lungs, the illness becomes pneumonic plague, the form that can pass from person to person through the air. Both septicemic and pneumonic plague can also develop directly, without a bubo appearing first.
Left untreated, bubonic plague kills between 30-60% of patients. The septicemic and pneumonic forms are always fatal without treatment.
Pneumonic plague treatment: antibiotics within the first 24 hours
Pneumonic plague is curable, but only if treatment starts quickly. The WHO warns that without treatment it can kill within 18 to 24 hours of the first symptoms.
Common antibiotics can cure the infection, and recovery rates are high when patients are treated within about a day of falling ill.

Speed is what decides the outcome. Doctors are advised not to wait for laboratory confirmation and to start antibiotics as soon as plague is suspected, according to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).

The drugs themselves are not rare or specialized. They are standard, widely used antibiotics, and patients usually need a course of up to two weeks. To stop the infection spreading, patients are kept in isolation, and wearing masks helps protect those around them, the WHO says.
Preventive antibiotics and isolation for close contacts

People close to a patient are treated as well, even if they have no symptoms. Both the WHO and the CDC recommend a seven-day course of preventive antibiotics for close contacts of anyone with pneumonic plague.
The WHO does not recommend a plague vaccine for the public. It reserves vaccination for high-risk groups, such as laboratory staff who work with the bacterium and health workers.

articles.title: California pair charged with abusing at least 14 surrogate-born children
articles.summary: Guojun Xuan and Silvia Zhang were arrested at their Arcadia mansion after 21 children were removed from their custody last year.

blocks.text: A California pair has been charged with multiple counts of abusing at least 14 surrogate-born children - some as young as two months old - and dissuading a witness.
"The number of children who were subjected to this alleged horrific abuse is unprecedented," Los Angeles District Attorney Nathan J Hochman said in a statement.
Guojun Xuan and Silvia Zhang, who US media describe as a couple, were arrested at their Arcadia mansion on Tuesday.
The pair pleaded not guilty at a Pasadena courthouse, the BBC's US partner CBS News reported.
Xuan, 66, and Zhang, 39, are accused of conspiring to subject 15 of the 16 children living in their home to repeated physical abuse, after 21 children were removed from their custody last year.

The pair ran their own surrogacy company and are accused of making false statements to at least two women who became surrogates, indicating that Zhang was struggling to conceive, according to the criminal complaint.
As of May 2025, Zhang maintained a spreadsheet that tracked 21 children, including those born to surrogates.
Officials said the investigation began that month when Zhang brought a two-month-old boy to the hospital with a head injury, telling medical staff that the baby had fallen from a bed.
The couple's lawyer Mitchell Krems said the allegation was a "mischaracterisation" based on the evidence he has reviewed, CBS News in Los Angeles reported.

Hospital staff informed law enforcement, and when police arrived at their home they discovered three different rooms called "learning centres" under the supervision of multiple nannies, which Hochman described as a "house of horrors".
The mansion allegedly had 32 motion-activated cameras which Hochman said were used by the couple to monitor the discipline given by the nannies.
Footage allegedly shows the nannies spanking, slapping or hitting the children.
One nanny, Chunmei Li, is accused of hitting the two-month-old baby who suffered the head injury two days before he was brought to the hospital.
Krems said Li was quickly fired, CBS News LA reported.

Li, 58, was previously charged with one felony count of child abuse under conditions likely to cause great bodily injury or death. Hochman said she was on the run with a $105,000 (£88,800) warrant for her arrest.
In July 2025, the couple's home was first raided by authorities, who took 21 children into state custody.
Arcadia Police Department said at the time the couple's house was first raided that the children ranged in age from two months to 13 years old, but most were between one and three years old.
Fifteen of the children were taken from the couple's home while six others were living elsewhere and also later taken into custody.
Krems said his client Xuan was innocent.
"He is being targeted for exercising his constitutional right to have a large family," CBS News quoted the lawyer as saying.
Investigators believe the surrogate mothers were from around the country and they were unaware they were carrying embryos for the couple at the same time.

Melissa Brisman, the attorney for two of the surrogates, told CBS News: "This is wonderful news that people will be held responsible for their actions and there will be consequences if you abuse the surrogacy system".
If convicted as charged, Xuan faces a possible maximum sentence of 17 years and four months in state prison, while Zhang faces up to 11 years and eight months. Li faces up to 12 years.

articles.title: Tito Sotto floats 'Tinikling' scheme using manager's checks
articles.summary: Senator-Judge Vicente “Tito” Sotto III on Wednesday floated a supposed scheme wherein manager"s checks that are unutilized or have become stale are being returned to the issuing bank, possibly to…

blocks.text: Published October 7, 2026 5:31pm

Senator-Judge Vicente “Tito” Sotto III on Wednesday floated a supposed scheme wherein manager’s checks that are unutilized or have become stale are being returned to the issuing bank, possibly to avoid audits.

This was revealed on the Day 35 of the impeachment trial, where witnesses from banks and financial firms were presented by the House prosecution panel to testify on Article 2 of the impeachment case against Vice President Sara Duterte, alleging her unexplained wealth.

“I’d just like to ask if you’re familiar with the term used by my banker friend, who told me that ‘yun daw pag-issue ng manager’s check, pagkatapos hindi ginamit, later on after the 31st of December, ibabalik, ang tawag daw do’n ‘Tinikling,’” Sotto asked Marwin Galvez, division head for Central Manila branches of Bank of the Philippine Islands (BPI).

(I’d just like to ask if you’re familiar with the term used by my banker friend, who told me that the practice of issuing a manager’s check, when it’s unused and is returned later after December 31st, is called Tinikling?)
“Gano’n daw ang ginagawa nung mga ibang umiiwas,” he added.
(That’s supposedly what some people do to evade something.)
The bank official said that he is not familiar with the term.
“Alam ko lang po ‘yung sayaw na Tinikling, Your Honor,” Galvez expressed.
(I only know the Tinikling dance, Your Honor.)

During the direct examination of Galvez, the prosecution flagged a P41.7 million worth of manager’s check linked to former president Rodrigo Duterte and VP Sara Duterte that was supposedly “floating” for years and was not being reflected in year-end balances.

Galvez confirmed the existence of such a joint peso time deposit opened on January 22, 2010, in the bank’s Julia Vargas Branch under the name “Rodrigo Roa Duterte or Rodrigo Roa Duterte and Sara Z. Duterte,” with a principal amount of P40,650,000.
He said that the time deposit had 12 rollover periods or renewals. At the last renewal in February 2011, he said the amount already increased to P41.7 million, including the interest.

In March 2011, the BPI official said a credit and debit memo showed that a manager’s check was purchased for P41.7 million. The manager’s check, however, remained unutilized after the validity period of six months.

Private prosecutor James Bryan Alih said that the prosecution intended to prove a "pattern," that a transaction in 2011 moved around for several more years and was later on used to purchase insurance policies.

“Ang punto lang naman po eventually is that ‘yung manager’s check na pinapaikot, hindi nakikita sa year-end balance kasi naka-float ‘yung pera na ‘yun. ‘Yun lang naman ‘yung gusto naming i-establish as a baseline,” Alih said.

(The only point is that the manager's check that is being circulated is not reflected in the year-end balance because the money is already floating. That's all we want to establish as a baseline.) — RSJ, GMA News
