blocks.text: The war Israel launched in response to 7 October has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians, the majority of them civilians, including about 20,000 children.

Netanyahu has also waged a years-long campaign to dismantle institutions protecting democracy inside Israel’s 1967 borders. Palestinians under Israeli military rule in the occupied West Bank do not have the rights of Israeli citizens.
Many Israelis opposed to this rightwing vision of perpetual war in a state with diminished institutions consider this election the most critical since Israel was founded in 1948, among them Margalit.

Nir Oz, like many communities targeted by Hamas, had its roots in the leftwing Zionist movement, and although the brutality of 7 October pushed some to the right, others saw their pain as bitter proof that war alone cannot offer long-term security.

“I don’t believe we can ignore the fact that Palestinians live here,” Margalit said. “We have to find a way we can live here with them and be secure. I don’t have an answer, I just know we are here to stay and they are here to stay. Maybe we need someone from the outside.”

articles.title: From films to streaming prices - how the Warner Bros deal could affect you
articles.summary: The deal is expected to alter the entertainment and news industries but could it mean higher prices for consumers?

blocks.text: From films to streaming prices - how the Warner Bros deal could affect you
Watch: What the Paramount and Warner Bros deal means for you
ByFrancisco VelasquezBusiness reporterReporting fromNew York and Regan MorrisReporting fromCalifornia
It has been months in the making but Paramount Skydance has finally completed its $110bn (£82.8bn) merger with Warner Bros Discovery.
The deal welds two legacy Hollywood powerhouses, uniting franchises like Harry Potter and Game of Thrones, into an entertainment behemoth named Skydance.
Yet behind this milestone lies strict rules about what the combined business can and cannot do - from how many films it must produce a year to the editorial independence of its newsroom.
Here are four ways this could affect you and the movies, TV and news you watch.
1. Streaming prices may rise

blocks.caption: Image caption, HBO Max is the company behind Euphoria, a series starring Zendaya

blocks.text: Image source, Eddy Chen/HBO
HBO Max is the company behind Euphoria, a series starring Zendaya

Warner Bros owns HBO Max, home to The Sopranos, House of the Dragon and Euphoria among others. Meanwhile, Paramount Skydance has Paramount+, which streams the likes of Yellowstone, Parks and Recreation and NCIS.
Combining HBO Max and Paramount+ into a single platform or bundle will likely squeeze subscribers' wallets over time.
While existing subscribers to both might enjoy short-term savings, analysts expect overall prices to rise as the combined giant seeks profitability.
The merged company, Skydance, carries a massive $80bn in debt from the deal, even as executives target $6bn in annual cost savings.
Analysts warn that consumers will ultimately bear the financial burden of the $110bn deal.

Mike Proulx, research director at Forrester, noted that with streaming services constantly raising fees to increase profitability and Skydance saddled with massive debt, price increases are likely to come.

While viewers will gain access to a broader catalog, as Skydance shifts toward a Paramount+ and HBO Max bundle rather than a single app, Proulx warns that "it's far-fetched to think it'll prevent downstream price hikes".
2. More film releases

blocks.caption: Image caption, Paramount and Warner Bros are coming together to form Skydance

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images
Paramount and Warner Bros are coming together to form Skydance
As part of a settlement deal with US states who had objected to the merger, Paramount Skydance has agreed to release a set number of films every year for the next five years.
For the first two years, that's 30 movies annually, and for the remaining period it has to release 32 films each year.
That's 156 movies in total - and the majority have to be "wide releases," meaning they must to be shown in cinemas.
The merged studio must also release at least four independent films each year.
If Skydance misses its movie quota, it could be forced to sell its 49% stake in Miramax – the studio co-founded by disgraced Hollywood mogul Harvey Weinstein.
Breanne Gilliam, a corporate lawyer at Maddin Hauser, said the film commitment is meaningful, even if it comes with an expiration date.
"Once those obligations expire, the company will have far more flexibility," she said.
"Temporary rules cannot permanently fix a structural market shift".
Once the five-year deal ends, Skydance could follow rivals like Disney and Netflix by prioritizing streaming over cinema.
As Disney's $71bn buyout of 21st Century Fox in 2019 proved, mega-deals can lead to fewer films in cinemas.
Before the acquisition, 20th Century Fox routinely released 12 to 17 movies annually in theatres, but under Disney that slate scaled down to just three to six a year.
3. Hollywood jobs could be hit

blocks.caption: Image caption, Members of the film and TV industry protested outside Paramount Studios in LA

blocks.text: Members of the film and TV industry protested outside Paramount Studios in LA
For those working behind the scenes, the merger of two historic studios has been described as a "disaster" by those on the ground.
Actors and writers recently gathered at Paramount Studios in Los Angeles to oppose the deal, accusing regulators of failing to protect industry livelihoods.
Criminal Minds star Kirsten Vangsness told the BBC she was "heartbroken".
"It's people that make this city," she said. "It's people that make entertainment, it's the everyday creatives that this industry is built on - this is who it hurts."
A report by consultancy CVL Economics for LA County estimated the merger could eliminate roughly 4,500 direct film and TV jobs, while causing $1.26bn in lost wages over three years.
The blow could hit a region that has already lost roughly a third of its film and TV workforce, about 50,000 jobs, since 2022.
Syleecia Thompson, a business professor at National University, said that "it hits small businesses, vendors, caterers and local communities".
She warned that Hollywood may become less of a "single location" and more of a "dispersed network."
Although the settlement establishes a workforce fund to retrain displaced workers, lawyers note it does not block job cuts.
"Nothing in the settlement limits layoffs," attorney Gilliam added.
4. CNN and CBS could change

blocks.caption: Image caption,  CNN White House correspondent Betsy Klein reports from outside the building

blocks.text: Image source, Reuters
CNN White House correspondent Betsy Klein reports from outside the building
To address concerns over journalistic independence at CNN and CBS, the settlement creates a news editorial independence board that will be appointed directly by Paramount.
The $110bn deal brings two major US television news operations under a single corporate roof. Before the deal, Paramount owned CBS News, and Warner Bros. owned CNN.

Both networks have faced intense political pressure - CNN was one of a handful of news organisations banned from the White House by President Donald Trump - as well as leadership shifts amid broader industry consolidation.

Paramount chief executive David Ellison has asked CNN boss Mark Thompson - the former director general of the BBC - to remain at the helm after the takeover closes. CBS News's editor-in-chief Bari Weiss will remain in her role.
Yet as Paramount targets billions in cost cuts across the merged company, staff fear the consolidation will trigger significant job losses at CNN and CBS.
Beyond potential workforce reductions, media advocates and legal experts remain deeply skeptical about whether it can ensure newsroom freedom.
Seth Stern, chief of advocacy at Freedom of the Press Foundation, described the Paramount-appointed board as "worthless".
"The board creates the same First Amendment problems it claims to solve, the government meddling in news," Stern said.
Gilliam agrees paper promises mean little without real authority. "An oversight board only has as much power as the agreement gives it. Oversight without authority is just observation," she said.
Get in touch
Are you affected by issues covered in this story? Share your experiences.

articles.title: EU seeks ways to make expansion more palatable to members
articles.summary: The European Commission has put forward ideas it hopes will both ease the EU expansion process and allay concerns among existing members. Several countries, not least war-torn Ukraine, are among the…

image.caption: Expansion was a key issue at 'Berlin Process' talks in candidate country Montenegro this month seeking to further Western Balkan integration into the EUImage: Regierung von Montenegro

blocks.text: The European Commission on Tuesday published a document called "Preparing for a wider Union," which sought to lay out new proposals on "the policy orientations and actions needed to prepare the [European] Union for future enlargements."

Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said that "Europe's future depends on the choices we make today," as she tries to encourage progress at the EU's leaders' summit this month and in other upcoming talks on the matter.

The EU's executive proposed an array of changes — including a gradual integration process for would-be members, new safeguards "to ensure that commitments undertaken during accession negotiations continue to be fulfiled steadily after accession," and changes to voting rules.

They were trying to strike a balance between simplifying the accession process, incentivizing candidate countries to continue to pursue it, and allaying concerns among existing members about potential risks or costs of expansion.

blocks.caption: Ukraine is the newest EU candidate country, seeking to accelerate the process amid Russia's invasionImage: Valentyn Ogirenko/REUTERS

blocks.text: Why is expansion coming back into focus?
In the quarter century after the end of the Cold War, the EU rapidly grew from a union of 12 member states to 28, before dipping back down to 27 when the UK left following 2016's Brexit referendum.
But the process has ground to a halt ever since, with a series of candidate countries stuck in lengthy negotiations and little apparent appetite among members to continue to expand.

In recent years, amid Russia's invasion of Ukraine and signs of the US vying for increased influence in parts of Europe, theoretical interest in expansion has picked up once more. But realizing the idea, with strict rules governing the accession process and the need for unanimous support among existing members for many core steps, has remained challenging.
EU enlargement: Montenegro on track to join bloc by 2028
What did the Commission say about expansion?
Von der Leyen said the Commission was trying to prepare institutions, adapt policies and adjust budgets to reflect shared realities to better facilitate and accommodate expansion.

"Enlargement of our Union is a geopolitical imperative," she said. "Today, we are laying the groundwork to ensure that a larger Union is also a stronger one: more resilient, more effective, and firmly anchored in the values and rules that define us."
She said that as countries progress on their path towards reform, "the EU must be ready to welcome them."

Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos said that Brussels' assessment "shows that the EU can accommodate a larger membership." But "there are areas where we see challenges we need to address," she acknowledged.
"One is the rule of law and sincere cooperation, where we are proposing stronger possibilities to prevent backsliding, including reducing funding or restricting voting rights," Kos said.
Why the US-EU rift is spilling into the Balkans
What changes are the European Commission proposing?
The Commission lays out a number of proposed changes or policies designed to smooth the accession process, including but not limited to:

items: Moving from unanimity to qualified majority voting among members in a number of the less significant votes about advancing or progressing membership bids
It makes no mention of changing the current requirement for a unanimous vote about finalizing membership applications, however
Gradual and accelerated integration of candidate countries to "bring tangible benefits to citizens and businesses," but which would remain "conditional and reversible"

"Stronger safeguards against serious backsliding on commitements undertaken during the acession negotiations" in future accession treaties, which could "in the most serious cases" extend to the suspension of voting rights
Introducing "targeted arrangements" to "significantly limit financial support and market access" for sensitive agricultural products from candidate country Ukraine

Ukraine's vast agricultural sector had prompted some concerns among EU members looking at how the bloc's budget could handle expansion, given that agriculture is a rare policy area where the bulk of spending and subsidies are orchestrated at the EU level, not by national governments

blocks.text: All these proposals will be subject to further discussion among European leaders and governments, with the next major meeting being next week's EU leaders' summit. Should they gain traction and progress, no doubt after some alterations and amendments along the way, they would ultimately have to face and pass various voting procedures to be implemented.

blocks.caption: Moldova's President Maia Sandu is also a staunch advocate of her country joining the EUImage: Vladislav Culiomza/REUTERS

blocks.text: What's the current situation with EU candidate countries?
A total of eight countries currently have formal candidate status, meaning they are seeking to join the EU and have at least begun the often lengthy process that involves.

Some hope to join the bloc sooner rather than later, not least frontrunner Montenegro, after years of negotiations. Kos told DW last week that Montenegro was currently on track to become the next EU member by 2028.
Others, like Turkey, have nominally been candidates for decades but have made no discernible progress for years.

Ukraine is the newest addition to the list, having only gained full candidate status in 2024, but it is also the one with the most pressing motivation to hurry the process along amid Russia's invasion.
Albania, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Georgia, Moldova, North Macedonia and Serbia are also all seeking membership.
A ninth country, Kosovo, is recognized as a potential candidate but not a formal one — with not all EU members recognizing Kosovo's unilateral declaration of independence from Serbia.

articles.title: Outcry in Trinidad and Tobago after passing of police bill that could threaten press freedom
articles.summary:
Journalists are calling for an urgent amendment to the Special Operations Bill, which boosts police search and seizure powers

Journalists in Trinidad and Tobago have called for an urgent…

blocks.text: Journalists in Trinidad and Tobago have called for an urgent amendment to a sweeping new bill that boosts police powers of search and seizure, which they argue threatens the country’s much-vaunted freedom of the press.
The government says the Special Operations Bill 2026, passed on 24 September, is designed to tackle alarmingly high crime and murder rates in the Caribbean nation.
The country has spent more than a year in an almost perpetual state of emergency, with police empowered to bypass normal constitutional rights around arrest, detention and search and seizure.
But journalists in Trinidad and Tobago have called for explicit exemptions in the new legislation to prevent police from searching and seizing their notebooks, phones and laptops.
In the past, journalists have been forced to challenge warrants empowering police to raid their homes and offices.

Although the country prides itself in honouring freedom of speech, ranking 19 out of 180 countries in the 2025 Reporters Without Borders press freedom index, this year it fell 13 places to 32, and journalists say they are deeply concerned about whether they can protect whistleblowers and vulnerable sources who share information on the understanding that they will be protected.

The president of the Media Association of Trinidad and Tobago (MATT), Prior Beharry, said the organisation had called for clause 15 of the bill to be urgently amended “to explicitly shield our devices and materials … and confidential source information from standard police seizure”.

Clause 15 prevents police from seizing “a tool of a lawful trade or business” or material protected by legal professional privilege. But MATT says journalism is not explicitly recognised as a protected trade, nor does the bill establish a procedure for handling confidential journalistic material discovered during searches. It wants the clause changed to “expressly name journalism as a protected lawful trade and safeguard journalists’ devices, materials and confidential sources”.

Beharry said the bill’s search‑and‑seizure powers were particularly worrying in a digital era where “the tools of a journalist is … usually [a] cell phone”. Though he said journalists had not been directly threatened under recent states of emergency, he warned that other restrictions were worsening.

“One of the issues we are having is the access to the government, the executive, including the prime minister, who has not had an official press conference for more than a year,” he said. “Ministries use state resources and we are not invited, but state media is invited.”

The independent journalist Pearce Robinson said the combination of surveillance capability, expanded search powers – without explicit protection for journalistic practice – and declining access to government ministers created a “concrete” threat to press freedom, with a particularly significant impact on investigative reporting.

“If your phone, your laptop and your notes can be searched or seized without explicit protection for journalistic material, that raises serious constitutional concerns,” he said. “Investigative journalism depends on people being able to speak confidentially.”

He also raised concerns about phone tapping and surveillance, pointing to an investigation by the Trinidad and Tobago Guardian which said that “judges approved 314 warrants to intercept communications in Trinidad and Tobago between 2020 and May 2026”.
after newsletter promotion
“My concern is not that press freedom has disappeared,” he said. “It is that several of these pressures … are accumulating at the same time.”

Pedro Cárdenas of press freedom and human rights organisation Article 19 expressed concern about the clause in the new bill. “It empowers law enforcement officers to seize any vehicle, article or document deemed likely to be of substantial value. We find this clause particularly problematic because it is vague and opens up to discussion what is substantial value or not,” he said.
He added that it “might directly counter” existing international human rights laws.
The office of the prime minister did not respond to a request for comment.

Stuart Young, Trinidad and Tobago’s former prime minister, branded the bill “unconstitutional and very dangerous”, adding that it “breaches fundamental and entrenched constitutional rights” and was passed “without a required constitutional majority in highly questionable circumstances”.
He warned that the government’s past use of emergency powers — including detaining citizens without charge — showed “the real likelihood of abuse” under the new legislation.

articles.title: France’s conundrum: How to cut spending amid protests
articles.summary: Prime Minister Lecornu is pledging to improve schools at a time when the government seeks to save billions. France's dilemma can be seen across the EU: How to cut spending when citizens are demanding…

image.caption: Protesters outside the Lycee Sophie Germain in Paris: French students are calling for better conditions in schools as the government seeks to save billionsImage: Eric Baradat/REUTERS

blocks.text: France’s Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu is unlikely to have had a quiet weekend. For almost two weeks, students across France have been protesting, angered by class cancellations, overcrowded classrooms and run-down school buildings. The protests have increasingly been overshadowed by serious clashes with police.
At the same time, the government accuses the left-wing party La France Insoumise (LFI) of exploiting the protests for political purposes and fueling the blockades.
On Friday, Education Minister Edouard Geffray tried to ease tensions by meeting with student representatives. It was unsuccessful.
Instead, a nationwide day of protest took place on Tuesday.

blocks.caption: Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu (left) and Education Minister Edouard Geffray both face increasing pressure as student protests continueImage: Telmo Pinto/NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: On Sunday evening, the prime minister took charge of the crisis. In a letter to several ministers, Lecornu called for concrete proposals: Class cancellations should be addressed more quickly, school buildings should be upgraded to cope with hotter summers, and the controversial university admissions system "Parcoursup" should become more transparent.

Initial decisions, along with funding and a timetable, are expected to be announced this month. But Macron's ally Lecornu faces one key problem: He has to promise young people more government support while his government is imposing an austerity budget on the entire country.
A signal to the markets

Last Thursday, the government submitted its 2027 budget proposal to parliament. The budget deficit is expected to fall from a projected 5.4 % of economic output this year to 5% in 2027. To make up the shortfall, the government plans to make spending cuts worth billions of euros. France is already subject to an EU excessive deficit procedure and is expected to bring its budget gap back toward the 3% limit set by the European Union.
Student protests in France: Schools shut as unrest grows

"It is an austerity budget," says Eileen Keller of the Franco-German Institute (dfi) in Ludwigsburg. At the same time, the draft is a signal to the financial markets. The government wants to show "that it is taking responsibility" and lay out a path toward reducing the deficit.
No majority in sight for the budget

The government plans to cut spending by the state itself, local and regional authorities, as well as in the social sector. Overall, Paris aims to reduce the budget by around €54 billion ($60.8 billion) compared with previously projected spending plans. Pensions alone are expected to make savings to the tune of around €5.5 billion, and more cuts are also planned in healthcare.

blocks.caption: There is currently no majority in the French parliament for the austerity budgetImage: Isa Harsin/SIPA/picture alliance

blocks.text: Whether the budget will actually be passed in its current form is still wide open. Lecornu's government does not have a parliamentary majority and relies on opposition votes. But with presidential elections coming next spring, an austerity budget is even less attractive to the opposition than it would otherwise be.
More money for schools — and more protests

The issue of education in particular shows that France's problem cannot be reduced to the formula "The state is cutting too much." The education budget is set to increase by around €1.2 billion in 2027. At the same time, the government expects around 1.7 million fewer schoolchildren by 2035.

blocks.caption: Many young people are angry about the state of the education systemImage: Nacho Doce/REUTERS

blocks.text: For Keller, this contradiction shows that money is only part of the problem. Public dissatisfaction is linked to what she calls "priorities" and the fundamental direction of the education system, including the transition from school to higher education.
Financing education is getting more costly

The difficult outlook for France is compounded by another factor: the financial markets. For many years, France was used to financing its high levels of debt at relatively low interest rates. But those days are over. The yield on 10-year French government bonds has risen sharply in recent weeks. At times, the spread over German government bonds widened to around 1.5 percentage points, the highest level since the euro debt crisis in the 2010s. The business daily Les Echos ran the headline on Monday that the country was in the "eye of the cyclone."

Market skepticism is hitting France at a particularly difficult time. With debt at around 119% of economic output, France is almost twice as heavily indebted as Germany, whose debt ratio stands at around 64%.
France students demand better schools

Step by step, old government bonds that were issued at very low interest rates are increasingly having to be replaced with new and more expensive debt. The effects of this are clearly visible in the 2027 budget. Estimated around €74 billion, the government will have to spend more on its interest payments than it can afford to spend on schools or defense. According to Finance Minister Roland Lescure, interest payments already consume more than half of the overall budget deficit.
Keller stresses that it is therefore crucial that France continues to be seen by investors as a "credible debtor." These days, however, that credibility depends on more than just economic data.
Markets keeping a close eye on election campaigns

In spring 2027, the French will elect a new president. "The election campaign, which is now gaining intensity, is being watched by the financial markets," Keller says. In an analysis for the dfi, she puts the need for fiscal consolidation at between €75 billion and €160 billion, depending on the calculation.

From the markets' perspective, political consensus on the need for the nation to tighten its belt would be helpful. But, at present, there is no sign of clarity. How the burden will be shared in the future is instead likely to become a central issue in the election campaign.
A French problem with a European dimension

France is an especially acute case. But many other European countries are also currently grappling with fiscal consolidation and how to finance the state. Europe wants to spend more on defense, modernizing its infrastructure and transitioning to renewable energy sources. At the same time, citizens still expect a certain standard of education, pensions and healthcare.

blocks.caption: Student protests are increasingly being overshadowed by violence. The signs are visible at many schools including the Lycee Vauquelin in ParisImage: Yves Herman/REUTERS

blocks.text: In France, this conflict can be observed almost in real time. The issue is not only whether the government can respond to the demands of young people, but also whether it can avoid further violence. In Paris, many are wary of the prospect of a new broad-based social movement, like the Yellow Vests protests of the past. For Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu, the coming days will be a major test.
This article was originally published in German.

articles.title: What is pneumonic plague and how does it spread?
articles.summary: The death of a worker from a Russian lab that researches plague has prompted questions about the disease.

blocks.text: Pneumonic plague is a really serious lung infection, often described as the most virulent form of plague.
There are two other types of plague: bubonic, which affects the lymph nodes; and septicaemic, which affects the blood.
Pneumonic plague can occur after an initial infection of one of these other types.
Symptoms include shortness of breath, chest pain, and often coughing up blood.
It's regarded as being more serious but less common than bubonic plague.
The global number of infections of all three types of plague varies each year, but it is probably somewhere between 1,000 to 3,000 cases.
Most of these are bubonic plague, and many of them occur in central Africa, but cases also develop in other places, including Russia, India, China, and the United States.
Prof Piero Olliaro is Professor of Poverty-Related Infectious Diseases at the University of Oxford.
He said: "Plague itself has not disappeared: the bacterium that causes it, Yersinia pestis, persists in animal reservoirs across many parts of the world.
"Around 200 rodent species can harbour the bacterium, with reservoirs found across the Americas, Eurasia and Africa.
"Sporadic human cases therefore continue to occur, but established surveillance, infection-control measures and effective antibiotic treatment are important tools for limiting their impact."
Plague is an infectious disease caused by bacteria usually found in small mammals and their fleas.
You can catch it by getting bitten by an infected flea or handling an infected animal.

But human-to-human transmission of pneumonic plague is also possible through coughing infected droplets into the air, which are then breathed in by another person, although this normally requires quite close contact.
You can also develop it if you have had septicaemic plague and the infection then spreads into the lungs.
It's thought that pneumonic plague was the main type of plague behind what is known as the Black Death, the massive outbreak that killed millions of people across Europe in the 14th Century.
Dr Zania Stamataki, Associate Professor of Viral Immunology at the University of Birmingham, says it is important that researchers are able to study diseases like plague.
"I understand why people find the idea of plague in a laboratory alarming, so it is worth saying why that work exists," she said.
"Plague is not a historical disease. It remains endemic in rodent populations across Africa, Asia and the Americas, and human cases occur every year, including outbreaks of the pneumonic form.
"Diagnostics, vaccine development and surveillance for antibiotic resistance all require laboratories that hold and study the live organism.
"This work is vital to prepare against outbreaks."
According to the World Health Organization, pneumonic plague has a very short incubation period - sometimes just 24 hours.
If it isn't diagnosed and then treated quickly, experts warn it is nearly always fatal.
But the good news is that plague responds well to antibiotics if the treatment starts early.
Dr Malick Gibani, Clinical Associate Professor in Bacterial Vaccinology at Imperial College London, says the infection is widely recognised as a serious threat to public health.
"Pneumonic plague is a very severe manifestation of plague disease.
"Some textbooks will say it has 100% mortality if left untreated, and it's difficult to have accurate figures in the modern age.
"It is treatable with antibiotics, particularly if started early.
"That's why anyone with high-risk potential exposure might be offered post-exposure prophylaxis with antibiotics and/or quarantine."
In the Russian case, it is still not yet clear whether the person who died was infected by pneumonic plague.

The authorities in Russia have issued a statement saying that tests had shown "no microorganisms associated with the patient's professional activities" – and so at this stage it is still not quite clear what has happened.
US President Donald Trump said Washington was looking "very strongly" at the case, while the Centers for Disease Control (CDC) said there was "no indication of a broader threat to the United States".
The UK's Health and Safety Authority said it was seeking more information, but that the risk to Britain's population was "very low".

articles.title: Munich up against at least six competitors for 2036 Olympics
articles.summary: The International Olympic Committee has revealed the six other countries intending to bid for the 2036 Olympic Games. This comes after Germany selected Munich as its Olympic candidate.

image.caption: Munich hosted the 1972 Summer Olympic GamesImage: Sven Hoppe/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Munich's bid for the 2036 Summer Olympics will be up against at least six candidates from Europe, Asia, and Africa. On Tuesday, the International Olympic Committee (IOC) announced that, in addition to Germany, Hungary, Turkey, India, Qatar, South Korea, and South Africa all intend to bid for the Games. All are currently engaged in the "Continuous Dialogue" stage of the bidding process with the IOC.

However, there could be further applicants, as the deadline for interested parties to submit a bid is October 31. The candidates are to present their plans virtually to the Future Host Commission in November. In March 2027, the IOC is to deliberate, analyze, and narrow down the field of applicants to a group selected to enter into the Strategic Dialogue stage.
A subsequent Targeted Dialogue stage with one or more bidders is planned for 2028, with the final decision on the 2036 Olympic host expected at the IOC Session in the summer of 2029.
However, the IOC did not disclose exactly which cities, alongside Munich, are in the running – although Ahmedabad, Doha, Budapest, and Istanbul are seen as possible hopefuls.

Munich secured its bid late last month after beating the Cologne/Rhine-Ruhr region in a vote by delegates of the German Olympic Sports Confederation. The city last hosted the Games in 1972. Berlin had withdrawn its bid in the days leading up to the vote.

blocks.caption: As a swimmer Kirsty Coventry won two Olympic gold medals for ZimbabweImage: Patrick Meinhardt/AFP

blocks.text: 'Best possible experience for the athletes'
"Wherever the Games take place, one thing must never change: athletes have to be at the heart of everything we do," IOC President Kirsty Coventry said.

"As an athlete, you spend years working to make your Olympic dream come true. The experience you have when you finally reach the Olympic Games stays with you for the rest of your life," added the former swimmer who won gold in the 200-meter backstroke for Zimbabwe at the 2004 Athens and 2008 Beijing Summer Games.
"That is why, for every future host, delivering the best possible experience for the athletes must always be the starting point."
Munich bid sees itself as well-positioned

The IOC is to evaluate the bidders' proposals based on "technical factors." These include a master plan for competition venues and the athlete experience, the financing strategy, political and public support, the capacity to deliver the event, and a sustainability strategy. The German Olympic Sports Confederation believes Munich is well-positioned in all these areas.

The Munich bid is not focused solely on 2036 but was also designed with 2040 and 2044 in mind. If it misses out on 2036, Munich can expect to face a similarly large pool of competitors for the following two Summer Games. According to an IOC statement, there are National Olympic Committees "taking part in noncommittal talks with the IOC about hosting future Olympic Games beyond 2036."
This article was adapted from German.

articles.title: Lionel Messi plays final Argentina national team game
articles.summary: Lionel Messi turned his official farewell to Argentina into a gala performance, contributing a penalty and two assists in a 3-0 win over Benin on Tuesday at the Monumental Stadium in Buenos Aires,…

image.caption: Argentina's forward Lionel Messi acknowledges the crowd following the international friendly football match between Argentina and Benin at the Mas Monumental stadium in Buenos Aires on Tuesday. (Juan Mabromata / AFP via Getty Images)

blocks.text: Soccer

Lionel Messi turned his official farewell to Argentina into a gala performance, contributing a penalty and two assists in a 3-0 win over Benin on Tuesday at the Monumental Stadium in Buenos Aires, where the crowd offered a deafening final ovation to the genius who defined the footballing pulse of a nation for two decades.
Superstar helps national team to 3-0 victory
In front of 85,000 fans, the superstar capped off an international career spanning 21 years, 126 goals, a 2022 World Cup victory, and two Copa America titles.

"It was a source of great pride to wear this jersey for over 20 years," Messi told the crowd, speaking into a microphone from the center of the pitch. "I never stopped fighting, never stopped giving my all. I would love to keep coming back forever, because playing for the Argentine national team is the most beautiful thing that can happen to you."
His teammates — many of them overcome with emotion — along with the coaching staff led by Lionel Scaloni and the fans, gave him a standing ovation.

"I'm going to miss you all. Now I'll be on your side, supporting the national team and the guys who come next," Messi promised. "When we're united, we're stronger than anyone and can overcome anything. Tough times lie ahead, because what this group achieved won't be easy to repeat."
Orchestrating the win

Following a corner kick taken by Messi, defender Nicolas Otamendi connected with a header to open the scoring in the 48th minute. Messi then provided an assist to young talent Nicolas Paz, who paid tribute to the star with an exquisite left-foot finish in the 61st.
Ten minutes later, Messi buried a left-foot penalty into the top corner, adding to his tally as the Albiceleste's all-time leading scorer.
"Ole, ole, Messi," the crowd chanted in his honour.

items: Ronaldo quits Portugal camp after learning he won't start game, vows to one day tell truth over exit

blocks.text: Despite still playing at a high level at age 39, Messi announced on Aug. 31 that the end of his time with Argentina was set.

Messi played his final match — his 208th for Argentina — amid a spectacular fireworks display. He wore a special edition Albiceleste jersey featuring wider vertical stripes than the standard design, a giant sun, and a golden No. 10 on the back. The back detail featured a goat's horns in the print — a nod to the "GOAT," referencing both the animal and his status as the "Greatest of All Time."

Ten minutes after kickoff in the international friendly, the referee paused the match to honor the Argentine captain. Rivals and teammates approached to greet him while fans rose for a standing ovation. Messi raised his hand in acknowledgment.

After the match ended, he thanked his teammates for the titles they had won and left them with a directive: "We need to build a strong, united group because there are people who want the national team to fail, and we shouldn't give them the satisfaction."
From heartbreak to World Cup glory

A successor to the legendary Diego Maradona, Messi made his senior national team debut in 2005. His journey was fraught with frustration until 2022, when he finally lifted the World Cup — a triumph that secured his place in the pantheon of the sport's greatest players and cemented his status as a national hero in Argentina.

Accompanied by his sons Thiago, Mateo, and Ciro, Messi was overcome with emotion as the Argentine national anthem played, sung by a veteran of the 1982 Falklands War. Goalkeeper Emiliano Martinez tried to comfort him by placing an arm around his shoulders.

items: More soccer coverage

blocks.text: "It's not a goodbye, it's a `farewell forever,' Captain" — that was the message Rebeca Arias and Daniel Lema emblazoned on a hat designed for the occasion. On the brim, they drew various depictions of Messi corresponding to each of the six World Cups he contested. The young couple traveled more than 1,000 kilometers (620 miles) from their native Tucuman to witness his final performance.
"We believe this is a unique moment. It's all worth it — being here, making the journey we did. Something like this might never happen again with a player," Arias remarked.

In the last World Cup, Messi went close to another title, falling just short after a 1-0 defeat to Spain in the final. However, the runner-up finish didn't overshadow his remarkable performance in the tournament — featuring eight goals and four assists.
"The match against England took a huge toll on us; the reality is that we were running on fumes," he explained, referring to the dramatic 2-1 semifinal victory.

His contribution was so pivotal that Messi has once again entered the conversation for the Ballon d'Or, competing against the two top contenders to succeed him: Spaniard Lamine Yamal and Frenchman Kylian Mbappe.
The Argentine star remains the only footballer to have won the award eight times.
"I am proud to be Argentine and to have been able to fulfill this dream with all of you," he concluded, before taking a solitary victory lap to cherish the fans' final chants of "Messi, Messi."
Messi receives honourary doctorate
Before his farewell at the stadium, Messi received an honorary doctorate from the University of Buenos Aires (UBA), a public institution.

The academic institution presented the honour at the national team's training complex in the suburb of Ezeiza. The star was awarded a diploma and a medal in recognition of his performance with the national team, as well as his influence both on and off the pitch.

articles.title: Germany shaken by espionage and treason allegations
articles.summary: The former head of Germany's foreign intelligence service, the BND, has been accused of spying for a foreign country. Never before has a German official of August Hanning's stature been accused of…

image.caption: Former BND chief August Hanning has been arrested on espionage chargesImage: Michael Kappeler/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: If the allegations are confirmed, it would be an espionage case of historic proportions for Germany: August Hanning, former head of the Federal Intelligence Service (BND), has been arrested, with the federal prosecutor accusing him of espionage, treason and attempted treason.

August Hanning, now 80, headed the BND from 1998 to 2005. But even before then, he had enjoyed a meteoric rise within the security apparatus. After leaving the BND, he served as state secretary in the Federal Interior Ministry, then moved into the private sector and worked as a security consultant.

According to the federal prosecutor's office, his informant was his former chief-of-staff, named in the statement only as Manfred D.*, who went on to hold this position under Hanning's successors from March 2012 to March 2026. D. thus had access to a great deal of classified information.
Former German spy chief arrested for espionage
Classified information from the chancellor's office

Manfred D. is alleged to have passed on nearly 2,000 BND documents — some of them highly sensitive — to Hanning over the course of several years in exchange for money. Hanning is then said to have used the information in his private consultancy business.

The most serious allegation is that Hanning is said to have maintained close contact with an employee of a foreign intelligence service for years and to have leaked classified information to him. It is not known which country was involved, but reports say it is not Russia.

Investigators also mention an analysis that Hanning is said to have prepared for an employee of another foreign intelligence service. However, it is not certain whether the analysis ever reached that person.

The classified information also concerned the routine meetings of the heads of German security agencies at the chancellery. Topics included, among other things, the Iranian nuclear program and analyses of the Russian armed forces.

Since intelligence from foreign partner agencies is also said to have been shared in this context, this could also undermine their trust in the German BND and lead to difficulties in future intelligence cooperation with Germany.
Hanning came under scrutiny in an entirely different context
"A good agent is one who doesn't draw attention to himself," Hanning was once quoted as saying. When he finally drew attention to himself, it was in an entirely different context.

In September 2025, the Hamburg state police searched Hanning's home and offices in connection with the famous case of the kidnapping involving Christina Block, heiress to the steakhouse restaurant chain Block House. State prosecutors in Hamburg accused her of having ordered the kidnapping of her two youngest children in late 2023 due to a custody dispute.

A little over a year before the operation to bring the children back, there is said to have already been a failed kidnapping attempt. At the time, there were suspicions that Hanning was involved, which he denies.

But during a search in 2025, investigators found an electronic storage device containing top-secret BND documents. The police handed the documents over to the federal prosecutor's office, which launched a covert investigation against Hanning and Manfred D. in May 2026. The most recent documents found so far are said to date from June 2022.
Greens demand consequences

Throughout its history, the BND has seen a number of espionage cases, some of them spectacular. In the 1960s, Heinz Felfe headed the "Counterintelligence: Soviet Union" division while simultaneously working for the Soviet secret service, the KGB.

In 2014, a BND employee was exposed as a spy for the US CIA. There is also an ongoing trial against a BND agent accused of betraying secrets to Russia's FSB in September and October 2022 — that is, after the start of the war in Ukraine. Yet never before has a former official of August Hanning's stature been at the center of suspicion of espionage.

"The BND launched extensive internal investigations early on and without delay, which corroborated the suspicions," said current BND President Martin Jäger. "For the BND and for me, there can be no compromises when it comes to internal security."

However, there was some fierce criticism from the political sphere. Günter Krings of the conservative governing party, the Christian Democratic Union (CDU), told the Rheinische Post newspaper: "The mere suspicion that a former BND chief is selling secrets is damaging to trust in our security agencies."

Konstantin von Notz of the environmentalist Green Party and deputy chair of the parliamentary committee that oversees the intelligence services said: "These are serious and grave allegations that have been leveled against August Hanning." Speaking on behalf of his party, he called for greater scrutiny of lobbying activities by former top officials and those with the highest security clearances. "These are clearly also a gateway for hostile intelligence services," von Notz said. The federal government must put an immediate stop to these "illegitimate practices."

Clara Bünger, domestic policy spokesperson for the socialist Left Party group in the Bundestag, went even further: "The investigations against former BND chief Hanning show once again: The intelligence services themselves are a security risk."
This article was originally written in German.

*Editor's note: DW follows the German press code, which stresses the importance of protecting the privacy of suspected criminals or victims and urges us to refrain from revealing full names in such cases.

articles.title: Paramount and Warner Bros merge into one Hollywood giant
articles.summary: Paramount has completed an $81 billion purchase of Warner Bros. Discovery, as its owner Skydance creates a new entertainment behemoth. Billionaire David Ellison's hostile takeover bid defeated rival…

image.caption: 'That's all folks,' Warner Bros. and Paramount and their subsidiaries will all be bundled under a new banner: Skydance Corp.Image: Samuel Boivin/NurPhoto/IMAGO

blocks.text: Paramount on Tuesday finalized its takeover of Warner Bros. Discovery, completing a hostile acquisition that was months in the making and almost faltered at several hurdles.
The takeover cost a total of around $81 billion (roughly €72 billion), or almost $111 billion including the Warner Bros. debts passed on as part of the deal.
The merger brings together two of the oldest US filmmaking studios and will form a new giant called Skydance Corporation.
Why Skydance Corp.? Who's behind the new behemoth?
The new name Skydance hails from billionaire investor David Ellison, who first bought out Paramount and its subsidiaries and then moved on to target the much larger fish that is Warner Bros.
The bid faced stiff competition in a bidding war with Netflix, and later scrutiny from US regulators and politicians, but ultimately went through.
"Today is a historic day, not just for Skydance but for our entire industry," said Ellison, whose family has ties to US President Donald Trump.
Skydance shares began trading on the New York Stock Exchange on Tuesday under the ticker SKYD, while Warner Bros. Discovery shareholders will receive about $31 per share.
The deal closed less than a week after a federal judge in California approved a settlement between Paramount and 12 US states that had sued to block the transaction on antitrust grounds.

As well as the two giant film studios, Paramount Pictures and Warner Bros. Pictures, the deal also brings together the CBS News and CNN news networks, and the HBO and CBS television brands. Ellison says he plans to merge the subscription streaming platforms Paramount+ and HBO Max.
Ellison will serve as chairman and CEO of the new company. Former Mattel boss Ynon Kreiz is operating as co-CEO in charge of day-to-day operations.

Skydance Corp. looks set to have a total revenue in the region of $70 billion, based on the performance to date of its component parts. It says it's targeting cost savings of around $6 billion within three years as it takes advantage of overlaps created by the merger.

articles.title: Russia responds to US help offer after death of plague researcher
articles.summary: The US and Russia have each offered to help each other tackling infectious diseases.

blocks.text: Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has urged people not to "listen to various rumours" after a Russian lab technician died at a plague research centre in Siberia.
Peskov called for people to follow only information from Russia's public health watchdog, which named the official cause of death of the lab technician as pneumonia of unknown origin.
BBC Russia editor Steve Rosenberg also asked Peskov about US President Donald Trump's offer of support to Russia.

articles.title: US, Israeli and European far-right figures to gather for conference in Israel
articles.summary: Trump’s counter-terrorism ‘czar’, Sebastian Gorka, was scheduled to speak at conference but White House says he will no longer attend A National Conservatism (NatCon) conference beginning today in…

blocks.text: A National Conservatism (NatCon) conference beginning today in Jerusalem advertises a talk from the Trump administration’s anti-terrorism czar alongside speeches from far-right Israeli politicians, European figures who have faced disciplinary action over alleged antisemitism, and Christian nationalist and far-right figures from the United States.

The Jerusalem event is perhaps the most significant recent gathering to feature large contingents of Israeli nationalists alongside Christian nationalists and far-right European nationalists from a milieu sometimes shadowed by accusations of antisemitism.

Sebastian Gorka, a senior White House official whose May anti-terrorism strategy promised to target and neutralise groups “whose ideology is anti-American, radically pro-transgender, and anarchist”, was scheduled to speak at the Jerusalem event, and his presence is still advertised on the website.

But when the Guardian contacted the White House for comment on Gorka’s attendance at the conference, a spokesperson advised that he would no longer be attending due to a scheduling conflict, and that he had condemned Hamas’s 7 October attack on Israel.

blocks.caption: Sebastian Gorka at the AmericaFest 2024 conference, sponsored by conservative group Turning Point in Phoenix, Arizona, on 20 December 2024.   Photograph: Cheney Orr/Reuters

blocks.text: From Israel, the program lists Bezalel Smotrich, the finance minister, self-declared “fascist homophobe” and internationally sanctioned extremist, and Rabbi Shmuel Eliyahu, who in 2023 called for an atom bomb to be dropped on Gaza and was earlier ordered to face disciplinary proceedings for racist incitement against Palestinians.
The Guardian contacted both men for comment.

From Europe come Hans-Georg Maaßen, who once led Germany’s domestic intelligence agency but in 2023 faced an expulsion attempt by his then party, the CDU, for “statements in the language of the milieu of antisemites and conspiracy ideologues”, and Austria’s Harald Vilimsky, whose far-right Freedom party has been subject to a policy of non-engagement by Israel’s own government.

According to Israeli media reports, Vilimsky has played a key role in building a rapprochement between the Freedom party – whose first two leaders after its founding in 1956 were former SS officers – and Tel Aviv. He has visited the country repeatedly and in January reportedly led a European delegation to the country that was received by Benjamin Netanyahu, the Israeli prime minister, despite criticism from Austria’s own Jewish community.

In a statement, Maaßen wrote: “I firmly reject the claim that I made ‘statements in the language of the milieu of antisemites and conspiracy ideologues’. This deliberately vague wording was never a concrete accusation but a politically motivated label, designed to damage my reputation and to discredit critics of the political mainstream of the time,” Vilimsky was also contacted for comment.

blocks.caption: Hans-Georg Maaßen, former head of the Germany domestic intelligence service takes part in a constituency meeting of the Christian Democratic Union (CDU) district associations in Suhl, eastern Germany, on 30 April 2021.  Photograph: Jens Schlueter/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: The American contingent includes William Wolfe, a self-described Christian nationalist who has called for “mass deportations, denaturalizations, and remigration” to preserve a white Christian majority, and Jonathan Keeperman, the publisher unmasked by the Guardian in 2024 as the man behind the far-right internet persona “L0m3z”.
Keeperman did not address questions sent to him when asked for comment. Wolfe did not respond directly to questions on his attendance at NatCon, instead sending personal insults.

Dr Brendan McGeever, co-director of Birkbeck University’s Institute for the Study of Antisemitism, said: “Many attendees at NatCon view Israel not just as an ally but as an embodiment of the exclusionary ethnostate they wish to establish. National Conservatism sees in Israel a blueprint for the realization of a white, Christian nation built on racialized exclusion, while far-right Israeli attenders at NatCon often argue that partnering with white Christian nationalists is the best way to protect Israel. It is racism that binds these forces together.”

Attenders will also share a stage with high-profile conservatives including Heritage Foundation president Kevin Roberts, and former deputy national security adviser Victoria Coates, who is now vice-president at Heritage’s Davis Institute for National Security and Foreign Policy.
The Guardian contacted Heritage with questions about their attendance at NatCon.

Last October Roberts defended Tucker Carlson after the broadcaster gave a friendly interview to the white nationalist and Holocaust denier Nick Fuentes, saying in a video that “the venomous coalition attacking him are sowing division”. He later called the phrase “a terrible choice of words”, and said he and Heritage would speak out against antisemitism. In July a Heritage spokesperson said the thinktank’s “record opposing antisemitism is long, consistent and public”. In May, Heritage elected Yoram Hazony to its board.

blocks.caption: Heritage Foundation president Kevin Roberts introduces former vice-president Mike Pence during an event to promote his new book at the conservative thinktank on 19 October 2022 in Washington. Photograph: Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images

blocks.text: Roberts and Wolfe are among the NatCon Jerusalem attenders singled out last month by the evangelical conservative commentator Erick Erickson, in a broadside against “a group of white guys” who “have subtly inserted themselves into conservative institutions and church organizations” and who “to varying degrees … embrace white nationalism, antisemitism”.

Erickson’s principal target was the shampoo tycoon and would-be “warlord” Charles Haywood, the subject of extensive previous reporting in the Guardian, but he also singled out Heritage fellow Scott Yenor, another Jerusalem speaker. He was supported in his efforts by other NatCon attenders, including the writer Rod Dreher.
The Guardian contacted Haywood and Erickson for comment.

Matthew Taylor, a senior visiting fellow at the Georgetown Center for Faith and Justice and author of the new book Defying Tyrants, said: “I think they were trying to find a way to kind of carve out a version of Christian nationalism that could synchronize with kind of European and Israeli politics … and I think what they’re discovering is kind of the impossibility of that.”

He added: “[Hazony is] running up against the limits of that project because the reality is that you can’t simply stir up abstract Christian nationalism. One side of the Christian nationalist coalition is very aligned with Israel, is very Christian Zionist, the other side is leaning hard into this antisemitic impulse.”

The gathering is the latest in a series of NatCon conferences held in the United States and abroad since 2019 by the Edmund Burke Foundation, whose founder is the Israeli nationalist and rightwing intellectual Yoram Hazony.
The conferences are high-profile gatherings of the international national conservative movement, which scholars describe as the most influential strand of an anti-liberal “New Right”.

Past NatCons have featured JD Vance, Viktor Orbán, Giorgia Meloni and Nigel Farage, and have drawn accusations of racism and extremism since a speaker at the first Washington conference argued for an immigration policy of “more whites and fewer nonwhites”. Conference organizer Hazony, reportedly said at that time that the speaker’s views were “legitimate and should be heard and debated”. In 2024 a Brussels mayor ordered police to shut the event down before a court overturned him.
The Guardian contacted Hazony for comment.

Gorka is listed for a 7 October plenary titled “The Meaning of October 7”, alongside Israel’s diaspora affairs minister, Amichai Chikli, and the former Polish president Andrzej Duda. The Guardian previously reported on a video in which Gorka offered Israeli leaders advice on Hamas: “Kill every single one of them. God bless Israel. God bless Judeo-Christian civilisation.”

In August 2024 Smotrich said of Gaza: “Nobody will let us cause 2 million civilians to die of hunger, even though it might be justified and moral, until our hostages are returned.” Britain sanctioned him on 10 June 2025, acting with Australia, Canada, New Zealand and Norway. It held him responsible for “inciting, promoting and/or supporting” abuses, “in particular acts of aggression and violence against Palestinian individuals in the West Bank”.

Rabbi Eliyahu, who for decades has served as chief rabbi of Safed, a public office in Israel, remarked of Palestinians in Gaza in a lecture his office posted to YouTube in November 2023, “Drop an atom [bomb] on them? It’s an option,” he said. The disciplinary hearing Israel’s high court ordered in 2020 was reportedly not held until June 2024, and its outcome kept from the public.

The conference’s co-sponsors include the Sovereignty Movement and Regavim, the organisation Smotrich founded. The ultranationalist Israeli television news outlet Channel 14 says it is producing the event with Hazony’s foundation and his Herzl Institute. The conference website does not currently list the channel as a partner.
The Guardian contacted Channel 14 for comment.

One panel is titled “Immigration and Cultural Replacement”. Maaßen’s talk is billed as “Why Elites Embrace Mass Migration as a Tool of Cultural, Racial, and Political Transformation”. A fellow panelist, Nathan Pinkoski of the Center for Renewing America, wrote the introduction to a 2025 edition of The Camp of the Saints, a novel Dreher at one time called “racist”. Dreher appears to have since softened that view.
The Guardian contacted Pinkoski for comment.
Vilimsky reportedly told a Budapest conference in April 2024: “We do not want Mohammed to become the most common name in our countries.” He is listed for a NatCon plenary on 7 October.

Gideon Sa’ar, the foreign minister, who last month welcomed a speech by the FPÖ leader, Herbert Kickl, at a Strasbourg event Vilimsky organised with Likud, as making possible “a substantive, open and sincere dialogue” despite the ongoing disengagement, is listed for the conference dinner on 6 October.

Wolfe told a Texas audience in February: “My boys all look like me. And I want my children to grow up in a country where they’re not minorities.” He has called Erickson’s essay “a call for the assassination of a group of conservative Christians”. His conference bio says he served at the state department and the Pentagon in the first Trump administration.

As previously reported in the Guardian Haywood’s private foundation gave the Edmund Burke Foundation, which organizes the NatCon conferences, $25,000 for “general operations” in the year to June 2023, its tax filing shows.

Hazony’s former communications director was among the Jewish conservatives who criticised him in January, after he blamed an “antisemitism-industrial complex” for failing to make the case against Tucker Carlson. He has since refused Carlson a speaking slot in Jerusalem, and on 28 September called the broadcaster’s show “the leading clearinghouse for antisemitism on the political Right in America”.

Taylor, the religion scholar, said: “[Hazony is] still trying to play an older game of drawing boundary lines and saying, oh, there is an antisemitic far right that is the fringe that we have to cut off … But Tucker Carlson is not [fringe]. Tucker Carlson is about as mainstream today in rightwing politics as you can get.”
The Guardian contacted the Carlson Network’s press office for comment.

McGeever, the antisemitism scholar, wrote: “Yoram Hazony may express bewilderment about this surge of antisemitism, but it is baked into the very political alliances he has forged. His allies have repeatedly promoted ideas about ‘globalist elites’ and ‘secret cabals’ which utilize the same structural logic of antisemitic conspiracy theories.”
The conference runs from 6 to 8 October at Jerusalem’s International Convention Center.

articles.title: Former UN food agency official claims he was fired for highlighting hunger in Gaza
articles.summary: Benjamin Davis appealing against dismissal from FAO, after being accused by director general of playing ‘political games’ A former senior UN food agency official has alleged he was fired last week…

blocks.text: A former senior UN food agency official has alleged he was fired last week for his work highlighting hunger in Gaza, and has launched an appeal against his dismissal.

Benjamin Davis said the leadership of the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) had refused to renew his contract as director of its rural transformation and gender equality division because his team had published a brief on hunger in Gaza and held a seminar on the subject last year, and because he had taken part in weekly “moment of silence” vigils on FAO grounds for those killed.

The seminar on hunger in Gaza last September triggered a complaint from the Israeli mission to the FAO, which also sent a diplomat to take pictures of staff taking part a moment of silence gathering last October, according to a FAO staff report filed at the time.

Davis, 62 and a Spanish-American dual citizen, left the FAO last week after 26 years of service. Video of the event shows FAO staff standing and applauding him as he left the Rome headquarters for the last time.

“It’s a nice feeling that I’m not alone, that other people are behind me in this,” Davis said. “I was stopped constantly in the hallways by people, even those that I didn’t know, just to shake my hand or just to thank me or just to say that they supported me or that they were upset.”

The FAO did not respond to the Guardian’s request for comment on Monday, but the organisation’s director general, Qu Dongyu, appeared to refer to Davis’s dismissal in public remarks last Tuesday, in which he threatened to fire more people for what he deemed to be political activism.

blocks.caption: Benjamin Davis had worked for the FAO for 26 years before his dismissal. Photograph: Giuseppe Carotenuto/FAO

blocks.text: “We are not going to allow you to play the game here of human rights,” said Qu, a veteran Chinese agronomist. “Of course human rights are very important, but they have a human rights agency in Geneva. If you want to take care [of human rights], go there.”

“Thats why [when] some senior members play political games here, I fire him,” he said, suggesting that Davis had violated staff regulations. “I’m a very soft person. I didn’t fire that many. I’m going to use my last year … to fire more if they’re against the law.”
Davis said he and fellow FAO staff members had been stunned by Qu’s remarks.

“Even more than the threat about firing people was just what he said about human rights. I think that really shocked people because it undermined the foundations of why we’re here basically, or why FAO is part of the United Nations and why the United Nations exists,” he said.
“We’re surely an organisation which is based on human rights, right?” Davis added, pointing to the FAO slogan: “Leave no one behind.”

The official letter informing Davis that his contract would not be renewed said that Qu was “no longer confident in your ability to discharge your obligations in the manner required of a senior international civil servant”.

The letter cited paragraphs in the official code of conduct for international civil servants regarding “honesty, truthfulness, impartiality and incorruptibility” and limits on public expression of personal views on “controversial matters”.
In his written response, Davis said that approach taken by FAO leadership was “simply wrong”.

“Silence in the face of suffering and injustice is not neutrality, it is complicity,” he wrote. “Shutting down discussion on the starvation of the Palestinian people weakens the reputation of the organisation and the legitimacy of our mandate. Being true to our mandate calls for a frank and open discussion around starvation, famine, and genocide in Palestine and elsewhere.”

Davis said that FAO leadership had previously criticised him for a briefing paper published by his team in May last year describing the level of hunger in Gaza and setting it in the context of international humanitarian law.

“The current conditions in the Gaza Strip … reflect a gross violation of the right to food and the unlawful obstruction of humanitarian assistance,” the report said. It was removed from the FAO website a few weeks later on the orders of its leadership.
Davis led a seminar on the same subject in September 2025, which led to a complaint from the Israeli mission to the FAO and other Rome-based international agencies.

Davis said he had also been criticised for taking part in moment of silence gatherings held by concerned staff in the FAO car park every Thursday, in remembrance of those in Gaza who had died of hunger. There was an altercation there on 23 October when a woman identifying herself as an Israeli diplomat appeared and took photographs of those attending.

“The person explained she was the permanent representative of Israel, and asked if we were allowed to do these events, and asked specifically who says we could not take photographs,” a report by a FAO witness on the day of the incident said.
On being told she could not take photographs, the woman complained to FAO security that she was being harassed, the report said. The Israeli embassy in Rome said it had no comment on the report.

Davis said that the Gaza briefing paper, the associated seminar, and the weekly moments of silence had all been approved by FAO management, and he had not been told at the time that they represented violations of the code of conduct. He said he had lodged a formal appeal against his dismissal.

“I filed the appeal mostly as a matter of principle, not because I’m looking for or expecting any monetary compensation or anything like that,” Davis said. “I have requested to be reinstated, and also for them to take back the accusations that they made against me.”

articles.title: Kenya confirms first Ebola case and says patient has died
articles.summary:
Health minister says 28 contacts identified after death of citizen who arrived from DRC on Saturday

Kenya ⁠has recorded its ⁠first confirmed ​Ebola case, a Kenyan citizen who had been living…

blocks.text: Kenya ⁠has recorded its ⁠first confirmed ​Ebola case, a Kenyan citizen who had been living in the Democratic ⁠Republic of the Congo and arrived in Nairobi on Saturday, the health minister, Aden ⁠Duale, has said.
The patient has since died, ​and 28 contacts ‌have been identified ‌so far including family members and health ‌workers, Duale told a press conference.
DRC has been battling its largest-ever Ebola outbreak, caused by the rare Bundibugyo species.

The outbreak was declared in mid-May but may have ‌started months earlier and has so far resisted containment efforts, with the central African ​country recording more than 8,000 cases and over 4,000 deaths.
The outbreak spread to Uganda, which reported 20 cases and two ⁠deaths, but the World Health Organization declared Uganda ​free ​of the disease in ​August.
Ebola spreads through direct contact ​with the ‌body fluids of ​infected ​people, living or dead. It can cause fever, vomiting, diarrhoea and, in severe cases, internal and external bleeding.

articles.title: From competing for food to a gold medal: the stories behind India’s Asian Games winners
articles.summary:
The country’s 85-medal haul included athletes who trained with limited money and borrowed equipment. Plus, the Mumbai performer turning everyday absurdities into comedy

In a country where…

blocks.text: In a country where cricket eclipses every other sport, the recently concluded Asian Games offered a much-needed reminder of India’s breadth of sporting talent. In this edition of the games, in Japan, India won 85 medals: 21 golds, 27 silver and 37 bronze medals. I admit I did not know many of the players competing, or even some of the sports they play before putting this piece together. Learning about the stories, I wonder why not.
There were individual breakthroughs, records broken and history made. There were also hard-fought team victories, including the Indian women’s hockey team gold medal after a 44-year wait.

Sports broadcaster Siddharth Pandey cited an old saying in the world of sport: “You cannot be what you cannot see.” For Pandey, one of the most heartening sights was families and communities rallying around the four female players from the north-eastern states. (The region has endured decades of conflict and is often overlooked in the national conversation.) “We simply cannot underestimate the impact these games and medals have on future generations taking up non-cricketing sport and wanting to excel in it,” he told me.

Recognition is also important. Vidya Pillai, the first Indian woman to win a snooker world championship has spoken about her sport not getting the attention or respect it deserves. She felt unacknowledged following her 2023 feat, despite the fact that it came after six unsuccessful world finals and she beat two former world champions along the way.
Behind India’s medal glory are dozens of athletes and families who have struggled financially, trained with limited facilities, and often without much institutional support.

blocks.caption: Indian athletes at the closing ceremony of the 2026 Asian Games, in Japan. Photograph: Chalinee Thirasupa/Reuters

blocks.text: So this week, I am sharing a sample of the many extraordinary stories from different parts of the country. These are only a fraction of the champions to emerge from the games, yet they provide a glimpse of the possibilities that can open up when a country sees and celebrates sporting talent across the spectrum.

Neeru Dhanda (gold in trap shooting): Dhanda’s family in Haryana’s Jind relies on the government’s food subsidy programme and she began her sporting journey using a borrowed shotgun with tin cans as targets. Right before the games began, the 26-year-old spent a few days in a hospital recovering from an illness instead of training. But last week, as rain lashed the shooting range in Urenocho, she became the first Indian woman to win an individual gold in trap shooting at Asian games. She won a second gold in mixed team trap event as well as a silver in the women’s team trap event.

Vithya Ramraj (gold in 4x400m): Ramraj was one of the breakout stars of the event with a three-medal haul. NDTV reported that her father had to borrow money to support Ramraj and her twin sister’s athletic careers. Alongside the team gold in 4x400m, she won a silver in the mixed 4x400m relay. She also broke Indian legend PT Usha’s long-held national record in 400m hurdles which won her a bronze medal.

Sahil Jadhav (gold in compound mixed archery team and men’s compound team): Not long ago, Jadhav contemplated quitting archery, frustrated by not making the progress he had hoped for. He had been forced to compete with borrowed arrows for selection trials, the New Indian Express reported, adding that his mother sold her jewellery to buy him professional compound bows. Now, the 25-year-old has two gold medals and an automatic entry to the 2028 LA Olympics.

Lalremsiami Hmarzote (member of the gold-winning women’s hockey team): The women’s hockey team forward once had to travel about 100 miles from her home to reach the only hockey academy in Mizoram. When she was growing up, her parents had no idea about what hockey and she played barefoot on dirt pitches. This month, playing her 200th international appearance, the 26-year-old struck gold. She scored the lone goal of the final against China, which Hockey India described as a “stunning reverse-stick strike”.

Ancy Sojan (silver in long jump): With colourful beads glistening in her hair, Sojan flung herself 6.53 metres in long jump, to win the silver medal. Earlier this year, the 25-year-old broke the national record set in 2004. Her journey, from a village in Kerala’s Thrissur district to the international stage, has not been straightforward. Last year, she was diagnosed with polycystic ovarian syndrome, forcing her to drastically change her diet and manage the medication-related weight gain she had before the tournament.

Aslam Inamdar (a member of the gold-winning men’s kabaddi team): Inamdar came to kabaddi, a south Asian contact sport combining elements of tag and wrestling, from humble beginnings – he was partly drawn to it because it was affordable and didn’t require expensive equipment. Coming from a village in Maharashtra’s Ahilyanagar, he worked odd jobs – from cleaning washrooms to working in the fields – so he could spend evenings training. “It still feels like a dream to me,” Inamdar told the Indian Express. “I often think about how someone who didn’t even have food at home now holds two international medals.” The 26-year-old was instrumental in helping India win their gold-medal match against Iran.
I would love to hear from you: which sportsperson from the Asian Games did you find most inspiring and why?
What else we’re reading about

blocks.caption: A tribute to pilot Smit Machchhar, whose swift actions helped save the lives of 174 passengers on a flydubai flight to Israel. Photograph: AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Flydubai incident | Indian pilot Smit Machchar is being hailed as a hero for helping to save 174 passengers on the flydubai flight to Israel last week, after his co-pilot made an apparent effort to crash the plane. After being stabbed, Machchar opened the cockpit door, allowing passengers and crew to enter and overpower the attacker. He is recovering in a hospital in Saudi Arabia, where the plane eventually landed.

Datacentres | Protests against water-guzzling datacentres erupting from the US to Australia are gathering momentum in India. South Asia correspondent Hannah Ellis-Petersen travelled to the small village of Tarluvada, in Andhra Pradesh, where the state government has been accused of fast-tracking plans for a $15bn AI datacentre for Google, allegedly to avoid stringent environmental scrutiny.

Art and design | Designer Vikram Goyal, celebrated for his signature repoussé brass work, brings his installation Wings and Tales to a Georgian townhouse in London’s Mayfair from 12 to 16 October. The exhibition includes furniture designs inspired by landscapes from the Indian epic Ramayana.
Guest shelf
A recommendation from someone with great taste
after newsletter promotion

blocks.caption: A detail of Al-Qawi Nanavati’s work.

blocks.text: Shireen Gandhy, director of Mumbai’s pioneering Chemould Prescott Road Gallery, founded in 1963, recommends the work of artist Al-Qawi Nanavati. “[She] is a young artist from Bombay whose practice is rooted in printmaking and making her own paper. Her mother’s passing left her with a void,” says Gandhy. Nanavati created Letters to My Mother, an epistolary artwork crafted in, as Gandhy puts it, “a deeply personal language that is not known to anybody but her. Using fabrics and saris that belonged to her mother, she creates this tactile imagery for these letters. I find it very moving and like alchemy.”
Count it
A number worth knowing

blocks.caption: Students at a cram school in Kota, where every year hundreds of thousands of students take the Indian Institutes of Technology exam. Photograph: Saurabh Das/AP

blocks.text: This is the number of students from disadvantaged communities who dropped out of some of India’s most prestigious institutions: central universities, Indian Institutes of Technology and Indian Institutes of Management between 2018 and 2023, according to Anubhuti Vishnoi of the Economic Times. The figure comes from an interim report by a committee set up by the supreme court last year to examine mental health and suicide prevention in higher education.
Vibe check

blocks.caption: Nitesh Shetty plays know-it-all for laughs. Photograph: Instagram/@ nitesh_shetty99

blocks.text: Nitesh Shetty’s sketches find absurdity in everyday life, turning familiar characters and social interactions into unexpected punchlines. This is what makes his work powerful: you’re laughing one moment and moved the next. There is a reel for every character imaginable: the person perpetually trapped in the limbo of land disputes, the man who is strangely knowledgeable about funerals, or the friend who has a unique dressing sense.

The 35-year-old from Mumbai didn’t plan on a career in comedy. “When you don’t know what to do, you try anything,” he told me. Now, Shetty rejects more conventional formats such as television in favour of challenging himself creatively. His advice for those who look up to him? “It’s a great time to build something. The [online] audience is ready-made for you. Be original and don’t follow trends.”
